You are correct, China has several issues, the Housing boom was not real and the demographic bomb is bearing down, couples have few kids or none at all and a greying population are two of the biggest. Conflating Housing with China's technologic rise in my view is a mistake
China is the World's first Electric state. China invested late in Solar and upscaled the production, reducing their costs by a whopping 95% and cornering about 90% of the worldwide market. Solar is the cheapest form of energy generation and it will keep getting cheaper and more efficient. You won't wake up tomorrow and Solar panels will be gone, quite the opposite. And since not many countries want to produce Solar, China remains at the top of the food chain. 
 The same thing with Batteries, now China has the lead in battery technologies with companies like CATL and BYD far and away the biggest battery manufactures with the best manufacturing technologies on the planet. Again battery prices are down 90% from just a few years ago. Battery EV's are now even cheaper than Gasoline vehicles not even counting the 1/10 energy usage vs Petrol.  These technologies are now at a basic level, and they will never go away and only keep improving faster. The same cannot be said for Gasoline technologies which are using the same basic basically technology from 120 years ago.  The electric transition is continuing to happen and now Electric vehicles comprise 65% of all new vehicle sales in China. The models produced are quite revolutionary with respect to digital features, styling and construction, even Ford CEO has been driving a Xiaomi SU7 describing it as "insane". This in turn and now has opened up a huge export market to Europe and worldwide. Electric vehicles and renewables have powered the Chinese Trade surplus to over $1.19Trillion, even in the face of tariffs. 
 China's investment in Chips, Software Telecom and foundry technologies has also been a big boon to China, reducing chip imports and the subsequent explosion in digital exports. Now with AI, China has been able to somehow keep up with the USA, not sure how they are doing it, but there may be some risk to US companies which are borrowing and spending $Trillions on data centers, just as the American public sours on the whole technology.
 The US on other hand, was well on it's way to a similar renewable transition, but now it reversed course favoring Fossils. Now GM Ford cannot sell their vehicles outside the US(Their sales in China went from ~5 Millions to barely 1.2Million( and most of those are electric). Chrysler.. nothing new, still on life support, their transition back to massive Hemi engines will not end well, they may not even be able to sell those in some states in the US. Apart from Tesla who benefited from the early US investments in renewable technologies to power a massive stock boom, the big three, no pun intended, are looking at a Dinosaur future.

 Which brings us to Climate.... It is getting Hot!!
 Everybody can see it, America's cattle herd has been decimated, Lake Mead, the biggest reservoir in the US is now heading to life support, leaving millions with the threat of water scarcity. The middle East Africa even Europe is starting to have droughts, before with a Goldilocks climate, farmers were sure when to plant, when to harvest, now with climate disruption brought on by global warming, it's getting more difficult to bring in a good harvest, and this is just the beginning. Warming is currently killing thousands slowly, within another decade we will start to 100's of thousands and then millions dying fast.
 Now as the world goes back to reality, that Climate change is bad, Those investments China made it Renewable technologies are going to pick back up again improve efficiency and cost, whereas countries that invested in Fossil technologies will essentially be left with massive massive dislocations as those industries are sidelined and $Trillions in investments rendered worthless. Countries like Russia, who instead of investing in Russia, decided to invest their oil fortune attacking Ukraine with Terrible outcomes. US has also spent too much fighting wars in the Middle East. Saudi Arabia, investing in Social capital like golf, gaming and concerts,  instead of building up resilient industries for when the oil taps run dry

American Structural Decay: NASA’s flagship Artemis program is mired in multi-year delays, supply chain breakdowns, and cost overruns on the Space Launch System (SLS). The aging International Space Station (ISS) suffers from structural leaks and operational fatigue, while private contractor mishaps (e.g., Boeing Starliner thruster failures leaving astronauts stranded) highlight a loss of institutional engineering rigor.

snippet.textDisplay:
Geopolitical primacy is forged when rising powers convert crippling existential crises into permanent structural advantages, executing a deliberate arc from vulnerable emergence to undisputed dominance.

1. State of Qin (4th–3rd Century BCE / 356–221 BCE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Dismissed as a semi-barbaric state on China's western periphery, Qin faced permanent encirclement and military pressure from the wealthier, culturally dominant Six States.

 * The Structural Pivot: Beginning with the Shang Yang reforms in 356 BCE, Qin dismantled its feudal aristocracy, bound agricultural yield directly to military rank, and established a rigorous legalist administration that out-mobilized every rival to achieve the first unification of China in 221 BCE.

2. Han Empire (3rd–1st Century BCE / 202–87 BCE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Founded in 202 BCE on the ashes of civil war, the early Han faced total economic devastation and military humiliation, forced into an asymmetrical tributary system (heqin) by the Xiongnu nomadic empire following the near-capture of Emperor Gaozu at Baideng.

 * The Structural Pivot: Decades of frugal statecraft during the Rule of Wen and Jing built a massive treasury, enabling state monopolies on salt and iron. Under Emperor Wu (Han Wudi), this fiscal baseline funded an elite standing cavalry that launched deep-desert offensive campaigns, shattering Xiongnu dominance and securing the Silk Road by the late 1st Century BCE.

3. Roman Republic (3rd–2nd Century BCE / 264–146 BCE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: The Second Punic War brought Rome to the brink of total annihilation after losing entire armies and an entire generation of political leadership to Hannibal at Cannae (216 BCE).

 * The Structural Pivot: Rome weaponized its republican social contract and institutional resilience. Refusing capitulation, it adopted a war of attrition (Fabian strategy), reverse-engineered Carthaginian warship designs to build a Mediterranean navy from scratch, and systematically dismantled Carthaginian and Hellenistic power to achieve undisputed Mediterranean hegemony by 146 BCE.

4. Mongol Empire (Late 12th–Mid-13th Century / 1189–1279 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Trapped in endless, fratricidal tribal warfare on the harsh Eurasian steppe, the early Mongols were impoverished, fractured, and continually manipulated by neighboring regional dynasties.

 * The Structural Pivot: Unifying the tribes in 1206, Genghis Khan systematically dismantled traditional clan lineages, replacing tribal loyalty with a decimal military structure (mingghan) based strictly on merit. Combining nomadic mobility with siege engineering, psychological warfare, and sophisticated intelligence networks, the Mongols established the largest contiguous land empire in human history by 1279 CE.

5. Ottoman Empire (Late 13th–16th Century / 1299–1566 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Originating as a minor border principality (beylik) surrounded by the Byzantine Empire and hostile Turkic rivals, the early Ottoman state faced near-total collapse following a devastating defeat by Timur at the Battle of Ankara in 1402.

 * The Structural Pivot: The Ottomans institutionalized the Janissary corps—history's first professional standing infantry—and combined gunpowder artillery with meritocratic civil administration. This allowed the empire to capture Constantinople in 1453 and reach its zenith of global power under Suleiman the Magnificent by mid-16th century.

6. Ming Dynasty (Mid-14th–Early 15th Century / 1368–1433 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Decades of Mongol Yuan rule, rampant epidemics, collapse of agricultural supply chains, and chaotic civil war left East Asia economically drained and structurally shattered.

 * The Structural Pivot: Emperor Taizu (Zhu Yuanzhang) overhauled the agrarian baseline through land surveys (Fish Scale Maps), extensive reforestation, and self-sustaining military agricultural colonies (weisuo). This built a massive fiscal foundation that funded the Great Wall and sponsored the global maritime expeditions of Zheng He by the early 15th Century.

7. Portugal (15th–16th Century / 1415–1580 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: A demographically tiny nation of barely one million people tucked onto the Atlantic coast, completely blocked from European land trade routes and surrounded by dominant Castilian power.

 * The Structural Pivot: Beginning with the conquest of Ceuta in 1415, Portugal channeled state resources into nautical science, cartography, and ocean-going caravel design at Sagres. By pioneering a "fort-and-factory" (feitoria) maritime network, Portugal bypassed Ottoman and Venetian trade monopolies to dominate the global spice trade by the mid-16th century.

8. Spain (Late 15th–16th Century / 1492–1598 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Divided into rival kingdoms, economically impoverished, and fighting centuries of religious fragmentation during the Reconquista, early Iberian states lacked central fiscal and military authority.

 * The Structural Pivot: Dynastic unification under Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492 combined with the development of the Tercio—a revolutionary combined-arms infantry formation—allowed Spain to project military power across Europe while extracting American silver bullion, establishing global Habsburg hegemony during the 16th century.

9. Dutch Republic (Mid-16th–17th Century / 1568–1648 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: A small, swampy cluster of provinces facing the full military might of the Spanish global empire during the Eighty Years' War (1568–1648).

 * The Structural Pivot: Lacking territorial depth, the Dutch created modern corporate finance—establishing the Bank of Amsterdam, the world's first public stock exchange, and low-cost merchant shipping fleets (Fluyt). They leveraged capital markets to out-finance their occupiers, achieving formal independence and global commercial primacy by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

10. Great Britain (Late 17th–19th Century / 1688–1815 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: A demographically minor island state facing severe population and resource deficits against the dominant land armies and wealth of Bourbon France.

 * The Structural Pivot: Following the Glorious Revolution of 1688, Britain avoided costly continental land wars and engineered a revolution in sovereign finance. The founding of the Bank of England (1694) enabled low-interest borrowing to fund continental proxy armies while the Royal Navy secured global trade routes, culminating in undisputed global primacy following the defeat of Napoleon in 1815.

11. United States (Late 19th–Mid-20th Century / 1865–1945 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Severely fractured by a devastating Civil War, the U.S. began its industrial rise as a heavily indebted agrarian nation vulnerable to European economic and naval domination.

 * The Structural Pivot: Washington maintained strategic insulation from European Great Power rivalries, using high protective tariffs to shelter infant industries while integrating a massive continental market through transcontinental infrastructure. Passing European industrial output by 1890, the U.S. converted its unassailable manufacturing base into global financial and military primacy by 1945.

12. Modern China (Late 20th–21st Century / 1978–Present)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Emerged from a century of foreign exploitation, severe poverty, and geopolitical isolation, lacking modern industrial infrastructure and technical capital.

 * The Structural Pivot: Operating under strict strategic patience (zhanlue dingli) following the launching of Reform and Opening-up in 1978, China mobilized its labor base, invested heavily in state-led infrastructure, engineering education, and supply-chain integration, transforming itself from an impoverished agrarian state into the world's primary industrial power and high-tech competitor.

The common historical thread across all twelve powers is absolute: external crises do not destroy rising states; structural rigidity does. True geopolitical primacy belongs to the states that turn existential threats into catalysts for institutional, financial, and technological renewal.

Combining nomadic mobility with siege engineering, psychological warfare, and sophisticated intelligence networks, the Mongols established the largest contiguous land empire in human history by 1279 CE.

5. Ottoman Empire (Late 13th–16th Century / 1299–1566 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Originating as a minor border principality (beylik) surrounded by the Byzantine Empire and hostile Turkic rivals, the early Ottoman state faced near-total collapse following a devastating defeat by Timur at the Battle of Ankara in 1402.

 * The Structural Pivot: The Ottomans institutionalized the Janissary corps—history's first professional standing infantry—and combined gunpowder artillery with meritocratic civil administration. This allowed the empire to capture Constantinople in 1453 and reach its zenith of global power under Suleiman the Magnificent by mid-16th century.

6. Ming Dynasty (Mid-14th–Early 15th Century / 1368–1433 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Decades of Mongol Yuan rule, rampant epidemics, collapse of agricultural supply chains, and chaotic civil war left East Asia economically drained and structurally shattered.

 * The Structural Pivot: Emperor Taizu (Zhu Yuanzhang) overhauled the agrarian baseline through land surveys (Fish Scale Maps), extensive reforestation, and self-sustaining military agricultural colonies (weisuo). This built a massive fiscal foundation that funded the Great Wall and sponsored the global maritime expeditions of Zheng He by the early 15th Century.

7. Portugal (15th–16th Century / 1415–1580 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: A demographically tiny nation of barely one million people tucked onto the Atlantic coast, completely blocked from European land trade routes and surrounded by dominant Castilian power.

 * The Structural Pivot: Beginning with the conquest of Ceuta in 1415, Portugal channeled state resources into nautical science, cartography, and ocean-going caravel design at Sagres. By pioneering a "fort-and-factory" (feitoria) maritime network, Portugal bypassed Ottoman and Venetian trade monopolies to dominate the global spice trade by the mid-16th century.

8. Spain (Late 15th–16th Century / 1492–1598 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Divided into rival kingdoms, economically impoverished, and fighting centuries of religious fragmentation during the Reconquista, early Iberian states lacked central fiscal and military authority.

 * The Structural Pivot: Dynastic unification under Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492 combined with the development of the Tercio—a revolutionary combined-arms infantry formation—allowed Spain to project military power across Europe while extracting American silver bullion, establishing global Habsburg hegemony during the 16th century.

9. Dutch Republic (Mid-16th–17th Century / 1568–1648 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: A small, swampy cluster of provinces facing the full military might of the Spanish global empire during the Eighty Years' War (1568–1648).

 * The Structural Pivot: Lacking territorial depth, the Dutch created modern corporate finance—establishing the Bank of Amsterdam, the world's first public stock exchange, and low-cost merchant shipping fleets (Fluyt). They leveraged capital markets to out-finance their occupiers, achieving formal independence and global commercial primacy by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

10. Great Britain (Late 17th–19th Century / 1688–1815 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: A demographically minor island state facing severe population and resource deficits against the dominant land armies and wealth of Bourbon France.

 * The Structural Pivot: Following the Glorious Revolution of 1688, Britain avoided costly continental land wars and engineered a revolution in sovereign finance. The founding of the Bank of England (1694) enabled low-interest borrowing to fund continental proxy armies while the Royal Navy secured global trade routes, culminating in undisputed global primacy following the defeat of Napoleon in 1815.

11. United States (Late 19th–Mid-20th Century / 1865–1945 CE)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Severely fractured by a devastating Civil War, the U.S. began its industrial rise as a heavily indebted agrarian nation vulnerable to European economic and naval domination.

 * The Structural Pivot: Washington maintained strategic insulation from European Great Power rivalries, using high protective tariffs to shelter infant industries while integrating a massive continental market through transcontinental infrastructure. Passing European industrial output by 1890, the U.S. converted its unassailable manufacturing base into global financial and military primacy by 1945.

12. Modern China (Late 20th–21st Century / 1978–Present)

 * The Crippling Crisis: Emerged from a century of foreign exploitation, severe poverty, and geopolitical isolation, lacking modern industrial infrastructure and technical capital.

 * The Structural Pivot: Operating under strict strategic patience (zhanlue dingli) following the launching of Reform and Opening-up in 1978, China mobilized its labor base, invested heavily in state-led infrastructure, engineering education, and supply-chain integration, transforming itself from an impoverished agrarian state into the world's primary industrial power and high-tech competitor.

The common historical thread across all twelve powers is absolute: external crises do not destroy rising states; structural rigidity does. True geopolitical primacy belongs to the states that turn existential threats into catalysts for institutional, financial, and technological renewal.

snippet.textDisplay: It's misleading to compare this to the real-estate bubble, because those empty apartment or office buildings are not being exported. A large part of the excess production capacity in PV and EVs has been redirected from the Chinese domestic market to exports. For example, solar power output in Pakistan (without government subsidies) grew from 15 TWh in 2023 to 51 TWh in 2025. EV sales in Peru, Colombia and other countries are growing rapidly. So while subsidies for PV and EVs in China have achieved the strategic goal of reducing China's dependence on fossil fuel imports, it has also created economies of scale that are now allowing Chinese manufacturers to undercut and elbow out competitors internationally, in all kinds of markets. In places like Thailand, most internal combustion engined cars used to be Japanese brands, but amongst EVs, China is now in the lead because Japan is still stuck in the fossil age. Meanwhile, solar and EVs are still growing in China, in the case of solar at a slower pace than before and in the case of vehicles, in an overall shrinking vehicle market (which is also true in Europe). EVs are cannibalizing the ICE vehicle market in China and elsewhere. Battery prices in China keep falling and new technologies such as sodium ion will drive down prices even further, enabling variable energy sources such as solar and wind to compete for an ever greater share of total energy production.

So, the Chinese BEV market has competition from the Chinese BEV market so I'm not sure how to take some of the discussion.  China is a place where one good idea turns into everyone's good idea and people all rush into that market.  BEV is the wrong market for that to have happened but it was brought on by the CCP, based on how their subsidies worked.  The CCP gave money directly to the companies based on PRODUCTION, and it was a significant subsidy.  This created a BOOM in BEV production, most of it was a money grab by companies that did very dubious things just to get the subsidy money.  Most of those companies are gone now, with people and even members of the CCP having pocketed lots of money.

China is a place where if the govt. wants to pump money into something, there's a few million people wanting to cash in on what that money is doing, and there's party officials finding ways to benefit themselves via some "company".  THAT is the real story.

All of this doesn't negate the highly qualified companies such as BYD that's existed for a long time and has been in manufacturing for all that time, including the production of ICEV.  The highly qualified companies are the ones exporting to other countries.  The subsidy that the CCP was giving to companies for BEV is gone now.  The winners are those companies that built a brand and production mastery and quality along the way, once again like BYD.

This is the statement for BYD:   BYD’s annual production growth for new energy vehicles (NEVs) has accelerated rapidly over the last five years, climbing from under 600,000 units in 2021 to over 4.6 million in 2025. While this massive scaling has established the company as a global leader in pure electric vehicle (BEV) deliveries, the brand’s quality remains mixed, with independent data identifying specific areas for improvement in paintwork and electronic systems.

BYD now has to deal with the laws of other countries and quality now matters, because when a vehicle has issues they have to get fixed, or there could be recalls, which has already happened.  The point that can be missed though is there's substantial investment behind the company including from Western investors which makes them a standout in this market.  They WILL get better at manufacturing, as opposed to Tesla whee even though they can can production routines to improve their quality, they're STILL having issues after a fairly long maturity period.

I would have liked to seen a comparison using Toyota since they're the global leader in auto production.



For your coal vs. solar panel thing you compared panels in full production AFTER installation to a new coal plant buildout.  What about the continued cost of mining, transportation and processes involved in burning that coal to make energy which solar panels don't require any inputs?


ALL countries that have oil reserves have either seriously drawn down their supplies or COMPLETELY drawn down their supplies.  The world is missing millions of barrels of oil a day.

For the US:

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve has declined to approximately 289.7 million barrels as of late August 2026, reaching its lowest level in over four decades due to compounding political decisions and international supply shocks. This depletion was significantly accelerated by a coordinated 172-million-barrel release in March 2026, which was enacted by the U.S. and allied nations to stabilize global energy markets following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.


So we're at a 40 year low, so apparently we have the same problem China does, along with the rest of the world.  So how is this a "China" thing?  You touched on the wrong topic here because Asia is SUFFERING, as in ALL of Asia is suffering because of the war created by trump.


You missed the point of solar panels.  Once again it's called "everyone and their brother wants to cash in on Chinese govt. subsidies"   It's not that a handful of companies there can't be successful, it's that there are TOO MANY companies making the same thing.  Same issue with BEV.  The solar panel companies in China are competing against the solar panel companies in China.


You showed a drop off in solar panel production but that drop off was in production without comparing it to global production where they STILL clearly lead.


I would say this video in fact gets close to being propaganda.  Your comparisons and the way you used data paints SOME form of a picture, but without putting that picture into a global context and doing global comparisons it's just useless.

snippet.textDisplay:
I have about an essay worth of thoughts on this. And ill try to be succinct. 

I want to start by saying I am not a defender of China/CCP by any means - i think its possibly the largest source of evil out there today. And I want to say i broadly agree with the thrust of this video, in that what China is doing is a facade and an unsustainable house of cards  (particularly in terms of demographic crisis).

The however comes when you realise that they realise this. And that their strategy, while it makes no sense seen from a western economic perspective- does make sense from theirs. They move from generating one 'false' bubble based on printing money to another. In the west we have hangups about the consequences of that oncoming crash. In China, they know the crash is coming anyway. They have nothing to lose by proactively generating these investment bubbles. Because when they pop, they ultimately are left with the infrastructure anyway. And they can print more money to generate the next bubble which builds on top. Ultimately, they will have built 21st century infrastructure- even if theres no one to occupy this. 

Think about the dot com crash. Yes, wildly overvalued. It caused a crash. But ultimately it was about home Internet and it generated a load of infrastructure quickly, and what now? We all have home Internet- the infrastructure remained.

China currently have a unique ability to generate these bubbles- due to scale and control. They can scale with mass subsidy in the hope an industry outcompetes rivals like no other economy. The hope is some of it sticks in the autumn of their demographic crash, and they have a productive economy left over anyway out then other side of the turmoil.

They build expensive public transport connections in the middle of nowhere in the hope a neighbourhood will grow. Madness. But sometimes- the neighbourhood does grow. If it doesn't. We'll you have a connection to nowhere but excellent and efficient rapid transit across the rest of the city. 

I say this not to defend them, as the downfall will come and it will come with human consequences all of us but not least the chinese people.

However there is something we can learn in the west. In that you can build it. If you want it. China's approach to speculative investment through printed money may be too far- but just look at the results. And the cost of not learning is western industry being outcompeted by a model which can do these things. 

We need a reevaluation of what we use out financial levers for. What we should be doing is learning from China that you must pump money into sectors in a strategic way to develop that productive capacity - in order to compete. And stop seeing macroeconomics as household finance- in order to fend off China. But also to improve our own economic futures.

In the essay, entitled "I Know What America’s Leading C.E.O.s Really Think of Donald Trump," Jeffery Sconnenfeld PhD, Yale School of Management political-economist argued that Donald Trump’s corporate backing was at an all-time low for a Republican nominee. He specifically critiqued several of Trump's central fiscal and trade policies as anti-business: 

Import Tariffs: Proposing sweeping 10% to 20% baseline tariffs on all foreign imports.

Federal Reserve Independence: Suggesting interventions that would strip the central bank of its autonomy to control interest rates.

Currency Devaluation: Seeking to artificially devalue the U.S. dollar to boost manufacturing, which economists warn could fuel inflation. 

Sonnenfeld concluded that these heavy-handed central planning initiatives align far more with the state-controlled philosophies of Karl Marx than the free-market, laissez-faire principles of Adam Smith.

snippet.textDisplay:
@paul.9828 Okay, sure, the Xintai quarry case is real, but that was fraud, not hydroseeding.

Hydroseeding involves spraying seed, mulch, fertilizer, and a green tracer so they can see coverage. It can look like painted grass. It is still an attempt to grow a slope, not a coat of camouflage on dead turf.

One factory cheating an inspection does not turn a standard engineering practice into a national character trait, though (which is what Paul Warburg seems to be implying with this video, and what you seem to be implying with the weak phrase "well known for").

Dyeing vegetables is a separate issue. Illegal adulteration has happened in China, as it has elsewhere, but does not make the original comment an accurate description of hydroseeding.

Apples to oranges = flawed analysis.  Oligopoly economy (West) vs Hybrid (China) is hard to compare.  If you're going to look at debt then you need to be thorough so include Government (National, Regional and Local), Corporate, Bank and Personal.  In many western countries personal debt is large, in China negligible.  That's a fairly important failure in your analysis.

Whenever there has been a massive growth in debt such as in China, there is a crash but this is happened in a command economy that is different to previous credit expansion examples / anything ever seen before so it's hard to predict what's going to happen in China.  Whenever countries have had large government debt, it drags down on growth and that's your problem in the US.  I don't think the US will be the world's reserve currency in twenty years time.  The Chinese are already slowly selling down their US holdings and trying to trade in their own currency so being the world's reserve currency won't help in the longer term.  Europe's adopting systems to cut the US dollar out.  Australia's cut its holdings of US dollars etc.

Coal compared to Solar is another apples to oranges.  Does your coal price include a carbon price?  The current US administration may be run by the fossil fuel lobby and in climate denial but the rest of world is not (as much).  Solar may only produce when the sun is shining but coal is the opposite - hard to turn off at non-peak times.  Therefore you need peaker plants usually gas to complement and they're expensive.  Sodium ion batteries are only just going into production and CATL says they expect the price to drop 90% so batteries will not be so expensive in the future.  In California and Australia, batteries are becoming a main source of peak demand time electricity because they are already cheaper then gas.  Meanwhile Trump is subsidizing coal to keep it going.  Is that really all that different to what China is doing?  Your fossil fuel story is also highly flawed.

"Just Happened"? Nothing you have described is new. China have been driving an infrastructure-led growth model for decades. This has always suggested an economic failure must come at some point but the only major financial disasters have been triggered by Wall Street greed. The thing is, the capitalist system means there is an accountability in western financial markets that eventually pops bubbles. Chinese commerce (and remember the Chinese were commercial titans many centuries before Adam Smith mapped out free market mechanisms) has never been capitalist and even communism has not defined Chinese instincts in this respect.

Where the ill-informed in the West have moaned about Chinese cheap labour giving them an unfair advantage in manufacturing, the actual advantage is their expectations on the use and returns on capital. In public spending, the ghost cities are one outcome but a lot of the infrastructure spending has been roads and railways and ports and energy that are, and will continue to be, very productive.

A few hundred million dirt poor, dissatisfied Chinese were enough to overthrow a ruling structure with millennia behind it. Chinese leadership now is always conscious that there are probably double that "few hundred million dirt poor" Chinese and, for a Government that stakes it's foundation on the legitimacy of revolution, they need to ensure that they don't also feel "dissatisfied". Economic growth is the absolute prerequisite for their leaders to keep the populace satisfied. They have, and must continue to drive that with the highest priority while we in the west will wait for the bubble to pop.

Meanwhile the auto industry example is a good one to illustrate what these Chinese government strategies are also driving. The unparalleled growth of an educated, innovative workforce. The industry may not be profitable (enough, in the western sense) it is developing products at a rate no manufacturer in the west can match. Western auto makers are burdened by financial hurdles and resulting analysis paralysis, IP rights protecting the minimal innovation that does occur, labour markets where fewer and fewer people want to work in manufacturing and boxing aspirations within the walls of what has always worked before. Chinese automakers have none (almost) of those burdens and, as a result, are bringing products to market in a timeframe that no legacy auto makers can match.

While the ridiculous situation in the Straights of Hormuz is irritating China, most also recognise it is strengthening China's position on the world stage. At the micro economic level, the elevated gas prices are pushing western consumers to electric (Chinese dominated) vehicles and away from ICE (legacy automakers) even though the gas price may come down again, the damage is done. Consumer awareness of the quality and price of Chinese vehicles has skyrocketed and this and their rapid innovation will secure an ever increasing share of the global market.

Chinese economic growth seems unsustainable, but it also seems to be working.

Selling at below cost of production or domestic price is the definition of "dumping",  and is illegal under most countries' trade agreements - this is here tariffs are typically applied. The reason is that dumping is destructive of nations' own manufacturing sectors, so they have a national interest in protecting them behind tariff walls. Assuming your analysis is correct, China has been obliterating whole manufacturing sectors at a time. 
Utility-scale solar regularly replace solar panels because solar panel degrade unequally, and replacing them permits the utility to balance the panels' production. 
I think your analysis of batteries is correct - for lithium-based chemistries. Not for the new sodium-based chemistries, which are about half the cost (and lack almost all the problems that lithium batteries have). Both of these may be eclipsed by "solid state" batteries, should they prove out. Sodium batteries are especially suited to large utility-sized installations, and solid state are especially suited to automotive installations.

Paul, It's nice that you are beginning to try to understand China and it's economy. I think you've still got a ways to go to get a good grasp on this. I will just mention a couple of things I think you have missed. 

For all the west's hoping that China will join us in the capitalists' world, China is not a capitalist country. We would be best advised not to measure China's economy based on our capitalistic ideas. That's not how they operate. They don't rely on market forces, never have and don't want to. They operate a top down, controlled economy. The government picks business winners and losers. Whether that is to build houses or cars. What the market forces want is not part of the equation so best not to compare to western economies.

Second, the narrative that you are saying "people" believe and push about China's economic mastery of the planet is bought and paid for by the CCP. They have been telling us that they are the best in the world for the last couple of decades now. Not because it is true, but that's what they want and they are paying media outlets to push that narrative. The fact that you are trying to disprove that narrative only means that their disinformation campaign worked.

The shock to the oil markets due to Trumps war on Iran has not brought down the global economies in large part because China was able to pivot away from gasoline usage by citizens this summer because the large base of EVs and solar panels already installed. I was in China this summer, gasoline was more expensive on purpose (government economy control) but most people didn't care because they have already switched to electric. In effect China saved us from the worst of Trump's idiocy and has left China in a strong position for if/when they are involved in a war.

Here's the thing: You have balance the grid somehow; solar and wind just need more of it. You can do that with natural gas, but batteries are way better. So batteries will continue to replace natural gas peaking plants. That will allow for more solar and wind; and the more solar and wind you have, the more reliable it gets, because different areas are windy and sunny at different times, and electricity can be moved around. So it's not really valid to stack batteries on top of solar to evaluate cost.

16:19 Also, you imply that "most people want to consume the most energy" at night, the time of day that solar isn't producing power, but that's not true. Energy demand drops quite low at night, year-round. Also wind and solar are surprisingly complementary: solar produces more at mid-day and summer; wind produces more at night and winter. This is why energy propaganda always focuses on one or the other in isolation.

19:52 China doesn't have a chokehold on rare earth metals, because they aren't really rare. What they have that's rare is cheap labor.

I don't disagree with much of the points you make in the video but I think there is a lot of nuance to add. China is in the process of phasing out fossil fuels in a deliberate sequence, which is the main reason they pushed so hard into solar, EVs and batteries. They are using coal to back this process up and for security reasons because it's the easiest fossil fuel to stockpile and store and they are less reliant on foreign suppliers for it. The reason they don't subsidize solar anymore is that it does not need it anymore. If I remember from my college days way back, once energy conversion efficiency crossed 19-20% it became competitive with fossil fuels. Existing quality commercial panels have 22-24%. This beats fossil fuels w/out subsidies everywhere but extreme northern latitudes. Tandem perovskite/silicon panels are being piloted now with 28-30% efficiency, which would make them the cheapest of all sources and is bad news for fossil fuels. When I was in college efficiency was just 15-16%. 

China added 315 GW of solar in 2025 and has 500+ GW of solar and wind under construction now. They commissioned 78 GW of new coal in 2025 but coal generation actually dropped YoY. China's transmission network still carries 42% coal and only approx 20% wind/solar because transmission expansion is slower than renewable expansion. So, coal is being used as a grid crutch until more transmission is built, more storage is deployed and more industrial load is co-located w/ renewables. Coal plants will increasingly become stranded assets as these items are put into place. 

The enabling technology for this is really the LFP lithium-ion battery invented at the University of Texas, commercialized in Quebec and matured in China. This is the cheapest, safest and most durable lithium-ion battery chemistry. China dominates its production and prices have dropped dramatically going into 2024 and continue to drop while at the same time energy densities have significantly increased. The LFP used as a grid storage battery paired with renewables significantly changes the economics. It is also an enabling technology for affordable EVs. CATL and BYD (among a few others) are scaling LFP production like crazy. These are also being deployed with renewables all over the world with massive growth going from 90 GWh of grid storage in 2024 to 307 GWh in 2025 including the US. There is a major effort with Western economies to create western LFP supply chains. If you don't believe me check out pre-revenue Canadian microcap Nano One Materials who has managed to attract major global partners Rio Tinto, Sumitomo and Worley to develop and roll out LFP cathode production outside of China. The US DoD also thinks this is critical and awarded a grant to them to retool the Quebec cathode plant to their process. China has restricted exports of their LFP technology. Nano One does not use China's technology. China is also developing Sodium-ion batteries for grid storage. LFP for grid storage works great for frequency control and load balancing up to 6 hrs allowing renewables to be used as a baseload while Sodium-ion works great for longer time periods, like overnight enhancing the baseload ability.

China has watched and learned the geopolitical energy lesson as Russia weaponized gas, Saudi weaponized oil, US weaponized LNG, sanctions and maritime control, OPEC manipulate supply, US shale reshapes global pricing and Europe struggle when gas was cut-off. Concluding that energy dependence=geopolitical vulnerability. I mean look at the comical rebuffing of Russia's desperate pleas to build a new gas pipeline into China. For China electrification is the only way to go. They are exporting this solution all over the world to countries in similar situations who also see the same things China sees. So, I don't think they just jumped on a trend to jump on a trend, they have a coherent and very long-term plan. They are in the early/middle stages of executing it so it is harder to see but the steps they are taking point to it. So far, they are having a lot of success. I have read where they are forecasting peak oil demand for them in 2027. If that forecast is accurate it will be the beginning of the end of an era.

I asked the Chinese AI about it and then crosschecked with claude.
"Is it true that thousands of completed residential complexes are standing empty in China?"
Deepseek said.
Yes, there are indeed numerous residential complexes in China with extremely high vacancy rates after completion, and in some cases, entire new towns have turned into "ghost towns." This is mainly reflected in the oversupply of tourism real estate and blind expansion in certain cities.

📊 Current National Housing Inventory
According to the National Bureau of Statistics, as of the end of July 2026, the total area of commercial housing available for sale nationwide was approximately 759 million square meters (down 0.8% year-on-year). Among this, the inventory of housing under 3 years old was about 556 million square meters (down 3.6% year-on-year). Although the volume remains large, the inventory has been declining for five consecutive months, indicating that the market is actively digesting existing stock, and not all buildings are sitting empty.

🏚️ Typical "Ghost Town" Examples

· Yintan, Rushan (Weihai): The supply of sea-view apartments is massive, and peak-season foot traffic is far below capacity. One statistic suggests it can accommodate about 500,000 people, but the permanent resident population is extremely low, with very few lights on at night.
· Beijing-Tianjin New Town: Positioned as the "largest villa district in Asia," of the 3,000 villas sold over a decade, only about 10% are occupied, leaving roughly 90% vacant.
· Kangbashi, Ordos: Once dubbed a "ghost city," it was planned to hold one million people, but in late 2010, the permanent population was fewer than 30,000. In recent years, it has regained vitality through industrial introduction and destocking.
· Langfang: Boosted by the Beijing-Tianjin integration, housing prices once surged to 21,000 RMB per square meter. After the frenzy faded, prices dropped to about 4,000 RMB per square meter, with noticeable vacancies in some areas.

🔍 Causes of the Vacancy Phenomenon

· Oversupply of tourism real estate: "Ghost mansions" appear in coastal and mountainous areas, where young people can rent an entire unit for only about 400 RMB per month, and the community facilities gradually decay due to lack of maintenance.
· Over-reliance on investment: Some projects were sold but never occupied, or after speculative bubbles burst, large numbers of units were dumped on the market, leading to vacancies.

Currently, overall inventory is declining, but structural oversupply (especially in remote tourism projects) still exists. Are you focused on a specific city, or would you like to understand the investment risks behind vacant properties? Let me know your focus, and I can provide a more detailed analysis.
I asked claude if it was playing down the problem. No — if anything it's fairly balanced, not downplaying it. It states plainly that ghost towns exist, structural oversupply persists, and gives real examples with real numbers. The caveats it adds (declining inventory, seasonal buyers, investment-driven vacancy) are accurate context, not spin — they're the same nuances that Western outlets like the NYT and Brookings raise, not a whitewash.
If anything, I'd say it slightly understates the scale relative to some other estimates — the figures I found elsewhere cite 65-80 million vacant units as a total stock estimate, which is a much more dramatic number than the "759 million sqm, declining 0.8%" framing suggests. That NBS metric only counts unsold new inventory — it doesn't capture already-sold-but-empty units, which is a huge chunk of China's vacancy problem (the investment-driven vacancy DeepSeek does mention, but doesn't quantify). So the answer's honest about the existence of the problem, but its headline stat is narrower in scope than the "ghost city" phenomenon as a whole — worth keeping in mind if you're trying to gauge total severity rather than just current unsold new supply..
I am always skeptical on China stories on both sides.

Domestic energy resources: If/when China finish scaling up from TMSR-LF1 (which picks up from where Oak Ridge's MSRE left off in 1969) the energy situation gets turned on its head.

The best fuel for this kind of nuclear reactor is thorium - and thorium is the primary waste product of rare earth mining (more than everything else combined)

It's worth noting that these nuclear reactors are hot enough to act as drop-in replacements for combustion plant in existing gas/coal power stations and it appears that those power stations have been built over the last 20 years with an eye to doing exactly that - there are vacant areas adjacent to the turbine halls in nearly all sites which are the right size to fit (A Molten salt nuclear reactor design large enough to replace coal burners is 1/4 the size of the combustion plant, including containment and heat exchangers)

This matters: Renewables - wind/solar/etc are a stepping stone. In order to reduce global carbon emissions we'll need about 6-8x the existing electrical generation that currently exists - electricity is only 1/3 of our global carbon emissions. Renewables can (at best) slightly outproduce existing carbon-burning electrical generation.

The USA threw away a multidecade lead in 1972 for various political reasons. In about 15-20 years we're likely to see countries representing 6-7 billion people lining up to purchase chinese nuclear power stations and moving off oil as fast as they can.

The carbon emissions issue and global warming is a "Lily pond puzzle" - the longer we sit on our hands, the more drastic the action will need to be. Right now we're at about day 20 of 30 and the lily covers 0.1% of the pond - noticable, but that lily doubling every day means that if we wait to day 29, the lily covers half the pond, will wipe out the pond on day 30 and the action needed to cut it back is vastly more effort than it was at day 20.

The big issue with global warning and climate change isn't sea level rise, wilder weather and crop failures. If warming waters trigger undersea methane clathrate blowouts that turn into a chain reaction then we can look back 250 million years to see what happens next - the short version being "Everything dies" (97-98% biomass dieoff and global oxygen levels crashing to 11-12%. No warm blooded creature can survive with oxygen levels that low, nor can most insects or cold blooded land animals or fish.)

If sea level rises 5-10 metres, China will need to move 400-600 million people off the coastal plains. In such an event, it's just as well all those ghost cities exist and are being maintained at "caretaker" level.

China is closely tracking the US history of boom/bust cycles. People who emphasize the booms are presenting a distorted picture, and likewise for those (like Paul in this video) who emphasize the busts. The better answer is the long term trend

Paul's presentation of PV is data based but wrong, because it uses a snapshot in time of battery pricing that ignores the dynamic downward pricing trend. The world is only a few short years away from $US 50/kWh large scale installed storage capacity, which will add about $5/MWh to the levelized cost of PV with 4 hour battery storage. That type of deployment at scale covers about 80% of grid annual demand. The other 20% is a future problem that has a myriad of solutions including thermal storage, wind, hydro, long distance power supply, dropping battery prices, and perhaps even hydrogen. PV production capacity will have periods where it is 'over-built' but they will be short-lived and *more* production capacity will be needed.

My primary thesis is that China's major issue is an inability to effectively allocate capital. The central government drives the targets of investment through expressed preference rather than pure central control. That's why here is such an extreme herding into certain areas.

China has - as you pointed out - massive numbers of underproducing or stranded assets as well as both known and undisclosed demographic problems. To pay for the gaping hole in the national asset and human balance sheets they need to manufacture and sell for cash flow rather than profit. Since their domestic consumption is far too low to generate these cash flows they must export. So if you want to throttle China, reduce their ability to export. Obvious, right?

Unfortunately western businesses usually operate for profit above cash flow. The higher cost structure creates higher prices for domestically manufactured goods, which is politically unpalatable. We are in an era of strategic deglobalization, so it's going to happen anyway. This is already creating discontent among western populations, which is being amplified by the anti democratic forces of the world in an effort to fracture the formal and informal alignment of interests the rich western, net consuming countries have assembled. See MAGA, or AfD, or  France, Nederlands, etc. Nationalism is the dysfunctional form of deglobalization, but obviously outright war is rose. 

Standards of living in the western world are likely to stagnate. The demographically growing areas are likely to benefit-Africa and India primarily. I believe Carney is correct to rebase the western alignment among the middle powers, which if it manages to include India could ultimately create a new equilibrium with much reduced US centrality. I believe this will be quite a long and volatile road but it may make more people richer and more secure than the Pax Americana, which seems to have plateaued.

Look it is a fair assesment but I think a few oversights. I think the first is super obvious and that is these Chinese companies who are subsidy darlings begin to capture foreign exports as the subsidies disappear. They divert that production capacity meant for domestic subsidized markets towards an export market they begin to easily dominate because China is the economic gym they practiced in. It is no wonder then you see Chinese EV's, robotics, and solar dominate exports globally even if by your calculation demand growth within China may have cratered. It's a pattern where large subsidy programs are followed by a dumping program as they cutback on subsidies and those products have to find external markets. Look at how they penetrated the EU EV market; to shock and displace German vehicles on their own home court not even the US big autos have been able to make such a dent.

Second point is 300% debt level is so unsustainable that I have to question your methodology here. It's true China spends with deficits on these subsidy programs but it also is true they are dollar for dollar more efficient spenders. Meaning a dollar their gets you further in program delivery than it would in a nation like the US. So what you may presume as them needing to spend so much on subsidy might actually be 3 times smaller than you would think. Plus the Chinese also display a measure of fiscal discipline in how they are mission focused on a target, they work towards that, and when they reach it they then scale back. Now again China's money manipulation and opaqueness might be the reason behind that but it is what it is on the Bond market compared to the US.

What follows is not intended to be an ideological or political criticism of China or its people. Nevertheless, it's simply a fact that China's Bubble Economy will collapse soon. Just like Japan's did in the early 1990s, and for the same basic reason: They can no longer exploit the comparative economic advantage they have had from cheap and abundant skilled labor. Their currency has become so powerful that they cannot compete on price alone anymore. 
But, unlike Japan, they have not developed a commercially viable fallback position. Japan cleverly knew the growing price of the Yen would eventually mean Japan cannot simply undercut the competition, they needed to be able to compete head-to head, on quality, and (importantly) Brand Reputation. Nowadays a Toyota isn't cheaper than an Audi, but it doesn't need to be. It is as good as, or better than, a similarly priced Audi. AND the market trusts Toyota as a brand. That was no accident.
In comparison, China is not trusted particularly as a trade partner, and China has established essentially zero trusted brands either. All their cars are forgettable here--today-gone-tomorrow "brands" like "BYD" or "Chery" or Three Swallows or whatever.  The only Chinese brand I can think of that has bucked that trend and actually built a solid best-in-class brand reputation is DJI (the bigest supplier of drones in the world) - a real innovator that stands behind its products and the market respects it. But DJI is an outlier. 99% of Chinese goods are produced in anonymous factories with some random log shoved on them to whatever the customer specifies. The world butys it because (and ONLY because) it is cheap. 
The question is what will China's Command Economy do when its middle class all suddenly become unemployed, and their properties become worthless almost overnight? The Leaders won't accept responsibility and resign, that's for sure. Much more likely, they will either force the workers back to their agrarian home-provinces and keep them poor and desperate, OR they will foment a foreign 'war' to rally the people behind them (they'll "wag the dog" as it were), or both.

What happened in China with joining the world economy starting in the 80s is very much to be expected. There was mass mobilization of hundreds of millions of workers who were sent to farms all over the country, often thousands of miles from home, under Chairman Mao and his most radical supporters. University professors, cab drivers, lawyers, ordinary citizens and the educated were sent to work the fields, often without motorized equipment during the Cultural Revolution.  

When China came out from that political phase with Mao Zedong's death in 1976, and the Gang of Four were removed from power and imprisoned, Deng Xiaoping began the modernization and opening of China. They invited prominent expatriates who had fled China in 1948, including college professors, doctors, researchers, to visit China in some high profile gestures. (My friends were among those accepting the invite to tour some major cities.)  

However, the Communist Party infrastructure, including most notably those in the provinces, remained after China began modernization and incorporation of certain Western practices. While the central government modernized mostly in the prosperous Eastern Central regions incorporating such cities as Beijing and Shanghai, many provinces did not reap the effects of modernization. Occupants of these provinces were still being sent to faraway regions, not just for farm work, but now working in the industrial complex. Grandparents often raised their grandchildren. It was no longer under the auspices of the Cultural Revolution, but China's modernization. 

Provinces generally saw limited benefit from its families sent to work elsewhere.  However, the central government often made laws and proclamations to extend medical care, pay the elderly pensions, award college scholarships, or modernize in provincial regions around the country. As can be expected with centralized power in such a large land-mass country with a billion citizens, these efforts were true boondoggles. Communist party apparatus in the provinces often whittled down outlays, resulting in huge disconnects from the intended effects.  The COVID pandemic created even more of a disaster.

Hmm.

I agree that China has a tendency to “subtract value” from input products, by selling outputs for less than they cost to make. Ultimately the Chinese taxpayers foot this bill, ultimately to the advantage not of Chinese people, but foreign countries. Consider their steel industry, their solar panels, their EVs, etc. Who is buying them? It doesn’t seem to be the Chinese people.

I agree that the EV push is likely an effort to reduce their fuel consumption rate by half, which naturally would double the length of time the same fuel reserves would last.

But the argument about solar power makes no sense to me. If solar power produces 11% of power on the grid, it will never be a suitable power source to reduce demand on the grid from fossil fuels. Would not a concentration in nuclear power be more rational? You might argue they already concentrate on nuclear power, but that fails to explain why they should diversify (poorly) across both power generation systems?

Generally, yes. I agree that all China’s subsidies come back to (_perceived_) strategic wartime industrial capacity. I don’t think that you have properly explained their subsidisation of solar though. I don’t know why they did it, but this doesn’t seem likely to be the reason.

​​@alistercrowe8531multiple weird things.

1.  I'm in US suburbia and find it worth it to go offgrid at $0.20/kWh US, but then I'm using DIY ground mounted panels but with 3x panel costs compared to you.  I suspect the DIY and ground mount aspects overcome the more expensive panels and lower solar insolation for a better ROI overall.

2.  With all the battery subsidies by the government, not also changing grid buyback scheme for higher rates during peak (evening) is weird.  Then you'd get not only the current midday flattening, but peak shaving without even needing a VPP.  Just basic thermostat/EV charging level programming complexity for solar/battery system to get the majority of arbitrage benefits.

But, you probably need AC even when cloudy.  I don't, but your winter heating is likely much less than mine and you get much more sun in winter.

They all have resources problems, the most important being food and water.
They have also built gigantic dams in an earthquake ridden part of the world. This has to go under the motto "no risk, no fun."
We also don't know how good the Chinese economic foundations have been built. Building foundations is boring, but necessary, if anything is to stand for a long time.

The One Child Policy was a trend in Lysenkoism - the break/fix approach to large statistical patterns. China's leaders were told by socialists that population growth would push the population rapidly beyond economic means if they didn't put limits in place. So - Government made a decision. One of Millions of unilateral decisions in China - and any negative feedback is considered slander, misinformation. Especially if it embarrasses an official - only positive news is allowed on Chinese Social Media. Including disasters and fatalities. No negative news is permitted - companies can ask the police to have your social media posts removed for slander. Even if it's true. Truth is not a valid excuse in Chinese Law. Chinese Law bends to assist those in power and those with wealth. The public interest is in making powerful people happy, not in making the people safe from exploitation or cruelty.

The Chinese Socialists of the time were informed that a village mentality would make housing and food production scarce, and populations would move rapidly if people were to move from villages - where land cost and growing of crops was the limiting factor to family sizes - to an urban density that was safer, had fewer jobs, but the government would have provisions for winter, food access, water and material goods. 

The government implemented a village/city 'family passport' where you had to be granted permission to live in a City area, a City Hukou - which is City or Regional/Rural based identification. This system still exists - and affects access to banking, travel, schools, medicine and health care, also pensions. Some village Hukou residents can't deposit money in an ATM, they have to travel home to deposit money in their banks and this limits their ability to live in, or own property in cities. The Hukou system is also why China's Economics is highly implausible - they may have a registered population of 8 million people, but 25 million people might work in a city, rent apartments, houses, offices and shop stalls, buy and sell food, transport goods, and use utilities. This plays with the numbers - as obviously you can cherry-pick which number looks better for statistics and GDP. 

City Hukou was/is a marriage make-or-break scenario as traditionally - parents are the match-makers for their children. The wive's parents still demand dowry payments for daughters. Which they often get - due to the economic and gender / demographic imbalance in women. The scale of the problem is still quite bad - which is why the government had to restrict marriages to 22 for men and 20 for women. This was due to the widespread kidnapping of girls from cities and schools to meet profit demands in rural areas - "aunties" would set up gangs to kidnap girls from schools, bus stops, shopping centres and train stations in broad daylight, bribing and drugging children and fitting them in suitcases. A trend that also continued in Primary Schools being caught selling and trading young children to politicians for exploitation and blackmail. 

Profit motives in China is usually the reason why laws are implemented radically and with little to no thought of consequences. It's also why there's 90 million unfinished highrise apartments / homes, up to 130 million to 150 million if you also include private islands, Entire village/cities built to house people that remain unoccupied, Theme Parks, Train stations with no nearby streets or houses, Empty/unfinished offices and shopping areas, apartments and buildings unfinished or lacking current owners - due to the rapid influx of capital from bank loans to pay for these new buildings. 

The modern problem of China's population is 3 fold. 

Age demographics - too many people are elderly - and too many are on the pension system, the 1CP's influence affects people in their 30s to 60s - especially families and the marriage limits. Now, you can have 2 to 3 children, or more, but the marriage numbers are depressed because of the economic slide into recession. 

Second, the bulk of the population, the average age is in the 50s. Too many retired people, not enough health care, not enough funeral homes. Too many deaths, and the population is sliding rapidly into uncontrollable numbers as people don't retire or replace workers. Entire companies are folding because nobody can retire, nobody can go bankrupt in China. Their families are too poor generally to maintain a family business - because they have to have multiple children to pay for their 3 or 4 generations to live in the same house. When the children leave - the grandparents don't have a support network if their children can't support them. There's no health system to cover the vast numbers of elderly. 

Third, the housing problem makes debt a widespread calamity. The current size of China's banking debt is Enormous, i.e. 10x larger than the Global Financial Crisis - held by Chinese Banking institutions because they can't get the money back on these debts. Too many wealthy people have left China with Trillions of dollars in liquid assets, gold, crypto and other resources. The scale of the problem is moderately impossible - because they cannot admit to the problem.

Their strenght is also their weakness in some ways. Its known that China directly supports its industrial sector. Other nations do this too...but China does it in a very large way. This allows China to 'over night' scale up any form of industry to massive scale. Housing, robotics, electric cars. But this creates an issue...or actually several.
It creates near instant over supply. Too much is being made in a lot of cases overshooting the target market. This is rather problematic especially when markets true value lags behind actual demand. Real-estate is one of those sectors. It take a while for buildings to be constructed and occupancy often depends on sales during and after construction. This is also true for EV's. China has so many EV's produced that their own market can't absorb the numbers and the global market often doesn't want to or is unable to do so either. It does allow for a market takeover potentially but the overshoot means that financial investment made by the Chinese government evaporates. 
Another issue is that Government funded corporations are either pop-up corporations who suddenly exist with government finance and disappear when the money was made in a heartbeat. Another issue is that internal competition due to government funding creates strong competition causing many companies to fold and thus government investment getting lost.

Essentially speaking - While a government funding its internal industry seems like a winning concept to quickly get ahead in a sector on the global market; it tends to come at a heavy economic and industrial price. Over time such a system is unsustainable. 

There are other issues playing on the background like aging population (which is a slow burn I should mention; its not a real issue now but it will be in ten or twenty years). Others are rising competitors like India. But currently I feel China's government heavily investing in its own industry is a mixed blessing; it does have some pretty big downsides. One could start with stricter regulation...but ultimately one then comes out on already pre-existing systems...which is why these pre-existing systems exists in the first place.
Basically China is discovering what most of the western world had already learned. Heavy investment by a government in its industry causes a growth spurt followed by a massive loss of capital. A sun burning twice as bright burns half as long.

snippet.textDisplay:
I think the discussion about China would benefit from a little more balance.

China clearly has serious problems: the property bubble, local-government debt, industrial overcapacity and a declining population are all real. But focusing almost exclusively on those problems gives a very incomplete picture of what has happened over the last four decades.

More than 800 million people have been lifted out of extreme poverty. China has built enormous amounts of infrastructure and developed complete industrial supply chains, becoming a global leader in areas such as solar, batteries, EVs and increasingly advanced technologies.

**High-speed rail is a particularly striking example. By the end of 2025, China had more than 50,000 km of operational high-speed railway. For comparison, Japan's Shinkansen network is about 3,146 km. The entire EU had about 8,554 km of dedicated lines capable of 250 km/h or more in 2024. The United States has NO comparable dedicated 250+ km/h national network: Acela uses the 457-mile/735-km Northeast Corridor, much of which operates at substantially lower speeds, with 160 mph reached only on limited sections. And anyone who has travelled through China will know that some of its major high-speed railway stations are extraordinary pieces of infrastructure in their own right — vast transport hubs whose physical scale rivals, and in some cases exceeds, that of many airports.**

That does not look to me like a country that has simply “wasted” its investment capital.

I have made more than 150 trips to China over the years, and one thing that has repeatedly struck me is the quality of everyday life I have actually seen there. Modern infrastructure, convenient transport, safe and lively cities, affordable services and rapid technological development have surprised me very positively. That personal experience does not prove that China's economic model has no problems, but neither should it simply be ignored in favour of a collection of negative macroeconomic indicators.

Even the property story is more nuanced than “millions of useless empty homes”. China undoubtedly overbuilt, but it also still has a huge stock of older and lower-quality housing that is planned to be replaced or demolished. Population decline reduces long-term housing demand, while urbanisation, smaller households and replacement of obsolete housing work in the opposite direction.

The interesting question is therefore not simply how much debt China accumulated, but what China obtained in return for that debt.

There has undoubtedly been waste and misallocation. But on the other side of the balance sheet are infrastructure, industrial capacity, technology, dramatically lower poverty, a middle-class population larger than the entire population of Europe, and a substantial improvement in living standards.

“China has serious problems” and “China has been remarkably successful” can both be true at the same time.

It's not the only option.  There are decades of old, second hand vehicles in various states and prices for all comers. The relatively new Chinese vehicle is a poor choice for the poor. You're better off with a vehicle that has been popular and therefore has lots of parts available. Bonus points for parts bin vehicles which share components with lots of other models.

I did this with my last vehicle. Bought cheap and parts that needed replacing were easy to find, quick to get and easy to replace myself if needed. Because it shared loads of components with multiple different models with very long production runs. Loads of 3rd party choices as a result with good competition on new parts. And loads of second hand availability and competition. Plus loads of guides and videos on how to diagnose and repair problems.

That is what you do when you're poor. You don't buy anything that's new or from a relatively new manufacturer / newish model. 

It's the same principle as buying an early model Tesla second hand - a terrible idea for the poor, even if it's relatively cheap.

snippet.textDisplay: Paul, love your work—nobody does deep, well-researched analysis like you. One nuance that might help: "ghost cities" weren't just the state overbuilding with money it didn't have. Research (NBER, IMF, PBOC surveys) shows Chinese households, facing capital controls and few investment options, used housing as a PRIMARY SAVINGS VEHICLE—various surveys put real estate at somewhere between 60-70% of household assets around 2019. That drove speculative purchases and vacancies, especially in lower-tier cities. At the same time, local governments are structurally dependent on land-related income (which made up roughly a third or more of local revenue in recent years) while covering the large majority of government spending, and are judged on GDP growth, so they push big new-town projects ahead of actual demand. one ckgsb analysis shows land-transfer revenue rising from 5.9% of local-government revenue in 2000 to 42% in 2020, and land-related revenue including associated taxes exceeding half of local revenue. In short: it's both—households storing wealth in homes + local land-finance incentives—not one cause alone, and the two reinforced each other.

A lot of what people see from China is smoke and mirrors. Much of their AI is not real, or it's not that good, for example. Some of it, of course, is decent. But it's not up to par with the latest from the United States. However, it is cheaper, which makes it attractive to some companies and individuals. It's "good enough" without breaking the bank. A lot of China's robotics, for example, is fake. 

When you see the dancing or fighting robotics, for example, they're not using AI at all. They're just radio controlled units, no different from your toy RC car. Almost every video you've seen online with those robots is staged. 

They're choreographed, and they make many takes, capturing the video when things go right. These robots all have a handler and are radio controlled by the handler. Like puppeteers, I noticed that many of them wear a lot of black clothing to help conceal themselves a bit more. 

But unlike what you see from Boston Dynamics, these robots are all just knock offs of Western designs, with none of the compute behind them. 

Some of China's AI trade shows are also embarrassing. Chinese companies were trying to convince people their latest AI could fully interact with you when, in reality, it was just a person talking to you through a microphone while hidden. Similar to how they do this trick at amusement parks. They also had a big CCP sponsored agricultural company that claimed to have created GPS and AI-tracking farm equipment that could harvest farm fields using GPS with minimal human input. The tractor would just follow a predetermined route and stay on course while harvesting crops. 

And in reality, the tractors didn't actually work. Plus, never mind that John Deere here in the United States actually perfected this technology for real 20 years ago, and that it required little human input, with mainly supervision and small corrections from an operator. And 5 years ago, almost no human input was needed for their latest tech, aside from the initial setup. (Supervision is still required if the operator has to take over for any reason since AI and GPS aren't foolproof by any means.) 

So China is really good at propaganda and putting on a good show to make people think they're highly advanced. But the reality is that China isn't nearly as advanced as they want you to think it is. China has a boatload of major issues across the country right now. China has a long way to go to iron out many of these core issues.

@Apollorion Making the two statements that China is authoritarian and that China is not communist are unrelated, both can be true at the same time. I think you started from an assumption that all discussions must be binary, which is a very common mistake to make (I make it myself quite often too).

RE: P.S. Agreed, in the case of capitalism and communism I think we're talking about a definition of ownership: Who gets to own the produced goods? Capitalism says the owner of the means of production, communism says those who need it should own it. The third option often gets conflated with communism, and that's socialism, since socialism says the worker should own the produced goods. In the case of autocracy versus democracy I would argue that has two dimensions: The first dimension is the level of power concentration (A.K.A. centralisation), the more concentrated the more autocratic and the more spread out the more democratic. The second dimension is consent.  You can have a democratic-in-the-first-sense society where 50% plus one of the votes can put any law in place regardless of how it treats a minority in the lack of consent-space extreme, in the middle of consent-space you can have a polder-model society where the main affected groups get a voice, while at the extreme point of consent-space you have a society where nobody can affect anyone without their consent.

​​@maxpool162That is an issue I have with the presenter.  His macro analysis seems cogent generally but such things are inherently unproveable especially in military analysis.  However an economic analysis begs for numbers to see the relative effects.  So that was a missed opportunity.

In the US where complex tariffs on panels come in at 165-250%, solar and batteries still have the best ROI (if you consume electricity.  Commercial ROI in solar vs solar markets isn't always great).

So, to your point, at the point of usage, solar and batteries have a huge ROI even at triple the price.

No, we don't. In fact, the so called climate crisis is a scam using manipulated statistics and buggy computer models*. I worked in the energy industry for 40 years and the FACT is, solar + wind simply cannot power a national grid.
Ate you aware that if you run the clock back on ANY of the 40 or so climate models, say back to start in 1980, then run them to predict the weather up through 2024 not one single model is within 65% of the weather that actually happened. If you go outside the mainstream media, especially the US media, it's been reported & discussed when that test was done back in 2024 a bunch and notice a lot of the imminent doomsday talk has quietly disappeared.

And clouds reflect sunlight (anywhere from 30 to 60% reflectance) which MASSIVELY affects surface heat gain which affects air temperature. Its the #1 driver of what the global temperature is, not CO2. Also, WATER VAPOR (in the upper atmosphere) is the biggest greenhouse gas, not CO2. And jet airliners have been putting tons of water vapor into the critical zone (higher than natural clouds) every flight. THAT might be having more effect than CO2 which has several regulation mechanisms like 'ocean sinks' and increased plant growth.
Anyway, it's all about energy density which old-fashioned generators have when turned by some fuel burning heat conversion device (gas turbine, diesel engines, steam boilers fired by coal, oil or natural gas or nuclear heat) and solar just isn't dense enough 24/7/356

​@opal3380during the summer, we do hit 90 degrees during the day. We have a high efficiency gas furnace and a heat pump that we use to heat and cool our home to use as little natural gas as possible. We also have a smart thermostat. With internet, I can check the temperature in the house in real time anywhere in the world.
The trick is to run the furnace fan during the day while the sun is up. This pre-cools the house to around 63° during the morning without the heat pump having to turn on until late afternoon or evening once the house warms up to about 20.5°. the furnace fan uses about 1/4 to 1/3 of the energy of the heat pump and is easily covered by the electricity generated by the solar panels. 
Even for those that don't have a furnace, the same can be accomplished with a heat pump and solar combination to pre-cool the house with solar energy. The house is being used as a thermal battery.
