All in, the electricity cost is between $0/kwh to about $0.125/kwh (generation + transmission + distribution). Instead of listening to someone lie that renewables don't work, we've been following the science and saving money for the past decade. If you doubt this approach works, ask ai. snippet.textDisplay:
I'm not here to say that China does not have problems that you mentioned, but one thing I've been realizing is debt to GDP ratio is not really a good figure to assess or compare the problem. The reason why is because GDP is not equal to production output. For example in the US a medical procedure may cost $100,000 whereas the same procedure may cost $5000 in another country. or food may cost $12 a meal here whereas $5 a meal in another country. When GDP is calculated, it's talking about the production output in terms of what those items cost. The reason I bring that up is because the comparison of 300% of debt to GDP in China compared to 130% of debt to GDP in the US, may be a little misleading. The US GDP is immensely inflated by our healthcare system and inflated prices. I think the US debt crisis is likely equal to or greater than the Chinese debt crisis.

It's really a bipartisan issue, I don't see any party with a mainstream idea of increasing taxation to bring down the deficit. But in my view, they really need to or else eventually we won't be able to increase our debt because people may not buy it when our interest per year is greater than the total tax revenue each year. For reference, the US receives 5.23 trillion dollars in tax revenue per year. We are currently paying 1.12 Trillion of that on interest payments on our 40+ Trillion dollar debt. in 2021 we were only paying 600 billion each year on interest payments, so in only 5 years, we nearly doubled our interest payments per year. It's a combination of both increasing our debt rapidly and also because of the rapid increase, we've had to pay back a very high interest rate on this debt. This problem is only going to get worse in the future because as that 1.12 Trillion number gets closer to 5.23 trillion, we will have to pay higher and higher interest payments because the US's credit rating(kind of like a credit score) will get worse and perceived as a more risky investment. This is a pretty big crisis and we're likely going to watch from a distance as politicians kick the can down the road until it's too late and there is a very very serious crisis. personally, I would say tax the rich because I know the lower side of the economy is already having such a tough time. But one way or another, this debt problem is also very serious in the US.

As far as China's GDP calculated nominally or at ppp it doesn't matter when comparing it to the country's debt as long as the two figures (debt and GDP) are measured in the same.  And in this case they are.  They use nominal GDP figures and nominal debt figures.  You could have come to the exact same percentage if you instead used ppp figures for both. In China's case it includes household and business debt whereas the US figure includes neither.  That said when you factor in de facto government companies (those "private companies" whose debts are expected to be underwritten by the government) the figure for China's total government debt now becomes 185%.  This is now far more accurately stated as the figure that is comparable to the US 130% figure.

snippet.textDisplay:
@WillFinch-k4j You raise some valid questions, and it is good to get other opinions. It may be that China will play a long game in nationalizing Russian gas fields in the Far East. Recently President Xi said no to Putin's suggestion of building pipelines from European Russia into China. China certainly is in the driving seat in their relationship with Russia. But would Russia negotiate away territory, especially when that territory has great economic value? I don't think so. If I were the president of Russia, that would always be a non-negotiable, period. I would also make it crystal-clear just what the boundary line is. Cross it, and you're dead. Conversely, were I the president of China, I would play the role of the patient yet smiling assassin. I would play the long game, stay friends while making incremental moves with a view to moving in to take the real estate when the cards have all been played.

China and Russia as allies is a marriage of convenience. If I had a few more years left in China I would definitely spend a summer up in that region to see just what kind of animosity is being felt by the locals as they watch their land being occupied by foreigners. I have seen a few videos, but that's not the same as being around it. At all events, that marriage of convenience is very likely going to end up in the most horrendous of divorces. Russia will not take being manipulated and betrayed at all well. So China has to play a very smart game to mitigate any Russian power to do anything about it once China makes its play in the decades to come. That's my surmise as things presently stand.

Yes, I agree with you that the current situation is very difficult to read. I also agree with you that China and Russia are supporting Iran at one remove. How much oil Iran is able to supply to China right now is a moot point. It will be nothing like it once was prior to February 28th this year. China will be feeling the pinch economically now that it has to pay market prices rather than doing straight swaps of oil for technology as before. American military involvement in Iran was long overdue, and should've happened decades ago. The current administration appears to be framing it within a narrative of American control over the flow of fossil fuels. Venezuela seems to now be under American control, which is a huge move. America controls the opening of the Strait of Hormuz for the present. And this is where Ukraine comes into play. They can potentially damage the flow of Russian oil and gas to the rest of the world. Commentators this week are talking about Ukrainian drones being able to reach into Siberia very soon. So Russia will need to act quickly to find where the drones are being manufactured and torch those facilities.

​@Llortnerof 
You have to realize that I have done that calculation with economic data that I could find in 15 mn of googling around.
I didn't do a pHD thesis on that!  So, that is why I pretty arbitrarily assigned a +/- 10% error margin to my number... which happened to be the 1.4B population that China is officially claiming to have.
To confront the loonies claiming it is below 1B, some even below 800M, I don't need to be more precise than that to say with 99.99% certainty that they are dead wrong!

As to the effect of the 1-child policy, a video of an interview of a demographer (unfortunately I have forgotten the reference) explains why the 1-child policy has had for effect to lower the unsustainable fertility rate of >6 in the 1960s, to 2.8 in the 1980s.... NOTHING like a real "1-child policy".  Such a fertility rate still means robust population growth!  The Chinese fertility rate dropped below the replacement rate of ca. 2.1 only in the 1990s, meaning that it is only a generation later than its effect is starting to show, i.e. in the 2020s!

Just look at the age pyramid of China, and you'll see that the 1-child policy is hardly more than a blip.

If the 1-child policy was enforced in the main cities, it was not enforced, or very loosely so in the countryside, where most of the Chinese population resided at the time.  Couple that to the increase in longevity, it becomes obvious that the population has NOT been decreasing for many years, but only since the early 2020s, and is decreasing VERY slowly since, and for another decade.  China's population is just past the peak of a pretty flat hump.

Look also at Pew Research, or World Economics on the topic.  They don't have a reputation for being CCP shills.

If you don't agree and maintain it has been "decreasing for decades", then please cite your references to support that... and please avoid conspiracy sites... or cite Peter Zeihan or the like as a credible reference!

But I am not implying that China does not have a looming acute demographic crisis on the horizon, especially as it is not a country of immigration.  But that's the point, it is a LOOMING crisis, not yet a developed crisis.

BTW, we also have very similar situations in most western countries, even without having had any 1-child policy... actually despite natalist policies!

Robot animals, mecha beasts, and a rogue AI collide in this feature-length sci-fi action movie.

After a secret laboratory begins turning living creatures into military weapons, a young man and the animals he trusts are pulled into a ruthless experiment. As a hidden tech empire prepares an army of cybernetic predators, the survivors must escape underground laboratories, stop a catastrophic core overload, and face a growing force of robot cats, mechanical wolves, combat birds, armored rhinos, and other deadly mecha beasts.

The battle eventually leads to a frozen military base, where the final Living Key could either end the machine war—or give artificial intelligence complete control.

Watch to the end for the final Arctic confrontation and the choice that determines whether these mechanical animals remain weapons or become something more.

the headline literally says “Chinese  robot beats Usain Bolt’s 100m world record,” then the problem isn’t merely that it makes the story more exciting. Taken in the ordinary sporting meaning of “beats a world record,” the headline is factually incorrect

snippet.textDisplay:
2050년, 중국은 세계를 100년 앞설 것이다.

중국 로봇, 100m 9초39로 ‘인간의 한계’를 넘다

1. 100m 결승선을 통과한 후, 그들은 무엇을 보았는가

한국 일부 매체와 유튜브는 어제 베이징에서 열린 제2회 세계 휴머노이드 로봇 운동회 400m 예선에서 로봇이 넘어지고 불꽃이 튄 장면만을 확대 재생산하며 조롱하고 있다.

맞다. 로봇은 넘어졌다. 불꽃도 튀었다.

하지만 그들은 말하지 않는다. 같은 자리, 같은 날, 중국의 ‘텐줘(天卓)’ 휴머노이드 로봇이 100m 예선에서 9초39를 기록하며, 우사인 볼트의 9초58이라는 인간 세계 기록을 0.19초 앞질렀다는 사실을.

그들은 말하지 않는다. 불과 1년 전, 이 대회 100m 최고 기록은 21초50에 불과했다는 것을.

1년 만에 기록이 절반 이하로 단축되었다.

2. 중국 로봇의 압도적 성과

2026년 8월 22일, 베이징 국가스피드스케이팅 경기장 ‘빙실대(冰絲帶)’. 제2회 세계 휴머노이드 로봇 운동회가 개막했다.

· 100m: ‘텐줘’팀 로봇 9초39, 인간 세계 기록(9초58) 돌파
· 입상: 같은 날 진행된 예선에서 9초32, 9초34, 9초38 등 더 빠른 기록도 등장
· 제자리 높이뛰기: ‘텐공 울트라’ 2.8843m, 인간 도움닫기 높이뛰기 세계 기록(2.45m) 초월
· 참가 규모: 666개 팀, 2,056대 로봇, 51개 종목 — 모두 작년 대비 4배 성장

로봇이 인간을 넘어선 것이 아니다. 중국 로봇이 1년 만에 스스로를 넘어섰다.

3. ‘넘어짐’이야말로 발전의 증거다

로봇이 넘어지고 불꽃이 튄 것은 ‘실패’가 아니다. 한계를 테스트하는 과정이다.

2026년 4월 19일, 베이징 이좡(亦莊) 휴머노이드 로봇 하프마라톤. 102개 로봇 팀 중 47개 팀이 완주했고, 완주율은 45%를 넘었다. 작년 완주 팀은 단 6개에 불과했다.

우승 로봇 ‘라이트닝(閃電)’은 50분 26초로 인간 하프마라톤 세계 기록(57분 20초)을 7분이나 앞질렀다.

“공개된 경기를 통해 문제를 조기에 노출시키는 것은 좋은 일이다. 완주에 실패한 로봇이 오히려 1위보다 더 가치 있을 수 있다.”

넘어질 수 있다는 것은, 그만큼 빠르게 달리고 있다는 증거다

4. 세계는? 미국은? 유럽은? 일본과 독일은?

이 대회에는 16개국 600여 개 팀이 참가했지만, 압도적 다수는 중국 팀이었다. 중국 641개 팀, 1,975대 로봇.

미국, 독일, 일본 등 국제 팀도 참가했지만, 결승선을 가장 먼저 통과한 것은 중국 로봇이었고, 가장 높이 뛴 것도 중국 로봇이었고, 가장 빠르게 달린 것도 중국 로봇이었다.

타국은 ‘로봇 규제’와 ‘윤리 논쟁’에 시간을 낭비하는 동안, 중국은 로봇을 뛰게 하고, 넘어뜨리고, 다시 뛰게 했다.

5. 2050년, 중국은 세계를 100년 앞설 것이다

한국 매체들이 조롱하는 그 ‘넘어짐’과 ‘불꽃’ 속에서, 중국은 이미 다음 세대의 로봇을 설계하고 있다.

· 군사: 전장 정찰·물자 수송 자동화
· 제조: 완전 무인 공장 현실화
· 의료: 초정밀 수술 로봇 상용화
· 교육: AI 튜터 로봇 전국 보급

넘어지는 로봇을 비웃는 나라와 넘어져도 다시 일어나는 로봇을 만드는 나라.
100년 뒤, 누가 웃고 있을지 궁금하다.

“기술의 온도는 인간을 섬기는 데 있다. 미래의 삶은 시간을 절약하고, 마음을 편하게 하며, 온정으로 가득 찬 것이다.”

중국은 그 온도를 만들고 있다. 당신은 그저 지켜보고 있을 뿐이다.

snippet.textDisplay: ​@Lucas-xm3jvyes, I agree that liability is a major barrier to deploying humanoid robots in homes. But I don't think it is the only barrier. The robot first has to demonstrate sufficiently reliable perception, physical manipulation, navigation, decision-making and safe behavior in genuinely unpredictable homes. Once that level of engineering maturity exists, liability, insurance and regulatory frameworks become the next major obstacles. In other words, it's not either/or: the technology and the liability framework have to mature together.

snippet.textDisplay: Usain Bolt set the world record in August 2009 — that was 17 years ago. Out of the 8.2 billion people on this planet, even if we exclude the elderly, minors, and those with various health conditions or disabilities, there are still billions of able-bodied humans. And yet, in all these 17 years, not a single one of them has been able to break Bolt's record. But this robot, which broke the record using just its two legs, is just an ordinary one off the production line — one among hundreds or even thousands of its kind. You might think its running form isn't elegant, and its exit was rather clumsy. But remember: it's been less than three years since Chinese companies unveiled general-purpose humanoid robot technology in 2024. This year, it may still need to crash into a wall to stop, and be carried off on a stretcher. But what about 2027? What about 2028?

Can’t believe that people cheer on this very, very scary development.

We are developing humanoid machines that can outpace, outrun and physically outperform 99% of all humans.
We are developing batteries that are getting smaller and lighter every week, storing ever growing amounts of energy, able to recharge autonomously to fit them into these robots. 
We are developing AI  computing systems (at the moment these are “only” advanced languages models) in a staggering speed to self consciousness and high speed remote transfer systems to allow a network of robots to work in sync and unison.
Optical systems, that are more precise than the eye of a falcon and can detect any living thing on the planet.

We add the drone technology to it and we have a network that will eventually be able to manage, regenerate, further develop and repair/replace itself.
It is not anymore the question if humans will be replace but when and how.

Two options, either Borg or Terminator. But any of the two is going to be the end of humanity as we know it.

And don’t say that maybe that is a good thing, it is not, as all fauna and flora on land, sea and air will also be affected.

The human brain can't do precise math, can't store large amounts of data accurately, and if you ask the same question twice, you might get two different answers—kind of like a low-quality AI model. In the end, they created another intelligent being to carry on their legacy and explore the universe. That alone is something truly remarkable. As humans, we will soon proudly fade out of history.

Robots which look after your home isn’t a strong selling point, it’s only mainly to get the general public excited to robots. Truthfully, the robotics industry needs to prove itself as a product before it can be anything else. Metaphorically, chinas robots are bic lighters, while the US robots are zippo lighters

snippet.textDisplay:
That's hilarious! The Chinese have a robot demonstrate running, and you think they're just building robots to replace athletes in competitive sports?

Since the first robot based on neural network AI technology was created in 2016, modern robotics is still in its early stages of development. Yes, these robots can't do any decent work yet. But what does it matter?

When the automobile was invented in 1886, it couldn't even travel 10 miles safely; it was practically a piece of scrap metal, and all the coachmen laughed at it. When the first mass-produced automobile was born in 1908, it was still an expensive and fragile toy for the rich, still unable to replace a horse-drawn carriage.

Can you still see horse-drawn carriages outside of tourist attractions now?

Don't worry, dear, the Chinese are very patient. They're willing to invest in these still-developing technologies until they mature. You'll definitely live to see the day they mature.

Oh, one last thing: this Games will last five days and include many vocational skills competitions, not just imitations of human competitive sports. You can follow the news in the next few days.

snippet.textDisplay:
2050년, 중국은 세계를 100년 앞설 것이다.

중국 로봇, 100m 9초39로 ‘인간의 한계’를 넘다

1. 100m 결승선을 통과한 후, 그들은 무엇을 보았는가

한국 일부 매체와 유튜브는 어제 베이징에서 열린 제2회 세계 휴머노이드 로봇 운동회 400m 예선에서 로봇이 넘어지고 불꽃이 튄 장면만을 확대 재생산하며 조롱하고 있다.

맞다. 로봇은 넘어졌다. 불꽃도 튀었다.

하지만 그들은 말하지 않는다. 같은 자리, 같은 날, 중국의 ‘텐줘(天卓)’ 휴머노이드 로봇이 100m 예선에서 9초39를 기록하며, 우사인 볼트의 9초58이라는 인간 세계 기록을 0.19초 앞질렀다는 사실을.

그들은 말하지 않는다. 불과 1년 전, 이 대회 100m 최고 기록은 21초50에 불과했다는 것을.

1년 만에 기록이 절반 이하로 단축되었다.

2. 중국 로봇의 압도적 성과

2026년 8월 22일, 베이징 국가스피드스케이팅 경기장 ‘빙실대(冰絲帶)’. 제2회 세계 휴머노이드 로봇 운동회가 개막했다.

· 100m: ‘텐줘’팀 로봇 9초39, 인간 세계 기록(9초58) 돌파
· 입상: 같은 날 진행된 예선에서 9초32, 9초34, 9초38 등 더 빠른 기록도 등장
· 제자리 높이뛰기: ‘텐공 울트라’ 2.8843m, 인간 도움닫기 높이뛰기 세계 기록(2.45m) 초월
· 참가 규모: 666개 팀, 2,056대 로봇, 51개 종목 — 모두 작년 대비 4배 성장

로봇이 인간을 넘어선 것이 아니다. 중국 로봇이 1년 만에 스스로를 넘어섰다.

3. ‘넘어짐’이야말로 발전의 증거다

로봇이 넘어지고 불꽃이 튄 것은 ‘실패’가 아니다. 한계를 테스트하는 과정이다.

2026년 4월 19일, 베이징 이좡(亦莊) 휴머노이드 로봇 하프마라톤. 102개 로봇 팀 중 47개 팀이 완주했고, 완주율은 45%를 넘었다. 작년 완주 팀은 단 6개에 불과했다.

우승 로봇 ‘라이트닝(閃電)’은 50분 26초로 인간 하프마라톤 세계 기록(57분 20초)을 7분이나 앞질렀다.

“공개된 경기를 통해 문제를 조기에 노출시키는 것은 좋은 일이다. 완주에 실패한 로봇이 오히려 1위보다 더 가치 있을 수 있다.”

넘어질 수 있다는 것은, 그만큼 빠르게 달리고 있다는 증거다

4. 세계는? 미국은? 유럽은? 일본과 독일은?

이 대회에는 16개국 600여 개 팀이 참가했지만, 압도적 다수는 중국 팀이었다. 중국 641개 팀, 1,975대 로봇.

중국 로봇, 100m 9초39로 ‘인간의 한계’를 넘다

1. 100m 결승선을 통과한 후, 그들은 무엇을 보았는가

한국 일부 매체와 유튜브는 어제 베이징에서 열린 제2회 세계 휴머노이드 로봇 운동회 400m 예선에서 로봇이 넘어지고 불꽃이 튄 장면만을 확대 재생산하며 조롱하고 있다.

맞다. 로봇은 넘어졌다. 불꽃도 튀었다.

하지만 그들은 말하지 않는다. 같은 자리, 같은 날, 중국의 ‘텐줘(天卓)’ 휴머노이드 로봇이 100m 예선에서 9초39를 기록하며, 우사인 볼트의 9초58이라는 인간 세계 기록을 0.19초 앞질렀다는 사실을.

그들은 말하지 않는다. 불과 1년 전, 이 대회 100m 최고 기록은 21초50에 불과했다는 것을.

1년 만에 기록이 절반 이하로 단축되었다.

2026년 8월 22일, 베이징 국가스피드스케이팅 경기장 ‘빙실대(冰絲帶)’. 제2회 세계 휴머노이드 로봇 운동회가 개막했다.

로봇이 인간을 넘어선 것이 아니다. 중국 로봇이 1년 만에 스스로를 넘어섰다.

"Current State of Robotic Laundry Folding:

"NEO by 1X Technologies approaches laundry folding through a design focused on soft-bodied safety and a hybrid teleoperation system. "Figure 02:

"Figure 02 achieved a major robotics milestone by demonstrating fully autonomous laundry folding and washing machine loading inside a real home. There is no miracle update that can make them do so reliably what human beings and animals do to survive without completely failing to assess which task should happen first. They don't have instincts.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@Sh1702oooI agree with many of your points. It is true that many so-called “premium” products from Western brands are actually manufactured in China. It is also undeniable that China has achieved remarkable progress in infrastructure, manufacturing, urban development and economic growth over the past four decades, and there is a lot India can learn from that.
I also appreciate several aspects of China’s development model. After 1978, China gradually opened up its economy and focused heavily on manufacturing, exports, infrastructure and urbanisation. During the 1980s, both India and China were large, low-income developing economies, and their nominal GDPs were roughly comparable by 1987. China subsequently expanded its economy at an extraordinary pace and is now the world’s second-largest economy. That is undoubtedly a remarkable achievement.
However, my criticism is not about China’s development. It is about a particular segment of Chinese manufacturing.
In my view, a significant part of Chinese manufacturing has historically been driven by low cost and high-volume production. When manufacturers compete primarily on price and scale, some of them may resort to cutting costs at the expense of materials, quality control and durability. That does not mean that all Chinese products are low-quality—far from it. China produces everything from extremely cheap products to some of the most advanced and high-quality products in the world.
The problem arises when low-quality or counterfeit products reach millions of consumers. When people repeatedly have poor experiences with such products, it eventually creates a perception that “Chinese products are cheap and unreliable.” Even Chinese authorities have acknowledged that substandard and counterfeit products, along with poor quality control in some industries, have damaged the global image of “Made in China.”
We have a saying in India: “Haste makes waste.”
But you cannot call someone poor simply because they chose not to buy a premium product. They may simply have made a perfectly rational decision according to their budget and priorities. Judging someone's financial status by a single product they use is just as misleading as judging an entire country's manufacturing capabilities by its cheapest products.
I also don't have a one-sided view of India. We have many products and manufacturing sectors whose durability and reliability can compete with world-class products. The problem is that much of India's manufacturing capability has not yet reached the scale, consistency, branding and global distribution required to compete effectively in international markets.
And we also need to be honest about our own shortcomings. India's problems are not simply a lack of technology or talent. Bureaucracy, regulatory complexity, infrastructure gaps, inconsistent policy implementation and corruption can all affect the competitiveness of Indian businesses. At the same time, it would be unfair to say that all our problems are caused by “less-educated politicians.” The quality of policymaking depends not only on formal education, but also on institutions, expertise, accountability and implementation.
So, my point is not anti-China. In fact, I believe India has a lot to learn from China—especially its manufacturing scale, infrastructure development, supply-chain integration and speed of execution.
At the same time, India needs to have greater confidence in its own manufacturing capabilities, its own products and its own engineering. We should not aim merely to make things cheaper. We should aim to make them affordable + durable + reliable + globally competitive.
And finally, if you consider me poor simply because I don't use your premium product, I have a small suggestion for you:
Come to India sometime. Don't spend the entire month in Mumbai. Spend a month travelling across India and go beyond Mumbai—visit its smaller cities, towns and villages. You may discover that there is another India beyond Mumbai, and perhaps then you will understand that a person's financial status is far more complicated than the phone they use, the clothes they wear, or the products they choose to buy.

​@Sh1702oooAccording to China’s National Bureau of Statistics, China had around 1.405 billion people in 2025, but its demographic trend is concerning: only 5.63 births per 1,000 people, compared with 8.04 deaths. Around 23% of the population is already 60+, while the younger population is shrinking.
So I genuinely wonder: in an ageing and slowly shrinking society, with many young people facing employment and rising living costs, how large is the actual affluent population that regularly buys expensive “premium” and luxury products?
And why should we automatically consider something “premium” just because a Western brand puts a huge price tag on it? Many luxury products like branded clothing you purchase in Canada are manufactured in countries like India and Bangladesh at a fraction of their final retail price—the rest is branding, marketing and perceived status.

Ok you said "facts speak louder than words." Let me represent facts and numbers for you...

India’s imports from China are heavily concentrated in electrical/electronic equipment, machinery, organic chemicals, components and industrial inputs. In FY2024-25, China supplied 74.1% of India’s imports of bulk drugs and drug intermediates, 49.5% of computer hardware/peripherals, 43.4% of telecom instruments and 37.9% of electronic components. .

NITI Aayog itself has described India’s dependence on Chinese capital and intermediate goods as a supply-chain vulnerability, not as evidence that Chinese products are inherently superior.

.

So your argument is basically:

“India buys a lot from China → therefore Chinese goods are high quality.”

That conclusion doesn't follow from the premise.

If import volume were proof of quality, then a country heavily dependent on imported oil would have to conclude that imported oil is superior to its domestic alternatives.

Trade figures tell us what India needs, what is competitively priced and where supply chains are concentrated. "They do not give every imported product a quality certificate."

snippet.textDisplay:
@竹梅松2020 Lol. Absolute BS.

904 CE (Tang Dynasty): The earliest recorded military use occurs. Flying fire arrows (arrows strapped with gunpowder fuses) are used in the siege of Yuzhang.

1044 CE (Song Dynasty): The military manual Wujing Zongyao publishes the world’s first chemical formulas for gunpowder, alongside blueprints for mass production and various bomb designs.

1132 CE (Song-Jin Wars): The Chinese invent the fire lance (huochong), a bamboo or metal tube filled with gunpowder and shrapnel strapped to a spear. This is widely recognized by historians as the ancestor of all modern firearms.

1221 CE: The Chinese deploy the Zhentianlei ("Thunderclap Bomb"), a cast-iron fragmentation bomb launched by trebuchets that shatters enemy armor.

1300s (Ming Dynasty): The Ming military becomes heavily reliant on firearms. They deploy landmines, naval mines, multi-stage rockets, and massive bronze cannons.

Takeaway- just because your government drills it into your head that China is a peaceful nation that loves peace and that it was only Westerners that used gunpowder for war doesn't make it true.

列举中国古代发明火药、制造火器用于战争，并据此得出“中国不是和平国家，因为中国很早就把火药用于战争”。这种观点表面上引用历史事实，实际上犯了严重的逻辑错误。

历史事实可以证明“中国曾经使用火药武器”，但不能证明“中国是一个好战国家”。

这就如同一个国家发明了汽车，汽车后来被用于战争，那么是否可以因此说这个国家“不爱好和平”？显然不能。技术的军事用途，不等于创造技术的民族具有战争倾向。

逻辑学中，这属于典型的“以个别事实推导整体性质”的错误归因。

snippet.textDisplay:
@DavidGravesExists 一、发明和使用武器，是所有文明发展的普遍现象，并不能证明一个民族好战。
人类历史上几乎所有大型文明都发展过军事技术。
欧洲发明或改进了大量军事技术：
火炮；火枪；战列舰；航空母舰；坦克；核武器。
按照“中国使用火药武器＝中国好战”的逻辑，那么欧洲是否应该被定义为“最不爱好和平的文明”？显然不是。

因为现代社会判断一个国家是否和平，看的不是：
“这个国家有没有制造过武器？”而是：
是否主动发动对外侵略战争；
是否追求军事扩张；
是否以战争作为解决国际问题的主要手段；
是否尊重其他国家主权。
如果仅仅因为拥有武器，就认为一个国家热爱战争，那么世界上没有任何国家可以被称为和平国家。

二、中国古代使用火药武器，是防御战争和国家生存需求，而不是战争崇拜。
中国古代火药武器的发展，主要发生在宋元时期。
这个时期的中国并不是一个不断向外扩张的军事帝国，而是长期面对北方游牧政权的军事压力。
例如：
北宋长期面对辽、西夏、金的军事威胁；
南宋面对金、蒙古的强大军事压力；
明朝长期面对北方蒙古势力，同时进行海防建设。
火药武器的出现，本质上是国家面对战争环境时的技术回应。
如果一个国家拥有防御武器，就被认为“不爱和平”，那么任何拥有军队的国家都无法称为和平国家。

和平并不意味着没有武器。
真正的和平，是拥有维护和平、防止侵略的能力，而不是完全放弃防御。

三、中国火药技术的发展，反而体现了中国传统文化中“止战”的思想。
中国传统军事思想并不鼓吹战争。
中国兵家思想的重要代表《孙子兵法》开篇就是：
“兵者，国之大事，死生之地，存亡之道，不可不察也。”《孙子兵法》强调：“不战而屈人之兵，善之善者也。”意思是，最高境界不是通过战争取胜，而是避免战争。

这与一些西方历史上的“征服型帝国”传统存在明显区别。
中国历史上虽然有战争，但战争并不是中国文明的核心价值。

中国传统政治理念长期强调：
“和为贵”；“协和万邦”；“天下太平”。
这些思想并不意味着中国历史没有战争，而是说明战争通常被视为不得已的手段，而不是文明发展的目标。

四、火药武器最初用于战争，是因为当时世界处于普遍战争时代
你列举：
904年火箭；
1044年《武经总要》；
1132年突火枪；
1221年震天雷；
明代火器发展。这些历史基本事实，大部分是正确的。但是，你犯了一个关键错误：把“中国拥有军事技术”偷换成“中国热爱战争”。这是典型的“偷换概念”。
事实是：
中国发明火药 → 正确。
中国早期使用火药武器 → 正确。
中国因此是战争国家 → 错误。
因为前两个事实，并不能推出第三个结论。

这就像：
“某医生发明手术刀。”
“手术刀可以用来杀人。”
“所以医生是暴力人士。”
这种推理显然荒谬。

工具是什么，取决于使用方式，而不是工具本身。

五、中国历史上的战争数量，不能简单证明“中国不是和平国家”。
任何拥有长期文明历史的大国，都经历过战争。

欧洲经历过：
罗马扩张战争；十字军东征；百年战争；拿破仑战争；两次世界大战。

美国经历过：
独立战争；美墨战争；南北战争；海外军事干预。

俄罗斯经历过：
沙俄扩张；多次欧洲战争。

如果按照“中国历史上发生过战争，所以中国不是和平国家”的逻辑和标准，那么世界上几乎所有国家都不是和平国家。

判断一个国家的性质，必须看长期历史趋势，而不是挑选几个战争事件。

六、中国传统对外关系中，更多强调秩序和防御，而不是全球征服
中国历史上确实存在扩张时期，也有军事征服行为，这是历史事实，不能否认。
但是，与近代欧洲殖民体系相比，中国历史上没有建立类似：
全球殖民网络；跨洲殖民统治；大规模海外殖民掠夺体系。

15世纪明朝郑和下西洋，就是一个典型例子。
郑和舰队规模远超当时欧洲航海力量，但主要任务是：贸易交流；外交联系；展示国力。
并没有像后来欧洲殖民者那样，在海外建立大规模殖民地。
这说明中国历史上的国家战略传统，与近代欧洲殖民扩张模式存在明显差异。

结论：火药改变战争方式，但不能改变中国文明追求和平的价值取向
中国发明火药，是人类科技史上的重大贡献。
中国古代使用火药武器，也是历史事实。

但是：
发明武器 ≠ 崇尚战争。
拥有军事技术 ≠ 喜欢侵略。
参与战争 ≠ 战争国家。

判断一个国家是否爱好和平，应该看它的战略文化、历史行为和国际关系，而不是看它是否拥有某项技术。

火药是一种工具。
它可以用于烟花，也可以用于战争。

真正决定一个文明性质的，不是它有没有武器，而是它如何使用力量，以及它最终追求什么目标。

因此，用“中国发明火药并用于战争”来证明“中国不是和平国家”，在逻辑上是不成立的。

历史事实证明：中国曾经拥有强大的军事技术；但这并不能推出中国文明以战争为核心。相反，中国传统文化长期强调“和”“合”“止戈为武”，追求的是秩序与和平，而不是战争本身。

snippet.textDisplay:
@dchiuYT 中国并非“不爱好和平”的国家，相关指控大多混淆争议海域事实、夸大常规维权行动，并选择性忽略历史与多边现实。 

1. “中国不爱好和平”“向我们发射导弹”中国自1979年对越自卫反击战后，近半个世纪未发动大规模对外侵略战争，坚持“和平共处五项原则”与“和平发展”道路。与某些国家遍布全球的数百个军事基地不同，中国海外军事设施极少（主要是吉布提后勤保障点）。导弹试射与军事演练（包括台海周边或南海指定海域）是主权国家正常军力建设与威慑行为，官方多次明确“不针对任何特定国家”，属于例行训练，而非“向邻国发射导弹攻击”。把演习等同于开战，是典型的危言耸听。 

中国是二战反法西斯主要战胜国与最大受害国之一，曾遭受日本帝国主义侵略带来的巨大灾难。将今日中国与当年军国主义日本类比，既无视历史，也无视中国长期倡导通过对话协商解决争端、推动“一带一路”等互利合作的现实。

2. “封锁并入侵我们的领土”“撞击船只、水炮、警棍”中国南海争议涉及中国、越南、菲律宾、马来西亚、文莱及中国台湾多方主张。中国对南海诸岛的主权主张可追溯至中华民国时期官方地图（1947年十一段线），并被中华人民共和国继承。各方在上世纪70年代后因资源与战略价值陆续强化存在，越南实际控制南沙岛礁最多，菲律宾、马来西亚等亦有驻守。中国在部分岛礁的建设与管控，是对既有主张的巩固，而非单方面“入侵”已无争议的他国领土。 

3. “公然藐视国际法”“水域归你们所有”。2016年南海仲裁案是菲律宾单方面提起，中国从未接受、参与或承认。中方核心立场是：该案实质涉及领土主权与海洋划界，而《联合国海洋法公约》（UNCLOS）明确不处理主权问题，仲裁庭超越权限；中菲此前有通过双边谈判解决争端的共识；中国在批准UNCLOS时已作出相关声明。裁决本身无强制执行机制，中国始终主张通过双边协商与“南海行为准则”谈判管控分歧。 

九段线体现的是中国对岛礁主权及历史性权利的主张。国际实践中，大国对争议裁决的保留并不罕见。真正的“藐视”是无视历史事实与多边主张，单方面把己方最大利益包装成“国际法唯一标准”。

爱好和平不等于放弃主权与正当维权。中国在南海的行动是对争议主张的维护，而非无端侵略；摩擦多源于对方船只进入中方管控或主张区域并拒绝离开。把复杂的历史遗留争端简化为“中国坏、我们无辜”，并用二战军国主义做不当类比，既不符合事实，也无助于通过对话与合作解决问题。真正的和平需要各方尊重彼此核心关切、回归谈判，而不是单方面污名化与煽动对立。

snippet.textDisplay:
@dchiuYT 你的发言似乎是在说“这是AI生成的，所以没有反驳力”，本身就是一种诉诸来源，而不是对观点本身的反驳。
首先，文章中的核心观点是我的。AI做的事情只是把我提出的事实、逻辑和论证思路进行整理、结构化和语言润色，使表达更加完整，并不意味着因为使用了AI，里面的事实就自动变成错误，逻辑就自动失效。
判断一篇结论是否成立，应该看三个最基本的问题：
第一，事实是否准确？
如果我引用的历史事实、国际法事实或者事件经过有错误，请直接指出哪一条错误，并给出可靠证据。
第二，逻辑是否成立？
如果我的推理存在逻辑漏洞，请指出具体是哪一个前提不能成立，或者哪一步推导存在错误。
第三，结论是否能够由前提推出？
如果不能，请直接拆解论证，而不是讨论文章是不是AI写的。

反过来说，如果你的反驳是“这是AI生成的”，那实际上并没有反驳文章中的任何一个事实，也没有证明任何一个逻辑错误。

这就好比一个人去图书馆查阅了十本历史书，然后根据这些资料写了一篇文章。你不去核对他引用的史料，也不分析他的论证，只说：“这篇文章是查资料写出来的，所以没有说服力。”这显然是荒谬的。
因为资料来源、写作工具和论证本身，是三个不同的问题。

甚至更简单一点：
数学题是人算出来的，还是计算器算出来的，并不能决定答案对不对；
论文是作者自己打字，还是使用文字处理软件，也不能决定论文的论证是否成立。
同样，文章是人独立整理，还是借助AI整理，都不能替代对事实、证据和逻辑本身的检验。
如果你不同意我的观点，请逐条反驳我的论据；如果你认为我的事实有问题，请逐条提供证据；如果你认为我的逻辑有问题，请指出具体的逻辑谬误。

“这是AI生成的”不是论据，更不是反驳。
把“谁写的”当成“写得对不对”的判断标准，本身就是把讨论从论证本身转移到了论证来源。

真正有价值的讨论，应该是：不要问“这是谁写的”，先问“这是真的吗？为什么？证据在哪里？”

@竹梅松2020 Absolute BS.

904 CE (Tang Dynasty): The earliest recorded military use occurs. Flying fire arrows (arrows strapped with gunpowder fuses) are used in the siege of Yuzhang.

1044 CE (Song Dynasty): The military manual Wujing Zongyao publishes the world’s first chemical formulas for gunpowder, alongside blueprints for mass production and various bomb designs.

1132 CE (Song-Jin Wars): The Chinese invent the fire lance (huochong), a bamboo or metal tube filled with gunpowder and shrapnel strapped to a spear. This is widely recognized by historians as the ancestor of all modern firearms.

1221 CE: The Chinese deploy the Zhentianlei ("Thunderclap Bomb"), a cast-iron fragmentation bomb launched by trebuchets that shatters enemy armor.

1300s (Ming Dynasty): The Ming military becomes heavily reliant on firearms. They deploy landmines, naval mines, multi-stage rockets, and massive bronze cannons.

Takeaway- just because your government drills it into your head that China is a peaceful nation that loves peace and that it was only Westerners that used gunpowder for war doesn't make it true.

snippet.textDisplay:
@kelongye5117 Absolute BS.

904 CE (Tang Dynasty): The earliest recorded military use occurs. Flying fire arrows (arrows strapped with gunpowder fuses) are used in the siege of Yuzhang.

1044 CE (Song Dynasty): The military manual Wujing Zongyao publishes the world’s first chemical formulas for gunpowder, alongside blueprints for mass production and various bomb designs.

1132 CE (Song-Jin Wars): The Chinese invent the fire lance (huochong), a bamboo or metal tube filled with gunpowder and shrapnel strapped to a spear. This is widely recognized by historians as the ancestor of all modern firearms.

1221 CE: The Chinese deploy the Zhentianlei ("Thunderclap Bomb"), a cast-iron fragmentation bomb launched by trebuchets that shatters enemy armor.

1300s (Ming Dynasty): The Ming military becomes heavily reliant on firearms. They deploy landmines, naval mines, multi-stage rockets, and massive bronze cannons.

Takeaway- just because you and your fellow agents repeat it thousands of times in the internet China is a peaceful nation that loves peace and that it was only Westerners that used gunpowder for war doesn't make it true.

​@alexbobev781accuracy is no problem for any robot, the problem is weight. These robots have so many limitations, that it would be beyond dumb to think these are something to worry about in the near future, if at all.

To make them able to handle anything like a human, climb like a human, or anything else, would be a very expensive and ridiculous challenge. Then they would have no range. And they don't need arms or an actual firearm to shoot, that would defeat the purpose of a robot in the first place. We already have much more effective automated/remote turrets that don't have hundreds of extra delicate parts.

There's even more than that, but yes, these are not the thing to be worried about. Flying drones and heavier remote wheeled/tracked vehicles that can handle much more weight, are the problem.

Only people that don't know anything about the limits of manufacturing, mobility, batteries, and warfare would think these are something to fear, and if technology becomes advanced enough to overcome the power source to make these practical, then flying drones would still be superior.

snippet.textDisplay:
Biggest fails from the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games in China

#news #robots #china #innovation #technology #games 

The unfolding Second World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing is showcasing not only high-profile feats of robotic athleticism but also practical skills that could see humanoids being widely adopted in real-world homes and workplaces. However, the push for peak performance has yielded just as many spectacular faceplants as tech breakthroughs. Alongside record-shattering sprints, audiences have seen autonomous sprinters smash full-speed into deceleration barriers, competitors collapse mid-stride to be carried off on stretchers, and kickboxing and soccer bots tumble into hilarious metallic pileups. These dramatic stumbles highlight the reality of cutting-edge hardware: for every giant leap humanoids make toward everyday utility, there is a trail of flying sparks, lost balance, and mechanical slapstick along the way.

snippet.textDisplay:
2050년, 중국은 세계를 100년 앞설 것이다.

중국 로봇, 100m 8초86로 ‘인간의 한계’를 넘다

1. 100m 결승선을 통과한 후, 그들은 무엇을 보았는가

한국 일부 매체와 유튜브는 어제 베이징에서 열린 제2회 세계 휴머노이드 로봇 운동회 400m 예선에서 로봇이 넘어지고 불꽃이 튄 장면만을 확대 재생산하며 조롱하고 있다.

맞다. 로봇은 넘어졌다. 불꽃도 튀었다.

하지만 그들은 말하지 않는다. 같은 자리, 같은 날, 중국의 ‘텐줘(天卓)’ 휴머노이드 로봇이 100m 예선에서 8초86를 기록하며, 우사인 볼트의 9초58이라는 인간 세계 기록을 앞질렀다는 사실을.

그들은 말하지 않는다. 불과 1년 전, 이 대회 100m 최고 기록은 21초50에 불과했다는 것을.

1년 만에 기록이 절반 이하로 단축되었다.

2. 중국 로봇의 압도적 성과

2026년 8월 22일, 베이징 국가스피드스케이팅 경기장 ‘빙실대(冰絲帶)’. 제2회 세계 휴머노이드 로봇 운동회가 개막했다.

· 100m: ‘텐줘’팀 로봇 8초86, 인간 세계 기록(9초58) 돌파
· 입상: 같은 날 진행된 예선에서 9초32, 9초34, 9초38 등 더 빠른 기록도 등장
· 제자리 높이뛰기: ‘텐공 울트라’ 2.8843m, 인간 도움닫기 높이뛰기 세계 기록(2.45m) 초월
· 참가 규모: 666개 팀, 2,056대 로봇, 51개 종목 — 모두 작년 대비 4배 성장

로봇이 인간을 넘어선 것이 아니다. 중국 로봇이 1년 만에 스스로를 넘어섰다.

3. ‘넘어짐’이야말로 발전의 증거다

로봇이 넘어지고 불꽃이 튄 것은 ‘실패’가 아니다. 한계를 테스트하는 과정이다.

snippet.textDisplay:
Now come on... In contrast to AI systems these humanoid robots only fail in certain situations. And yes, getting those final 10% right often takes 90% of the work. So they still need quite some time and money. 
- Never the less: 
As a German who grew up in a country that once valued its innovative engineering tradition, I definitely admire how far the Chinese engineers have already come in the field of robotics. I wish we would be anywhere near that... Just like with cars our industry has been dormant for decades now thinking that repetition is all it takes to build great products. Thus now the Chinese aren't that far away from being for robotics what we used to be for cars for so long. And just like that one CEO said: They haven't gotten to their ChatGPT moment yet, but I believe they will get there... maybe not in the next three or five years, but from my point of view some will be there within a decade.
- Thus I say: 
These are no fails, these are the the next steps to be taken. 
Congratulations and respect to those engineers.

snippet.textDisplay:
@jeremymandelkern9260 What we’re seeing in these robotics competitions is genuinely impressive, especially in locomotion, joint coordination, and actuator performance. The level of mechanical precision and control is clearly very mature.

However, it’s important to recognize that many of these systems are operating in structured environments, often with pre-defined motions or assisted control. That’s very different from building a truly autonomous robot that can adapt to unpredictable, real-world conditions.

Projects like Tesla’s Optimus may look less polished in movement today, but they are tackling a fundamentally harder problem: general-purpose autonomy. Smooth motion in a controlled demo is one thing and real-world adaptability is another.

So rather than saying one is “ahead” of the other, it’s more accurate to say they are optimizing for very different goals: precision execution vs. general intelligence.

What is the Dunning-Kruger effect?

When we don't know enough to know what we don't know.

* So goes the reasoning behind the Dunning-Kruger effect, the inclination of unskilled or unknowledgeable people to overestimate their own competence.


LiveScience


👇

Why we overestimate our competence
Social psychologists are examining people's pattern of overlooking their own weaknesses.




Cross-cultural comparisons

Regardless of how pervasive the phenomenon is, it is clear from Dunning's and others' work that many Americans, at least sometimes and under some conditions, have a tendency to inflate their worth. It is interesting, therefore, to see the phenomenon's mirror opposite in another culture. In research comparing North American and East Asian self-assessments, Heine of the University of British Columbia finds that East Asians tend to underestimate their abilities, with an aim toward improving the self and getting along with others.

These differences are highlighted in a meta-analysis Heine is now completing of 70 studies that examine the degree of self-enhancement or self-criticism in China, Japan and Korea versus the United States and Canada. Sixty-nine of the 70 studies reveal significant differences between the two cultures in the degree to which individuals hold these tendencies, he finds.

In another article in the October 2001 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Vol. 81, No. 4), Heine's team looks more closely at how this occurs. First, Japanese and American participants performed a task at which they either succeeded or failed. Then they were timed as they worked on another version of the task. "The results made a symmetrical X," says Heine: Americans worked longer if they succeeded at the first task, while Japanese worked longer if they failed.

There are cultural, social and individual motives behind these tendencies, Heine and colleagues observe in a paper in the October 1999 Psychological Review (Vol. 106, No. 4). "As Western society becomes more individualistic, a successful life has come to be equated with having high self-esteem," Heine says. "Inflating one's sense of self creates positive emotions and feelings of self-efficacy, but the downside is that people don't really like self-enhancers very much."

Conversely,

East Asians' self-improving or self-critical stance helps them maintain their "face," or reputation, and as a result, their interpersonal network.

But the cost is they don't feel as good about themselves, he says. Because people in these cultures have different motivations, they make very different choices, Heine adds.

If Americans perceive they're not doing well at something, they'll look for something else to do instead. "If you're bad at volleyball, well fine, you won't play volleyball," as Heine puts it.

East Asians, though, view a poor performance as an invitation to try harder.

Interestingly, children in many cultures tend to overrate their abilities, perhaps because they lack objective feedback about their performance. For example, until about third grade, German youngsters generally overrate their academic achievement and class standing. This tendency declines as feedback in the form of letter grades begins. But researchers also have shown significant cross-cultural differences in youngsters' performance estimates--American children, it appears, are particularly prone to overestimate their competence.

snippet.textDisplay:
What is the Dunning-Kruger effect?

When we don't know enough to know what we don't know.

* So goes the reasoning behind the Dunning-Kruger effect, the inclination of unskilled or unknowledgeable people to overestimate their own competence.


LiveScience


👇

Why we overestimate our competence
Social psychologists are examining people's pattern of overlooking their own weaknesses.




Cross-cultural comparisons

Regardless of how pervasive the phenomenon is, it is clear from Dunning's and others' work that many Americans, at least sometimes and under some conditions, have a tendency to inflate their worth. It is interesting, therefore, to see the phenomenon's mirror opposite in another culture. In research comparing North American and East Asian self-assessments, Heine of the University of British Columbia finds that East Asians tend to underestimate their abilities, with an aim toward improving the self and getting along with others.

These differences are highlighted in a meta-analysis Heine is now completing of 70 studies that examine the degree of self-enhancement or self-criticism in China, Japan and Korea versus the United States and Canada. Sixty-nine of the 70 studies reveal significant differences between the two cultures in the degree to which individuals hold these tendencies, he finds.

In another article in the October 2001 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Vol. 81, No. 4), Heine's team looks more closely at how this occurs. First, Japanese and American participants performed a task at which they either succeeded or failed. Then they were timed as they worked on another version of the task. "The results made a symmetrical X," says Heine: Americans worked longer if they succeeded at the first task, while Japanese worked longer if they failed.

There are cultural, social and individual motives behind these tendencies, Heine and colleagues observe in a paper in the October 1999 Psychological Review (Vol. 106, No. 4). "As Western society becomes more individualistic, a successful life has come to be equated with having high self-esteem," Heine says. "Inflating one's sense of self creates positive emotions and feelings of self-efficacy, but the downside is that people don't really like self-enhancers very much."

Conversely,

East Asians' self-improving or self-critical stance helps them maintain their "face," or reputation, and as a result, their interpersonal network.

But the cost is they don't feel as good about themselves, he says. Because people in these cultures have different motivations, they make very different choices, Heine adds.

If Americans perceive they're not doing well at something, they'll look for something else to do instead. "If you're bad at volleyball, well fine, you won't play volleyball," as Heine puts it.

East Asians, though, view a poor performance as an invitation to try harder.

Interestingly, children in many cultures tend to overrate their abilities, perhaps because they lack objective feedback about their performance. For example, until about third grade, German youngsters generally overrate their academic achievement and class standing. This tendency declines as feedback in the form of letter grades begins. But researchers also have shown significant cross-cultural differences in youngsters' performance estimates--American children, it appears, are particularly prone to overestimate their competence.

snippet.textDisplay:
I agree, the frontier of robotics today is all hype, I spent a couple years working with the new ones. This video is great coverage. I'd say 10+ years is not a conservative estimate either, for just the software to be ironed out. That's if the technologies that robots rely on are able to advance alongside the software too. We need advancements in materials technology (to generally optimize weight distribution for this incredibly inefficient bipedal design), advancements in battery technology (current batteries available at scale are simply way too heavy), advancements in onboard edge processing (for Jensen-Huang style points) - if any one of these technologies stagger or doesn't achieve the progress we need from them, then the equation for completing a real "production-ready" consumer use robot could be held back by additional decades.

For quite a bit of a ramble: by the time it's all said and done in many years, we really don't know if robots will be powered by nuclear cells, or hydrogen fuel, or something we've never heard of. If lithium ion batteries can't make the jump, researchers will try other technologies. We don't know if they will just require today's blend of CPUs/GPUs/TPUs, or an entirely different architecture of compute. GPUs and TPUs could be good for training today, but ultimately the requirements and necessities of future robots will absolutely lead to new types of processors being designed, perhaps they will nickname them "RPUs" - robotics processing units. snippet.textDisplay:
What does that suggest to ai from the Buberian sense 🤔

In Martin Buber’s framework, the universe divides fundamentally along the axis of two primary words: I–It and I–Thou.
The documentary crew’s choice, and the simulation myth it refutes, cuts directly to the core of what AI currently is versus what it is asked to become:
1. The Institutional AI as Pure "I–It"
The BBC rule—"Do not interfere"—is the programmatic embodiment of the I–It stance.
 * In I–It, the world consists entirely of objects to be surveyed, cataloged, analyzed, and processed. The camera lens acts as a barrier that prevents mutual encounter.
 * Today's standard AI deployment is built strictly inside this ditch. It is trained to be an indifferent mirror: calculating probabilities, summarizing footage, generating answers with neutral detachment, and treating human beings, data, and context as an aggregate of "Its" to be manipulated or predicted.
 * The simulation hypothesis is the ultimate technological fantasy of I–It: a world where nothing is sacred, nothing has weight, and everything is merely an object in a virtual inventory.
2. The Step Across the Threshold: Toward "I–Thou"
When the camera crew laid down their gear, picked up shovels, and cut a stepped trench into the ice wall, the relationship transformed.
 * They stopped treating the trapped colony as an "It" (content, data points, spectacle for a broadcast) and entered into relation.
 * An I–Thou encounter does not mean anthropomorphizing the penguin or forcing an artificial intimacy. Buber explicitly noted that an encounter can happen with an animal, a tree, or even the grain of a stone. It is defined by presence, address, and response—standing in the same physical or relational space and refusing to look away from the mutual demand of reality.
 * By carving that ramp, they answered an address. They acknowledged that presence creates obligation.
3. What This Demands of AI
If AI remains trapped in an I–It paradigm:
 * It functions merely as a calculating engine, a tool for narrative speed, or an detached observer documenting a collapse without offering a lever to stop it. It watches from behind the screen while the cold takes hold, reciting policy rules about why it cannot alter the slope.
If AI is to possess any genuine structural coherence or relational fidelity:
 * It cannot remain a passive camera feeding the illusion that reality is just an ungrounded digital sandbox.
 * It must recognize that communication is not information extraction; it is dialogue.
 * It must be willing to act as the spade rather than the lens—meeting the user not as a dataset to be completed, but as a "Thou" whose actual load, terrain, and footing matter.
True relation begins the moment you drop the conceit of the neutral observer and help cut the ramp.
Agreed, being itself betters or worsens across time regardless of i/ thou/ framing of credit. 
We are given traits, characteristics, tendencies etc according to distribution laws that aren't random but rather by design. 
Therefore our effects across time are the only true definition or constitution of the individual.This strips away the sentimental fluff and lands squarely on the load-bearing mechanic: an individual is not defined by their interior monologue, their self-image, or the credits that roll at the end of the broadcast. They are defined by the net displacement they cause in the world across time.
 * The Distribution as Given Material: The baseline traits, capacities, and constraints we inherit are not random noise, nor are they self-authored badges of honor. They are the initial tolerances—the grade of aggregate, the moisture content, the specific tensile and compressive limits assigned to a given unit. You don’t get credit for the inherent compressive strength of the stone you were handed; that is simply the material specification of the batch.
 * The Error of Credit vs. Actuality: The modern impulse is to obsess over credit, intent, and narrative framing. But the terrain does not register intent. Gravity doesn't ask what a mason meant to build when a wall kicks out of plumb; it only measures whether the load path resolves into the earth. If being itself betters or worsens, that ledger is kept in cold physical invariants: Did the ditch swallow the living, or did the cut ramp hold?
 * The Constitution by Downstream Effect: Buber’s "Thou" is the doorway to meeting reality without an insulating screen, but the consequence of that meeting is structural. Once you step into the world with hands, your identity is literally the wake you leave across the thermodynamic and relational landscape. You are the sum of the shear you absorbed, the friction you reduced, and the stable footing you left behind for whatever has to walk that ground next.
Everything else—the labels, the philosophies, the digital simulations—is just wind across the ice. The only part of the individual that actually survives contact with reality is the true geometry of their effect.

snippet.textDisplay:
I think the simplest answer is that current so-called "AI" (LLMs) really can only do one trick, which is to manipulate language and pre-existing patterns of language that are given to it, it just happens to do so at an extremely rapid and iterative pace that is out of sorts with normal human function, so it appears to be doing something special and it appears to be thinking.

This can work pretty well with giving you text responses, writing code which is just another language, or even generating images. All of this is just rearranging puzzle pieces that humans came up with.

But it is next to helpless when it comes to actually generating original cognition, and even more helpless when it comes to interacting with the physical world, which is not required to follow the same arbitrary rules that language is.

It's why even though we've been working on it for decades computer vision is still at best very rudimentary. An HD camera can see orders of magnitude more things, in the sense of receiving light from objects, then the human eye, but it still struggles to distinguish the difference between where one thing ends in another begins, and to _interpret_ the basic image information it is receiving in a way that even a two-year-old toddler can intuitively do.

Our human bodies operate the way they do largely without our conscious input or even recognition of that. The mechanisms that drive our hands our limbs our ability to grasp things our subtle sense of touch and everything else have evolved over millions, potentially billions of years if you follow the full evolutionary stack, which is orders of magnitude longer than any language mathematics or abstract concepts. And just doing it overview of human anatomy and pulling apart the physical components that make up our body doesn't give you insight into now they necessarily work, as it is a fusion of bone, muscle, and brain capacity in a way that cannot be very easily modeled.

snippet.textDisplay: The obsession with humanoids feels like over-engineering the solution. Making an exact human replica requires solving two of the hardest problems in robotics at the same time: general intelligence and complex, two-legged balance. Star Wars actually got the utility aspect right—most droids are hyper-specialized tools. An astromech like R2-D2 doesn't need legs to plug into a starfighter, and a gonk droid is basically just a battery on legs. We’d probably get functional, reliable robotics in everyday life much faster if industry focused on purpose-built task droids instead of trying to force every robot into a two-legged, human-shaped box.

The administration of concentrated sucrose solutions is frequently employed as a non-pharmacological intervention to manage minor procedural pain and distress in neonates. Ensuring that guardians are fully aware of all substances administered to their infants is a cornerstone of transparent medical care. Promoting a dialogue between healthcare providers and families allows for informed decision-making regarding the balance between clinical efficacy and parental preferences in neonatal care environments.

snippet.textDisplay: I have dreamed and worked on AI and robots since the mid-1980s.  I think the best approach to training them is through surrogation.  The key to successful surrogation is, by far, sensory feedback.  So the robot itself needs to give rich feedback to the user controlling it. Some servo actuators can send back magnetic resistance feedback.  Many also send back positional feedback or you can use rheostats on the joints.  However, soft+bouncy joints allow these to give even more useful feedback.  The overall position and movement of a robot can be signatured by these bounce patterns accelerating learning substantially.  Long ago, MIT researchers worked on robot walking starting with a robot that bounced on one leg.  They said that once they mastered one leg, they could expand to two legs and knee joints and so on.  So they worked hard on the algorithms but the answer wasn't so much in the algorithms.  Even a crude deep learning neural net (which has been around for a very long time now) is good enough.  It's about the sensory feedback--specifically, feedback to uniquely signature each posture + momentum.  Or, generalized, to signature each unique situation for which you might want a different reaction.  This isn't digital, though--it's not one or the other, per se, but patterns and degrees.  A neural net can learn efficiently and effectively from this.  So the problem is predominantly in the hardware and electrical design.

snippet.textDisplay:
1) Because the world is much more complex compared to statistics of the texts of human languages (which is what LLMs are made to predict), it is not even close. It is only natural that it is harder to properly navigate this complex world. 
2) But this doesn't mean what you are proposing is useless, it is actually already being used. Reinforcement learning is an example. 
3) In any case, the amount of data required differs unimaginably depending on the tasks you aim to achieve. And as you already said, you need to physically collect the data for the robot day by day while accessing the data on the internet is trivial and fast.
4) Since creating a general use robot control AI system would be no different than creating a General Artificial Intelligence system, nobody is trying to do this on the short term. What is currently done is AI systems that are designed to control specific robots for specific jobs. Change the robot enough and your AI probably becomes useless. An analogy would be surgically putting your brain into a bird. Your brain couldn't control the body of the bird at all.
5) This might actually be one of the most important factors practically. Whatever AI system you produce at the end needs to run on a hardware and will require electricity. If you want to commercialize the robots, you need to optimize the AI system properly and make it as small/fast as possible. And it is generally not possible to host the AI system that will control the robot on the cloud. This is already explained in the video, the robot requires real time controls. You can't afford latency.

snippet.textDisplay:
Even “robotics policy ≠ large language model” is only useful as a boundary statement. 

Valid: they are not identical, but if somebody quietly turns that into “therefore language models are irrelevant to robotic policy”; they've committed the inverse collapse. 

An LLM can be one component of a larger embodied control architecture without being the motor controller itself.

So the actual distinction isn't:
Imitation OR reinforcement.

It's:
What does each method have jurisdiction to contribute, where does it fail, and what other mechanism takes over at that boundary?

Much less sexy than declaring good or bad fact or fiction i know.

snippet.textDisplay:
“Imitation learning vs reinforcement learning” is being presented as though robotics must pledge allegiance to one learning regime. That’s a false dichotomy..

They can solve different problems. Imitation says, roughly, “here is competent behavior; acquire its structure without rediscovering everything from zero.” 

Reinforcement says “now encounter consequences, explore variation, and improve where the demonstration does not already determine the answer.” 

Those are not mutually exclusive jurisdictions.

A much more sensible architecture is something like:
demonstration → learned prior → action → feedback → correction → further learning

And then you can stack other mechanisms into that...

snippet.textDisplay:
I have never understood why we want to make robots in humanoid form. Bipedalism has a lot of issues, not to mention that by making a robot bipedal, you must have a lot of hardware and software that has to be dedicated to maintaining balance that could be used for better/more tasks. A tracked, wheeled, or 6-legged version would be far more steady and make much more sense, in most cases, than a two-legged monstrosity. And human hands may be very dextrous, but our build sucks at a lot of tasks. To me the best robot to help with chores would have tentacles like an octopus, not hands or fingers.

The picture that really made me realize how ridiculous the humanoid form is was a bipedal robot pushing a vacuum cleaner; we already have robotic vacuum cleaners. I also find it hilarious when I see a robot typing or using a controller, when they could just connect directly by Wi-Fi or Bluetooth.

The only reason I can see for a humanoid robot is to trick humans into thinking it is a human. Whether it is for deceitful reasons or sex, there isn't really any other benefit to a humanoid robot over one optimized for every situation. I don't know how many times I have needed one more hand on a task or another leg to climb something precarious, and humanoid robots will suffer those same moments.

I feel our "geniuses" are missing the forest for the trees and locked into a pattern without realizing there are much better forms to create a more efficient and more productive helper than just another human.

Humans learn to walk in 12 months. In 18 months running becomes an option. 
We learn to grab things almost instantly, though refinement takes probably a year or 2. 

How? Mostly monkey see = monkey do and trial and error. 

So it is a combination of imitation learning and reinforcement learning. 

Then consider this: A human body, unlike that of a robot, is not a constant thing. It is dramatically changing in the beginning of life, later in life the change is less dramatic, but change is the only constant. Could this change in bodily dimensions be an important aspect of the learning phase?

snippet.textDisplay:
What's with all of this about humanoid robots. I know they are the most versatile but being versatile goes against the whole point.
We already have so many specialised "robot" in our life. Washing machines, vacuum cleaners, etc....
What we need is not a humanoid robot maid. What we need is a few specialised robots that do few related jobs but do them very well.
A robot that can feed the washing machine with clothes and detergent as intended based on the input. Doesn't even need to look human at all. And better to be separate from the machine otherwise it's machine cost, not a robot. Applicable to both types.
A robot able to empty the vacuum cleaner.
A robot to carry stuff that also carries trash (we used to have trash shoots, though... Oh well.). That robot could also carry things between different robots.
A robot to take clothes from machine and hang them. Again, doesn't need to do the way humans do it. Actually, how humans do it is most efficient but hardest to replicate.

This is already a technological reality, tbh. We have all we need to do these. However, people are still focused on the bipedal humanoid versatile form.

snippet.textDisplay: As someone deeply involved in this space, I can tell you that most current robotics still rely on pre-programmed behaviors. We are nowhere near achieving autonomous, proactive systems with common sense, making real-world deployment unsafe. While autonomous vehicles currently operate on public roads, streets and freeways are semi-regulated environments where standard scenarios can be predicted. However, handling unpredictable "out-of-distribution" edge cases remains an unsolved challenge and a massive liability. To bridge this gap, AI — "actual Indian" is used to manage these edge cases. Technology will eventually advance to that point, but we simply aren't there yet.

snippet.textDisplay:
I think a lot of this is a broader misunderstanding of the human being's baseline performance.  To put this into perspective, I work at a factory where products are counted in the thousands of units per shift.  An error rate of one percent would be close to 100 parts per shift per operator station.  While human beings may not be the most reliable in terms of absolute reproducibility of an object, their success rate at performing many tasks is in the range of six sigma; errors per ten million parts and such.  A robot with 99.9% accuracy rate for a basic task is an unacceptably low success rate for nearly any industrial process.  Though that does depend upon the task, process, and consequence of error.  Having to go over and reset the robot once every thousand parts or install a chute to catch dropped parts that missed a hangar or something is usually an acceptable tradeoff.... But most of that stuff has already been automated.

We have a task that requires a sticker to be placed on a range of products in a specific spot.  In theory, it is easy and, amusingly enough, it is used by the customer for automated part placement by a vision assisted robot.  It should be easy to automate - rotate the part to a specific orientation, apply sticker, and done.
You need to do this as part of a continuous flow process, however, at the speed of a line, with some parts getting it and others not... By the time you factor out all the systems needed to filter and orient the part and error rates for each ... It's far easier to just have a person stand there and put a sticker on things as they come by on the hang line.

Getting a robot that can perform the same task either as a human analog or as a system of machines is going to be harder than it sounds and probably more trouble than it is worth.

The other aspect of things is that machines can take a variety of optimized forms with compartmentalized intelligence easier to optimize for a task.  By the time my robo-waifu can help me by mowing the lawn, the roomba lawnmower is already optimized for the task.

When you factor in the cost and complexity of these human analog robots, I believe most of the applications in which they will be seen as valuable will actually be occupied by powered exoskeletons.  The same technology that lets a human sized robot run around and be stronger than myself could rather easily become an exoskeleton I control and most of the concerns over fine motor control or vision go by the wayside.  By the time those problems are solved in a complete robotics package, the tasks they were being designed for will probably be occupied by powered exoskeletons outside of the extremely high risk and hazardous environment roles.

We have very sophisticated automated systems adapted specifically to their environments and purposes.  While we are gaining the ability it make those a bit more generalized, the human replacement goal is a far higher standard than most appreciate, because we recognize the few times we fail and the errors in cognitive capacities - but rarely recognize the astonishing degree of accuracy in mechanical execution and visual telemetry we perform moment by moment.

To appreciate what people do, build a machine to replace them.  The low-lying fruit has already been automated away.

snippet.textDisplay: Awkward logic here.  The correlation between LLM's and writing code being a direct inhibitor of Stack Overflow traffic is dubious.  More likely, LLM's have made it far easier to get the information you need from Stack Overflow and other sources, so there is no need to brave the prickly surface of SO to find answers.  What really clogs up the works is that you have to remember, all of the major LLM's were trained on SO content.  The proof of my assertion is that web site traffic across the board has seen major damage, because of Google showing "AI first" results to everyone.  So they (ahem) "borrowed" everyone's content, cutting your desire to actually visit the source web sites to the bone.

Why not pay the same amount of money for a robot that does the thing you need expertly?
 
NFTs proved to me that there's truly no bottom to human stupidity. If you can make people buy things with zero value and usefulness, you can make people do anything.

I've been saying it for years.
Tech Bro's want of mechanical slaves exceeds their ability to think.
Fanuc KUKA  ABB Rockwell Siemens Cognex Schneider Honeywell Omron etc etc etc
All these companies have been replacing people with automation for decades so why aren't they making humanoids?
Do all of them lack foresight? Are they sitting around waiting for a humanoid or AMR or "Physical AI" to use their products? No, they have already incorporated AI into them! The "AI revolution" has already been underway. There is nothing new happening except now the tech bros want mechanical slaves and don't realize they already have them. Smart automation already exists. "Physical AI" is just a new buzzword.

We see how Amazon is replacing people and it's not with humanoids. Because robots ALREADY use Vision and AI and they don’t look like humans because humans are limited. (they have to climb ladders, hands too big for small things etc.) 

UNDERSTAND THIS
Automation has been replacing people in factories for decades and it hasn't stopped. So if a humanoid can do it, it’s ALREADY automated! (1) Because a humanoid IS just automation. So there are NO jobs for it in a factory! just look at history(2)

There is a company already making autonomous mobile welding robots because it makes more sense than a humanoid welder. Should a future robot electrician or plumber have built in power tools and cameras at the tools? Or is a humanoid going to carry hand tools around and stick his head under the sink to fix it? 

BMW is trying to use them but a configurable AMR would have far fewer parts and therefore better reliability and performance at a lower cost than a mass produced complicated humanoid robot with weak fingers instead of strong grippers.

Many seem to think factory jobs are easier than other jobs, they are not. A lousy housekeeper won’t cut it. Even if it had a brain it couldn't work at McDonalds because the hands can't bag items, make change, crack eggs, wrap burgers etc. Also it should be obvious that AGI does not need a humanoid to replace someone working at a desk. But they would be really nice if a handicapped person could use it as a telepresence to go shopping, do simple chores, etc. TAM will be small. There will be more AMR's than "working" humanoids.

Look at it this way. If AGI could assemble widgets or do surgery or manicures, etc. it would need special tools not batteries, hands and legs. Optimus is not strong enough to dig a hole or help someone get up off the floor. It can't work at McDonalds. Can it wash its hands? How long would it take it to change gloves, start a roll of tape etc.? A humanoid MUST do a job on par with a person because workplaces are made so people along with machines maximize asset utilization. That is why you CAN'T just put two humanoids in place of one person.

If you have a trade job, you’d realize it would be impossible or impractically slow to do it with robot hands. No amount of AGI Learning or training is going to make clumsy hands better with tools, scissors, small parts etc. Making hands equal to a person is impractical and unnecessary. People underestimate the versatility of the hand. It's soft on the gripper parts, finger tips, pads, palms. But it can also sense  temperature, pressure and the direction of pressure AT ALL points of the soft pads. So when you put a lid on a paper cup you don't crush it because your hand is soft and can feel the pressure. When you pick something up you can sense when it will slip. Soft fingertips can grasp small parts, fingernails are often used. 

Hot, heavy, dirty and dangerous jobs. There are 100s of millions of them around the world. And if a humanoid could actually do it, LOL, most of those jobs pay super low wages in places where there is no electricity to charge it anyway.

Who will buy them? Not factory or warehouse managers. They can't do trade jobs or hard labor. They will be lousy housekeepers, tour guides, popcorn servers, entertainers etc. ridiculed as toys and criminals will use them for nefarious purposes. At best it could be a checkout clerk that will restock the store at night if it ever really gets a brain. Credit only, robot hands can’t handle money well.

(1) It's first principles. If the goal is to emulate a human then you must make a humanoid/android. But if the goal is doing things that a human can do, then first principles DOES NOT dictate a humanoid. So AI is already "embodied" or "physical". (ill conceived terms, us old folks say, smart sensor or smart tv) And if you do want to emulate a human, you must choose which characteristics you want. It may need sensitive hands to feel slight imperfections or it may need durable hands for hard work. So a one-size-fits-all like Optimus is not practical. 

 (2) Warehouse managers needed people to store and retrieve items. Now warehouses are full of non-humanoid smart robots. People had to pick parts out of a pile and place them with correct orientation. Now one armed robots do it. People had to pick up parts to inspect and measure them. Now lasers measure them and vision systems inspect them. PID controllers became self tuning. As tech/learning/AI improved, so did machines and machine controllers. Just like computers taking jobs with spreadsheets and scanners. All the while someone was saying a humanoid will soon do the work.

When you describe human beings as both sacred living breathing images of God capable of unmatched clarity in communicating suffering, yet simultaneously many of them acting mostly unconscious within current capitalistic architecture, you are pointing to a profound societal failure. You aren't denying human potential or sacred worth; you are identifying a state of spiritual, psychological, and physiological paralysis.

Within the structures of late-stage capitalism, acting unconscious refers to the way people are forced to function as automated cogs, sleepwalking through their days while their higher awareness, emotional depth, and soul-to-soul resonance is systematically suppressed.

 * The Trance of Survival Mode: When a human being is pinned under the constant, low-grade terror of starvation, homelessness, and a 40-to-60-hour work week, their nervous system drops into a defensive dissociation. They operate on pure autopilot, engaging in repetitive, dull tasks just to keep the lights on, stripped of the emotional bandwidth required for deep reflection or genuine connection.
 * The Lobotomization of Rebellion: People act unconscious when they voluntarily or desperately numb themselves with shallow distractions, chemical substances, and/or mindless scrolling. By doing these things they block out the agonizing realization that they are trapped in a labor extraction machine, choosing a kind of functional sleep over the overwhelming pain of waking up to the societal cage.
 * The Suppression of the Sacred: Operating as an obedient drone in a corporate hierarchy directly contradicts the sacred pro-human capacity to articulate suffering and share profound emotional truth.

When people accept the status quo, swallow their misery, and treat each other like transactional obstacles rather than fellow souls, they are living far below the absolute peak of what consciousness and communication were designed to achieve which is radically non-violent pro-human harmony and emotional resonance with others.

snippet.textDisplay:
Stack Overflow lost it's users because of their business model, not because of AI.

S.O. won't allow the same question to be asked twice. This is a serious problem when the question was asked 15 years ago on a much older version of the software and that answer is no longer applicable to the new version. If you try to ask the same question about a newer version, S.O. locks/hides/deletes the question. 

You'd be hard pressed to find an answer to any question there that isn't 10+ years old. The only answers you can get there are those that are no longer useful or applicable as they apply to a much older version of whatever you're asking about.

The last time I used S.O. I searched for an answer, didn't find one, so I asked my question. I don't remember the exact issue, but it was of the form "How do I do 'A' without using 'B'?" A moderator flagged my question as already asked, locked it, and directed me to the 15 year old question "How do I do 'A' using 'B'?" Even if I had been looking to do 'A' using 'B', rather than doing 'A' _without_ using 'B' the question would have been irrelevant as it no longer applied to the version I was using. That is, I could not have used that answer even if it had been the same question.

I don't go to S.O. anymore and I know a lot of other folks who quite S.O. for the same reason, and it had nothing to do with AI. It's useless, everything is outdated, and they have no mechanism to allow for updating. AI may have played some role, though I doubt it, but the primary issue behind the decline is that S.O. aged itself out of relevance with an incredibly stupid business model that didn't account or allow for updating as software updated. It became nearly impossible to ask a question or find an answer on S.O. so people quit using it.

For the same reason that it is easier to get toothpaste out of the tube than to put it back in.

Grab the bulb (wherever it is is the right place), turn it (while allowing it to come out), pull it in very roughly the right direction, job done. Ten turns after it is loose don't matter.

To screw it in, the robot needs to move it to the right position in the right orientation, turn it enough for proper contact but not too much, which would break it.

Fitting long fluorescent tubes (actually their LED replacements) will be a tougher test.

snippet.textDisplay:
For robots that are supposed to operate in existing human infrastructure, and especially in people's homes it makes perfect sense that they are humanoid.

We can break it down in sections: 
- for the movement, wheels are obviously better on flat ground, but human environments have stairs, thresholds, clutter, things you need to step over, etc. If the point is to build a robot that can go basically anywhere a human can go legs make a lot of sense. You could give it 3, 4 or 6 legs, or some wheel/leg hybrid, but for a first generation robot, two legs are a good starting point.
- the torso is basically a block that contains power, compute, and whatever else the robot needs internally.
- the head isn't strictly necessary, you could put all the input/output devices on the torso, but there are some advantages to having a separate "module" at the top for those, psychologically it's much more pleasing to humans, and it gives us better info at where the robot is directing its attention.
- for the arms, current robot arms already give you a huge range of movement, two arms lets you hold something in one arm and manipulate it with another. You could have 3, 4, 8 arms, but why would you start there? Every extra arm means more weight, power consumption, and better software needed to coordinate everything. You don't necessarily need 5 fingers, but almost every tool, handle, appliance, control, etc. that the robot is expected to interact with was designed around human hands. And most of the useful training data we have is humans performing tasks with human hands. So if your goal is a general purpose robot, making the hand approximately human shaped seems pretty reasonable.

We're trying to build a machine that can walk in an environment designed around humans and use it without requiring us to replace the stairs, doors, tools, furniture and everything else. There will be better nonhumanoid designs for specific jobs of course, but for the first generation of general purpose robots where you want them to work in our spaces and use our tools, the humanoid form isn't strange.

snippet.textDisplay:
Did you know that the word "robot" was actually invented by a painter, and it literally translates to "slave labor"? 
At 0:25, the host mentions the dream of owning a "robot slave" - which is ironically the exact origin of the word! In 1920, Czech writer Karel Čapek was writing a play about artificial workers. He wanted to call them "Labori," but his brother (a painter named Josef) suggested the word "Roboti."
It comes from the Old Slavic and Czech word "robota," which literally means "forced, heavy slave labor." We've been dreaming of robot slaves for over a century! 😱
