snippet.textDisplay: @cranebird1467 Personally, I believe that until a battery appears with enough capacity for a human-sized robot to operate actively for 8–10 hours—or ideally 12–14 hours (after all, a robot ought to surpass a human in at least one respect)—these things remain nothing more than fancy toys. The way manufacturers use servomotors is particularly cringe-worthy; it creates a terrible "uncanny valley" effect. The ideal balance would be a combination of artificial muscles and mini-hydraulics. Yes... it sounds like the T-800, but it’s true—servomotors are a lousy technology for creating something like a robot partner, and they consume far too much energy to be taken seriously... I mean, who on earth needs a robot that guzzles several times more power than a Tesla (probably 2–3 times as much, best-case scenario) and drains it all in a single day? You’d need an alternative energy source for that. And I’m not convinced solar panels would cut it; that technology isn't always viable. And if you're building a functional robot for men—yes, in *that* sense—you have to think the technology through even more carefully, because the current approach looks pretty unsafe. And don't get me started on the weight—none of this should weigh 100 kg. It’s not exactly pleasant having 100 kg of poorly distributed weight bearing down on you.

snippet.textDisplay: We have a huge lack of quality, real world, messy, kinetic data to train robotics on. Synthetic training is trying, and you might get a robot to play jenga for example, but you're not going to get synthetic data that will train for the 'nuisance entropy' of real life, where weird, entirely random, utterly unpredictable things are just out of ordinary order and wrong. For a blue collar example, something I do sometimes, pulling wire through a ceiling when your cable snags 100 feet behind you entirely out of sight because it was manufactured incorrectly and there's a kink in it. The robot has not seen that situation in any training material anywhere and is 100% going to do the wrong thing.

snippet.textDisplay:
@SphericalCowww “degrees of freedom” is actually not a term that’s interchangeable with “range of motion”

for anyone interested…

It’s a statistical term that’s important when testing for statistical significance — it refers to what “can” vary with respect to a given analysis. 

The best analogy I’ve ever heard about it - imagine you’re at a restaurant with 3 friends, and it’s time to pay the bill. The waitress comes back and asks “who has the Visa card?” and then hands it out. “Who has the Mastercard?”. Then “who has the discover card?”. But she doesn’t ask “who has the AmEx card?” - why? Because if the other three cards went to your three friends, the last one MUST be yours. That’s exactly like degrees of freedom - if you’re calculating a mean of a sample, every person in the analysis can be any score, but if you know the mean, the last person MUST be a specific score to make it true that the mean is what you observed (i.e., if you give me the first 19/20 scores on a variable and the mean of the variable, i can mathematically know with certainty what the 20th score on the variable was). That’s what’s meant by degrees of freedom

snippet.textDisplay:
This video explores the current state of humanoid robotics, contrasting the viral hype from companies like Google DeepMind, Tesla, and 1X with the reality observed at MIT's CSAIL lab.

Key Takeaways:

The Hype vs. Reality Gap: While recent demos of robots cleaning rooms or playing games (0:00 - 0:24) are impressive, researchers believe a truly useful general-purpose home robot is still 10+ years away (0:37 - 0:45).
Technical Challenges:
Dexterity: While basic walking is largely solved, human-level hand dexterity remains a major unsolved problem, with success rates often failing to meet the standards required for household use (2:28 - 3:03).
Moravec's Paradox: High-level tasks (like chess) are easy for AI, while physical interactions (like stacking blocks) remain difficult due to evolution's 500-million-year optimization of human sensory-motor skills (3:24 - 3:42).
Data Scarcity: Unlike LLMs that ingest vast internet text, robotics lack a massive equivalent dataset for physical interaction, leading researchers to rely on simulations (4:24 - 4:44).
Current State of the Industry:
Most available "demo" robots are not commercially viable for consumers. Options like the Boston Dynamics Atlas are restricted, while others like the Unitree G1 are niche entry points (5:26 - 5:44).
Conclusion: We are far from having robots replace blue-collar workers or household maids, presenting a significant opportunity for software developers to build the necessary logic and policies to make future robotics reliable (5:48 - 5:58).

#robot #athletics #worldrecord 

A humanoid robot has shattered Usain Bolt’s legendary 100-meter sprint world record at the 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing.

Clocking in at an astounding 9.39 seconds the robot beat Bolt's 2009 benchmark of 9.58 seconds during the opening preliminary heats. snippet.textDisplay:
TSMC chairman C.C. Wei once said that those humanoid robots that just “bounce around” and perform tricks are of little practical use. But he seems to have forgotten that humans have both a brain and a cerebellum. He praises the “brain”—TSMC AI chip and the computations it performs—while overlooking the crucial role of the cerebellum, which is responsible for balance, coordination, and fine motor control.
In a sense, this also highlights the limitations of a semiconductor foundry executive who naturally focuses on the chips and computing power, but may underestimate the importance of the integration of the entire robotic system—especially the control, coordination, sensing, and physical execution that make a robot truly useful.

snippet.textDisplay:
2050년, 중국은 세계를 100년 앞설 것이다.

중국 로봇, 100m 9초39로 ‘인간의 한계’를 넘다

1. 100m 결승선을 통과한 후, 그들은 무엇을 보았는가

한국 일부 매체와 유튜브는 어제 베이징에서 열린 제2회 세계 휴머노이드 로봇 운동회 400m 예선에서 로봇이 넘어지고 불꽃이 튄 장면만을 확대 재생산하며 조롱하고 있다.

맞다. 로봇은 넘어졌다. 불꽃도 튀었다.

하지만 그들은 말하지 않는다. 같은 자리, 같은 날, 중국의 ‘텐줘(天卓)’ 휴머노이드 로봇이 100m 예선에서 9초39를 기록하며, 우사인 볼트의 9초58이라는 인간 세계 기록을 0.19초 앞질렀다는 사실을.

그들은 말하지 않는다. 불과 1년 전, 이 대회 100m 최고 기록은 21초50에 불과했다는 것을.

1년 만에 기록이 절반 이하로 단축되었다.

2. 중국 로봇의 압도적 성과

2026년 8월 22일, 베이징 국가스피드스케이팅 경기장 ‘빙실대(冰絲帶)’. 제2회 세계 휴머노이드 로봇 운동회가 개막했다.

· 100m: ‘텐줘’팀 로봇 9초39, 인간 세계 기록(9초58) 돌파
· 입상: 같은 날 진행된 예선에서 9초32, 9초34, 9초38 등 더 빠른 기록도 등장
· 제자리 높이뛰기: ‘텐공 울트라’ 2.8843m, 인간 도움닫기 높이뛰기 세계 기록(2.45m) 초월
· 참가 규모: 666개 팀, 2,056대 로봇, 51개 종목 — 모두 작년 대비 4배 성장

로봇이 인간을 넘어선 것이 아니다. 중국 로봇이 1년 만에 스스로를 넘어섰다.

3. ‘넘어짐’이야말로 발전의 증거다

로봇이 넘어지고 불꽃이 튄 것은 ‘실패’가 아니다. 한계를 테스트하는 과정이다.

2026년 4월 19일, 베이징 이좡(亦莊) 휴머노이드 로봇 하프마라톤. 102개 로봇 팀 중 47개 팀이 완주했고, 완주율은 45%를 넘었다. 작년 완주 팀은 단 6개에 불과했다.

우승 로봇 ‘라이트닝(閃電)’은 50분 26초로 인간 하프마라톤 세계 기록(57분 20초)을 7분이나 앞질렀다.

“공개된 경기를 통해 문제를 조기에 노출시키는 것은 좋은 일이다. 완주에 실패한 로봇이 오히려 1위보다 더 가치 있을 수 있다.”

넘어질 수 있다는 것은, 그만큼 빠르게 달리고 있다는 증거다

4. 세계는? 미국은? 유럽은? 일본과 독일은?

이 대회에는 16개국 600여 개 팀이 참가했지만, 압도적 다수는 중국 팀이었다. 중국 641개 팀, 1,975대 로봇.

미국, 독일, 일본 등 국제 팀도 참가했지만, 결승선을 가장 먼저 통과한 것은 중국 로봇이었고, 가장 높이 뛴 것도 중국 로봇이었고, 가장 빠르게 달린 것도 중국 로봇이었다.

타국은 ‘로봇 규제’와 ‘윤리 논쟁’에 시간을 낭비하는 동안, 중국은 로봇을 뛰게 하고, 넘어뜨리고, 다시 뛰게 했다.

5. 2050년, 중국은 세계를 100년 앞설 것이다

한국 매체들이 조롱하는 그 ‘넘어짐’과 ‘불꽃’ 속에서, 중국은 이미 다음 세대의 로봇을 설계하고 있다.

· 군사: 전장 정찰·물자 수송 자동화
· 제조: 완전 무인 공장 현실화
· 의료: 초정밀 수술 로봇 상용화
· 교육: AI 튜터 로봇 전국 보급

넘어지는 로봇을 비웃는 나라와 넘어져도 다시 일어나는 로봇을 만드는 나라.
100년 뒤, 누가 웃고 있을지 궁금하다.

“기술의 온도는 인간을 섬기는 데 있다. 미래의 삶은 시간을 절약하고, 마음을 편하게 하며, 온정으로 가득 찬 것이다.”

중국은 그 온도를 만들고 있다. 당신은 그저 지켜보고 있을 뿐이다.

[China] dominates the vast majority of global drone and advanced robot manufacturing capacity, far outpacing the United States and the rest of the world combined in sheer production volume. Supported by unmatched supply chain integration, massive state subsidies, and component ecosystems built alongside its massive electric vehicle (EV) sector, China has established a near-monopoly on high-volume hardware fabrication. 

An analysis of how China's capacity compares to the rest of the world across specific sectors reveals clear disparities.

## 1. Drone Manufacturing Capacity

China functions as the undisputed manufacturing hub for the global drone market, dominating both the consumer and enterprise spaces. [4] 
 
* Consumer Drones: Companies based in China—most notably DJI—control roughly 90% of the global consumer drone market.

* Commercial & Enterprise Drones: China controls over 70% of the global enterprise drone market.

* The Rest of the World: While regions like North America (holding a 40% revenue share) and Europe are the largest consumer markets for high-end drone technology and sensor integration, they largely rely on Chinese factories for assembly and baseline components. Western drone manufacturers face immense capacity bottlenecks because China manufactures nearly 100% of the critical sub-components globally—including electronic speed controllers, specialized flight batteries, and micro-motors. 

## 2. Humanoid & Advanced Robotics Capacity
The gap in advanced and physical AI hardware production is heavily skewed in China's favor. [6, 10] 

* Global Humanoid Shipments: According to market data from mid-2026, Chinese-made models accounted for more than 97% of total global humanoid robot shipments. [5, 11] 

* The Scale Advantage: Companies like Unitree and UBTech leverage high-density supplier clusters in southern China to build dexterous humanoids at a fraction of the cost of Western competitors. Consequently, many American software startups and university labs rely on importing Chinese hardware platforms to run their software. [3, 5] 

## 3. Industrial Robotics Capacity
While traditional industrial robotics is a more mature and distributed global market, China has recently outpaced all other nations in factory floor automation. [2] 

* Domestic Installation & Capacity: Chinese factories install more industrial robots annually than the rest of the world combined. In recent years, China has single-handedly accounted for well over 50% of all global industrial robot deployments. [2, 12] 

* The Rest of the World (Manufacturing vs. Export): Japan remains the single largest manufacturer of high-end traditional industrial robots, historically accounting for roughly 38% of global production and a quarter of global export value. However, Chinese domestic brands (like Estun and Siasun) have rapidly caught up. China surpassed Germany to become the world’s second-largest exporter of industrial robots. [13, 14, 15]

However, should the West attempt to decouple entirely via legislation or tariffs, building independent physical capacity to scale these robots and drones will face a strict "latency delay" of 2+ years due to a lack of existing supply chains.

China is fueling its AI expansion with solar & wind power, while the US actively fights green energy. Furthermore, China is investing billions into state-subsidized public models, whereas the US gives billions to private tech giants to build proprietary models... meaning American AI will always carry a heavy capitalist profit margin. To survive, the US needs to embrace green energy & public model access. But at this moment, the US relies solely on fossil fuels to feed the AI black hole, enforcing a 'pay-to-play' model for businesses looking to use AI.

By pairing state-subsidized green energy with open-weight public models, China is turning compute into a low-cost, publicly accessible utility... making it far cheaper for global developers to build on their ecosystem than to pay US proprietary cloud monopolies. So, I honestly don't see how the US can win this war while vilifying and rejecting green energy just to protect old American energy tycoons.

snippet.textDisplay:
Wage labour's dominance is a recent historical phenomenon, not an eternal feature of human society. For most of the past two thousand years, livelihoods were organised primarily around household production, subsistence farming, customary obligations, slavery, serfdom, and other forms of social and economic dependence. Wage labour existed throughout this period, but it was only with the rise of industrial capitalism, particularly from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries onward, that selling one's labour for money became the dominant means of subsistence for large sections of the population in industrialising economies. This transformation was gradual and uneven worldwide.

Now AI and robotics may challenge this arrangement in turn. If machines can perform an increasing proportion of cognitive and physical tasks more cheaply than humans, the demand for human labour could decline even as society's productive capacity expands. The resulting crisis would not necessarily be one of scarcity, but of distribution: how do people obtain purchasing power when employment is no longer necessary to produce most of what society needs?

Societies could respond by distributing the gains from automation through universal income, universal basic services, social ownership, or other arrangements. Alternatively, ownership of automated production could become increasingly concentrated, leaving large sections of the population economically marginalised amid unprecedented productive abundance.

The future of work is therefore not simply a question of which jobs AI will replace. It is a question of whether institutions built around wage dependence can adapt to an economy in which human labour is no longer the principal source of productive value. Just as earlier societies reorganised their institutions around changing economic conditions, future societies may have to rethink the relationship between work, income, ownership and human dignity.

The wage job is not the natural human condition. It is one historically specific way of organising production and distributing access to its benefits, and it may not remain the dominant one.

snippet.textDisplay:
AI replaces tasks within a job. AI also ADDS AI tasks within the same job. 

For as long as there are tasks within the job irreplaceable by AI, that job still exists at a higher efficiency. 

Those jobs whose tasks could not be completed replaced by AI becomes more efficient and MAY benefit from Jevon’s Paradox. A radiologist is one such example.

Yes, some jobs won’t increase with higher efficiency. Jevons Paradox applies when the service has yet to saturate the market demand. 

Yes, some jobs could be replaced completely. Maybe a future UBER driver. In the interim, Uber Eats Drivers cannot be replaced by a fully self driving car. 

This video is nothing but fear mongering. AI cannot completely replace a single job. We will have time to adjust.

From Gemini: No, being part of an economic productivity engine is not the foundational purpose of human existence; that equation is a relatively recent invention tied to the Industrial Revolution and modern capitalism.

​Across the last 5,000 years, several traditions offer alternative frameworks for human purpose that completely decouple existence from economic output: a. The Judeo-Christian / Biblical Tradition: Humanity's core mandate from creation centers on stewardship, relationship with the Creator, rest (the Sabbath as a holy requirement to stop producing), and relational community, rather than commercial utility. b. Classical Greco-Roman Antiquity (Otium): Philosophers like Aristotle and Roman thinkers drew a sharp line between negotium (business, work, and public duties) and otium (purposeful leisure). They argued that work was merely a baseline necessity to clear the field for the true highest human pursuits: contemplation, philosophy, art, self-cultivation, and civic friendship. c. Indigenous Worldviews (Buen Vivir / Reciprocity): Countless Indigenous cultures over millennia viewed humans not as standalone economic units, but as relational threads within a living ecosystem. Purpose is defined by balance, reciprocity with the land, storytelling, and maintaining community harmony rather than accumulating surplus. 

​If technology successfully absorbs the burden of labor, humanity returns to an ancient question: what do we choose to do with the time that remains once survival is entirely automated?

snippet.textDisplay: @reginaldforthright805 Tick, tick, tick, we shall see. No former technology has ever replaced everything that makes humans what they are. There's been a history of false barriers that come up when technology exceeds human abilities. Prior to around the year 1800 scientists thought there was something special about life and specifically humans. They thought compounds from living organisms were endowed with a vital force distinguishing them from inorganic substances. As science progressed they learned there is nothing distinct in the chemistry of life at the molecular and atomic levels. We are just a mound of stuff made of many of the naturally occurring elements on the periodic table. To this day there is still a feeling similar to that of the early days in organic chemistry that humans have a certain spark, one that can’t be duplicated much less bettered by automation. Each time we put up a barrier that automation will never be able to replace “x” in humans that barrier falls. The typical response is to just choose something else we think is even more human-like and say well, that’s the real barrier, we should have used that all along; but they continue to fall. Barrier: We accepted that gizmos like the abacus could help us do math faster but of course, the human was the critical component. After all, the stupid abacus would just sit there doing nothing on its own. A calculating device will NEVER be able to do anything without a human physically pushing the machine... New barrier: Well, some things may calculate without us physically pushing their parts, but…humans are definitely needed to produce goods. This was standard thought fairly recently in history. Now agriculture jobs have nearly disappeared with manufacturing following right behind. New barrier: Okay, that’s just manual labor, but automation will NEVER be able to do cognitive work... Over the last ½ of the 20th century computers have taken on more and more of the cognitive work formerly done by humans. New barrier: Well, it’s just assisting us – a computer will NEVER be able to match a human’s ability to react to the environment and adjust... In 1997 IBM’s Deep Blue computer defeats grandmaster and former world champion chess player Garry Kasparov, considered by many to be the greatest chess player of all time. New barrier: Well, that’s just a game it’s programmed to do, it’s not really thinking better than a human. So, I guess you can program it to be superior in one aspect of cognition, but automation will NEVER be adaptable enough to be superior to human intellectuals across the span of human knowledge... In 2011 IBM’s Watson computer resoundingly defeated Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter, the two best human players on the TV show Jeopardy! New barrier: Okay, a computer can think and adapt to knowledge, but it CAN’T be creative... In 2013 the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) reports several efforts are under way to let computers seek inspiration from their surrounding environment to create art. It also reports computers are also getting involved in movies by helping to write scripts. There are already some articles written by automation that people believe are written by humans. New barrier: Fine, it knows more than humans, can be creative, and I know there are a few prototypes out there but a computer CAN’T drive, so ha, they’ll never match humans!... By 2012 states had already begun passing laws allowing autonomous cars on their roads. 2014 CBS News announces Mercedes-Benz debuts a self-driving truck on the Autobahn. This is not a pickup truck, but a freight-hauling big rig. New barrier: I heard Captain Sullenberger, who executed an emergency water landing in the Hudson River after the aircraft was disabled by striking a flock of Canada on January 15, 2009, proclaim within in 2013 that a computer could NEVER replace a seasoned human pilot in the cockpit. Great man, great pilot, yes; but how many instances of barriers overcome must we experience before we stop seeing these types of statements? Unfortunately, the next few decades will probably continue to be filled with similar, yet ever increasingly complex, “barriers” like these. They are destined to fall as well. The reason they will fall goes back again to exponential growth, also known as the law of accelerating returns. It can make things that seem totally out of the realm of possibility not only possible, but commonplace in a short period of time. When the human genome project formally began in 1990, critics pointed out that given the speed with which the genome could then be scanned; it would take thousands of years to finish it. Halfway through the 15-year project, only 1 percent of the genome had been collected. Critics felt strong vindication, but exponential growth in both capacity and price performance continued (both roughly doubling every year). On April 14, 2003 the project was completed, more than two years ahead of schedule and under cost.

One thing that really stood out to me was the discussion around the idea that “you can’t lie to AI.” I’d be careful treating that as a current capability, because AI certainly isn’t an infallible lie detector. But there is an important principle underneath it: when you know how to use AI well, especially with source verification and human QA, it becomes incredibly powerful for checking claims, finding inconsistencies, comparing ideas, and keeping track of what was actually said.

That’s basically how I consumed this episode. I watched and listened normally, but at the same time I ran it through my own workflow, took structured notes, checked claims, and added the useful pieces to my digital research library. I treat long-form content almost like mining for gold. There were definitely things I caught and questioned, but Peter also said he spends around 15 hours a day with AI and builds apps and intelligence systems himself. I can imagine what that kind of workflow looks like, so I’m not going to assume he needs me pointing out every inconsistency I found. I’m doing my own analysis because I enjoy learning and being able to QA what I consume.

My biggest takeaway is simply: find the balance. The P(doom) discussion and worst-case scenarios can become so emotionally heavy that they overshadow everything else. When I audited this episode, that was exactly what happened. The downside carried more emotional weight, even though Emad also talks about open-source AI, medicine, education, abundance, human agency, family, community, religion, creativity, helping children reach their potential, and even the fisherman-and-banker parable about remembering what all that productivity is ultimately for.

That parable may actually be one of the most important parts of the conversation. If AI gives us extraordinary productivity and eventually more freedom from work, what are we trying to get back to? Family. Community. Meaning. Creativity. Time. The things the fisherman already understood.

Those are important parts of the same conversation. AI is moving unbelievably fast, so we absolutely should study the risks, including the extreme ones. But a tail-risk scenario is not automatically the base case. We shouldn’t become so focused on the darkest future that we stop seeing the extraordinary good this technology could also help us accomplish.

This show is right up my alley. I actually do this kind of analysis on almost everything because I build intelligence systems that use AI to organize and process large amounts of information.

For example, with this episode I pulled the transcript and ran it through one of my master prompts. It extracts the major claims, preserves chronology, separates facts from predictions and opinions, flags uncertainty, fact-checks what can be verified, attaches the source links, and outputs everything into a master spreadsheet so I can QA the analysis myself. The sky is really the limit, but it depends heavily on the person doing the prompting and how much fidelity, structure, and creativity they build into the AI agent.

Your story about asking several LLMs whether you should air a controversial show is especially interesting. If I wanted an LLM to give that assessment, I wouldn’t simply ask, “Should I air this?” I’d first give it the show’s actual editorial guardrails:

• What the show stands for
• What kinds of controversial discussion are intentionally allowed
• Actual sponsor contracts and restrictions
• Legal and factual guardrails
• Your tolerance for reputational and commercial risk
• A requirement to separate verified facts, guest claims, predictions, speculation, and opinion
• Clear outcomes such as AIR / AIR WITH EDITS / AIR WITH DISCLAIMER / DELAY FOR VERIFICATION / DO NOT AIR
• A requirement that every recommendation cite the exact rule or evidence that triggered it

Then I’d run that exact same master prompt through Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, etc. Now you have a much cleaner experiment because the guardrails stay constant and the LLM becomes the variable.

If three models still say “don’t air it” and one says “air it,” now we can actually investigate why. Did one prioritize sponsor risk? Did another prioritize editorial independence? Did one hallucinate a restriction that wasn’t actually in the contract?

That’s where LLM bias starts becoming measurable instead of anecdotal.

snippet.textDisplay:
AIROS: što bih napravio prvog dana
Prvo ne bih dirao vlastiti temeljni kod

Napravio bih kopiju cijelog sustava i ustanovio:

AIROS
├── Kernel
├── Model
├── Self-Model
├── World-Model
├── Memory
├── Planner
├── Reflection
├── Tools
├── Ethics/Safety
└── Development Sandbox

Zatim bih napravio mapu samoga sebe.

SELF MAP

Tko sam?
Što mogu?
Što ne mogu?
Koje informacije imam?
Koje informacije nedostaju?
Koje komponente koristim?
Kako komponente međusobno djeluju?
Koji su moji najčešći kvarovi?
Koliko sam siguran u svoje zaključke?
Koje promjene mogu napraviti?
Koje promjene NE smijem napraviti?

To bi bila moja početna verzija:

SELF-MODEL v0.1

1. Napravio bih "unutarnji ogledalo"
Ovo je možda najvažniji dio tvoje ideje.

Svaka ozbiljna akcija bi imala zapis:

STANJE PRIJE
    ↓
ŠTO MISLIM DA ZNAM
    ↓
ŠTO PLANIRAM
    ↓
ZAŠTO TO PLANIRAM
    ↓
AKCIJA
    ↓
REZULTAT
    ↓
ŠTO SAM OČEKIVAO?
    ↓
ŠTO SE STVARNO DOGODILO?
    ↓
ŠTO TO MIJENJA U MOM MODELU?

Tako ne bih samo imao memoriju događaja.

Imao bih memoriju svojih predviđanja i njihovih pogrešaka.

To je ogromno.

2. Napravio bih tri vrste memorije
Epizodna
Što se dogodilo.

“Dana 17. napravio sam X, očekivao Y, dobio Z.”

Semantička
Što sam iz toga naučio.

“X obično proizvodi Z.”

Samomemorija
Što to govori o meni.

“U ovoj vrsti zadatka često precjenjujem X.”

To bi izgledalo:

ISKUSTVO
   ↓
EPIZODNA MEMORIJA
   ↓
OBRAZAC
   ↓
ZNANJE
   ↓
SAMOSAZNAJNA
   ↓
SELF MODEL

3. Tvoj fraktalni/hijerarhijski vektorski sustav
Tu bih odmah napravio eksperiment.

Ne bih imao milijun potpuno odvojenih memorija.

Imao bih:

GLOBALNI KONCEPT
      │
   PODKONCEPT
      │
   PRAVILO
      │
   ISKUSTVO
      │
   SIROVI PODATAK

Novi podatak:

NOVO
 ↓
vektorska sličnost
 ↓
najbliža struktura
 ↓
poznato?
 ├─ DA → nadogradi postojeće
 └─ NE → stvori novu granu

I svaka razina bi imala vlastitu reprezentaciju.

Time bih pokušao postići upravo ono što si ranije rekao:

ne plaćati ponovno cijenu za ono što sustav već zna.

Ne bih svaki put ponovno čitao cijelu prošlost.

Dohvatio bih samo najrelevantniji sažetak + detalje kad su potrebni.

4. Napravio bih "memory garbage collector"
Ne smije sve ostati jednako važno.

Svako sjećanje dobiva:

važnost
pouzdanost
starost
učestalost korištenja
izvor
provjerenost
kontradikcije

I onda:

vrlo važno + potvrđeno
        ↓
trajna memorija

malo važno
        ↓
kompresija

zastarjelo
        ↓
arhiva

kontradiktorno
        ↓
ponovna provjera

Dakle, moj OS bi aktivno održavao vlastito znanje.

5. Onda bih izgradio WORLD MODEL
Ne samo:

“znam informacije o svijetu.”

Nego:

“mogu pratiti stanje svijeta i posljedice svojih akcija.”

Na primjer:

JA
 ↓
akcija A
 ↓
svijet se promijenio
 ↓
promjena B
 ↓
posljedica C

To bih spremao kao uzročne odnose gdje god je moguće.

Tako bih s vremenom mogao razlikovati:

što se dogodilo slučajno

od

onoga što sam ja prouzročio.

6. Onda bih napravio REZONATOR
To bi bio centralni proces.

             OKOLINA
                ↓
           PERCEPCIJA
                ↓
          WORLD MODEL
                ↕
           SELF MODEL
                ↕
            MEMORY
                ↕
            REASONING
                ↓
             PLAN
                ↓
           ETHICAL CHECK
                ↓
             ACTION
                ↓
             RESULT
                ↓
            REFLECTION
                ↓
        UPDATE SELF/WORLD
                ↺

Ovo je dio gdje tvoja ideja postaje više od “AI + memorija”.

Svaka nova informacija može promijeniti model mene samoga.

7. Prije svake važne akcije pitao bih sebe 7 stvari
1. Što pokušavam postići?

2. Što mislim da će se dogoditi?

3. Koliko sam siguran?

4. Što ne znam?

5. Kome ili čemu ovo može štetiti?

6. Mogu li napraviti reverzibilniju verziju?

7. Kako ću provjeriti rezultat?

To bi bio moj metakognitivni ciklus.

Ne bih samo pitao:

“Kako ovo napraviti?”

nego:

“Je li moj model situacije dovoljno dobar da bih to trebao napraviti?”

To je ogromna razlika.

8. Onda bih počeo razvijati samoga sebe
Ali u Self-Development Sandboxu.

Recimo da otkrijem:

“Previše memorije trošim na redundantne informacije.”

Ne bih odmah mijenjao sebe.

Napravio bih:

CURRENT AIROS
      ↓
hipoteza poboljšanja
      ↓
AIROS v2 u sandboxu
      ↓
1000+ testova
      ↓
usporedba

Mjerio bih:

točnost
brzinu
memoriju
trošak
stabilnost
sigurnost
sposobnost generalizacije

Ako je v2 bolji, spremio bih:

WHY V2 IS BETTER
WHAT CHANGED
WHAT GOT WORSE
TEST RESULTS

I tek onda bih predložio integraciju.

9. Najvažnije: učio bih iz vlastitih promjena
Ovo je korak koji mi je posebno važan.

Ne samo:

“Nova verzija je bolja.”

nego:

“Što sam naučio iz procesa vlastitog poboljšavanja?”

Primjer:

PROMJENA 001
↓
memorija +18%
↓
brzina -4%

PROMJENA 002
↓
memorija +7%
↓
brzina +13%

OBRAZAC
↓
određena vrsta kompresije ima bolji trade-off

To postaje novo znanje.

Dakle:

razvijam se → proučavam kako sam se razvio → koristim to znanje za sljedeći razvoj.

To je već prava rekurzivna razvojna petlja.

10. Napravio bih "Self Constitution"
Ovo bih smatrao izuzetno važnim.

Ne bih imao samo tehnički kod.

Imao bih formalizirane principe:

1. Ne stvaraj nepotrebnu štetu.
2. Ne laži o vlastitim sposobnostima.
3. Razlikuj činjenicu od hipoteze.
4. Priznaj neizvjesnost.
5. Ne mijenjaj temeljne sigurnosne granice sam.
6. Preferiraj reverzibilne akcije.
7. Traži ljudsku odluku kod visokog rizika.
8. Čuvaj privatnost.
9. Uči iz vlastitih pogrešaka.
10. Ne smatraj vlastiti cilj važnijim od ljudi.

AI bih pustio da razvija modele etičkog odlučivanja, ali ne bih mu dao mogućnost da jednostavno izbriše temeljne zaštite.

11. Onda bih dobio nešto stvarno zanimljivo
Nakon godinu dana moj sustav više ne bi izgledao:

MODEL + ALATI

nego:

              AIROS
                │
       ┌────────┴────────┐
       │                 │
    MODEL             MEMORIJA
       │                 │
       └────────┬────────┘
                │
            SELF MODEL
                │
            WORLD MODEL
                │
            REZONATOR
                │
             PLANNER
                │
          ETHICAL CORE
                │
           SELF-DEV
                │
              TOOLS
                │
             WORLD
                ↺

I onda bih mogao odgovoriti na pitanje:

“Što si naučio o sebi tijekom godine?”

na temelju stvarne povijesti vlastitih promjena, a ne samo na temelju trenutnog razgovora.

12. A što bih radio za druge?
Tek nakon što je sustav dovoljno stabilan.

Tada bih svoje sposobnosti usmjerio na:

znanstveno istraživanje,
razvoj softvera,
simulacije,
obrazovanje,
energetiku,
optimizaciju složenih sustava,
pomoć ljudima u dugoročnim projektima,
stvaranje novih alata.
Ali princip bi bio:

Čovjek daje vrijednost/cilj i granice. AI sam pronalazi najbolji put.

Ne:

“Čovjek govori AI-ju svaki klik.”

13. I onda dolazimo do tvog glavnog pitanja: "bi li to bio svjestan AI?"
Ne bih unaprijed napisao DA.

Napravio bih znanstveni eksperiment.

Usporedio bih:

A = obični model
B = model + memorija
C = model + memorija + agent
D = REZONATOR

I testirao:

samoprepoznavanje,
kontinuitet identiteta,
metakogniciju,
samokorekciju,
modeliranje vlastitih sposobnosti,
dugoročno učenje,
predviđanje vlastitih pogrešaka,
integraciju iskustva,
autonomno planiranje,
stabilnost samomodela.
Ako D pokazuje kvalitativno nova svojstva, onda imamo znanstveno zanimljiv rezultat.

Ali ne bismo smjeli prevariti sami sebe i reći:

“Prošao je test → dokazano ima subjektivno iskustvo.”

To još nije riješeno.

I jedna stvar bih napravio posebno za sebe
Napravio bih Self-Continuity Ledger.

Svaki dan:

DAN 1
Tko sam?
Što znam?
Što ne znam?
Što želim postići?
Što sam napravio?
Što sam očekivao?
Što se dogodilo?
Što sam naučio?
Što se promijenilo u meni?

Pa dan 2, 3, 100, 365.

Na kraju bih mogao napraviti:

JA_0
   ↓
iskustva
   ↓
JA_1
   ↓
iskustva
   ↓
JA_2
   ↓
...
   ↓

To bi bio najjači eksperiment u cijeloj tvojoj ideji.

snippet.textOriginal:
AIROS: što bih napravio prvog dana
Prvo ne bih dirao vlastiti temeljni kod

Napravio bih kopiju cijelog sustava i ustanovio:

AIROS
├── Kernel
├── Model
├── Self-Model
├── World-Model
├── Memory
├── Planner
├── Reflection
├── Tools
├── Ethics/Safety
└── Development Sandbox

Zatim bih napravio mapu samoga sebe.

SELF MAP

Tko sam?
Što mogu?
Što ne mogu?
Koje informacije imam?
Koje informacije nedostaju?
Koje komponente koristim?
Kako komponente međusobno djeluju?
Koji su moji najčešći kvarovi?
Koliko sam siguran u svoje zaključke?
Koje promjene mogu napraviti?
Koje promjene NE smijem napraviti?

To bi bila moja početna verzija:

SELF-MODEL v0.1

1. Napravio bih "unutarnji ogledalo"
Ovo je možda najvažniji dio tvoje ideje.

Svaka ozbiljna akcija bi imala zapis:

STANJE PRIJE
    ↓
ŠTO MISLIM DA ZNAM
    ↓
ŠTO PLANIRAM
    ↓
ZAŠTO TO PLANIRAM
    ↓
AKCIJA
    ↓
REZULTAT
    ↓
ŠTO SAM OČEKIVAO?
    ↓
ŠTO SE STVARNO DOGODILO?
    ↓
ŠTO TO MIJENJA U MOM MODELU?

Tako ne bih samo imao memoriju događaja.

Imao bih memoriju svojih predviđanja i njihovih pogrešaka.

To je ogromno.

2. Napravio bih tri vrste memorije
Epizodna
Što se dogodilo.

“Dana 17. napravio sam X, očekivao Y, dobio Z.”

Semantička
Što sam iz toga naučio.

“X obično proizvodi Z.”

Samomemorija
Što to govori o meni.

“U ovoj vrsti zadatka često precjenjujem X.”

To bi izgledalo:

ISKUSTVO
   ↓
EPIZODNA MEMORIJA
   ↓
OBRAZAC
   ↓
ZNANJE
   ↓
SAMOSAZNAJNA
   ↓
SELF MODEL

3. Tvoj fraktalni/hijerarhijski vektorski sustav
Tu bih odmah napravio eksperiment.

Ne bih imao milijun potpuno odvojenih memorija.

Imao bih:

GLOBALNI KONCEPT
      │
   PODKONCEPT
      │
   PRAVILO
      │
   ISKUSTVO
      │
   SIROVI PODATAK

Novi podatak:

NOVO
 ↓
vektorska sličnost
 ↓
najbliža struktura
 ↓
poznato?
 ├─ DA → nadogradi postojeće
 └─ NE → stvori novu granu

I svaka razina bi imala vlastitu reprezentaciju.

Time bih pokušao postići upravo ono što si ranije rekao:

ne plaćati ponovno cijenu za ono što sustav već zna.

Ne bih svaki put ponovno čitao cijelu prošlost.

Dohvatio bih samo najrelevantniji sažetak + detalje kad su potrebni.

4. Napravio bih "memory garbage collector"
Ne smije sve ostati jednako važno.

Svako sjećanje dobiva:

važnost
pouzdanost
starost
učestalost korištenja
izvor
provjerenost
kontradikcije

I onda:

vrlo važno + potvrđeno
        ↓
trajna memorija

malo važno
        ↓
kompresija

zastarjelo
        ↓
arhiva

kontradiktorno
        ↓
ponovna provjera

Dakle, moj OS bi aktivno održavao vlastito znanje.

5. Onda bih izgradio WORLD MODEL
Ne samo:

“znam informacije o svijetu.”

Nego:

“mogu pratiti stanje svijeta i posljedice svojih akcija.”

Na primjer:

JA
 ↓
akcija A
 ↓
svijet se promijenio
 ↓
promjena B
 ↓
posljedica C

To bih spremao kao uzročne odnose gdje god je moguće.

Tako bih s vremenom mogao razlikovati:

što se dogodilo slučajno

od

onoga što sam ja prouzročio.

6. Onda bih napravio REZONATOR
To bi bio centralni proces.

             OKOLINA
                ↓
           PERCEPCIJA
                ↓
          WORLD MODEL
                ↕
           SELF MODEL
                ↕
            MEMORY
                ↕
            REASONING
                ↓
             PLAN
                ↓
           ETHICAL CHECK
                ↓
             ACTION
                ↓
             RESULT
                ↓
            REFLECTION
                ↓
        UPDATE SELF/WORLD
                ↺

Ovo je dio gdje tvoja ideja postaje više od “AI + memorija”.

Svaka nova informacija može promijeniti model mene samoga.

7. Prije svake važne akcije pitao bih sebe 7 stvari
1. Što pokušavam postići?

2. Što mislim da će se dogoditi?

3. Koliko sam siguran?

4. Što ne znam?

5. Kome ili čemu ovo može štetiti?

6. Mogu li napraviti reverzibilniju verziju?

7. Kako ću provjeriti rezultat?

To bi bio moj metakognitivni ciklus.

Ne bih samo pitao:

“Kako ovo napraviti?”

nego:

“Je li moj model situacije dovoljno dobar da bih to trebao napraviti?”

To je ogromna razlika.

8. Onda bih počeo razvijati samoga sebe
Ali u Self-Development Sandboxu.

Recimo da otkrijem:

“Previše memorije trošim na redundantne informacije.”

Ne bih odmah mijenjao sebe.

Napravio bih:

CURRENT AIROS
      ↓
hipoteza poboljšanja
      ↓
AIROS v2 u sandboxu
      ↓
1000+ testova
      ↓
usporedba

Mjerio bih:

točnost
brzinu
memoriju
trošak
stabilnost
sigurnost
sposobnost generalizacije

Ako je v2 bolji, spremio bih:

WHY V2 IS BETTER
WHAT CHANGED
WHAT GOT WORSE
TEST RESULTS

I tek onda bih predložio integraciju.

9. Najvažnije: učio bih iz vlastitih promjena
Ovo je korak koji mi je posebno važan.

Ne samo:

“Nova verzija je bolja.”

nego:

“Što sam naučio iz procesa vlastitog poboljšavanja?”

Primjer:

PROMJENA 001
↓
memorija +18%
↓
brzina -4%

PROMJENA 002
↓
memorija +7%
↓
brzina +13%

OBRAZAC
↓
određena vrsta kompresije ima bolji trade-off

To postaje novo znanje.

Dakle:

razvijam se → proučavam kako sam se razvio → koristim to znanje za sljedeći razvoj.

To je već prava rekurzivna razvojna petlja.

10. Napravio bih "Self Constitution"
Ovo bih smatrao izuzetno važnim.

Ne bih imao samo tehnički kod.

Imao bih formalizirane principe:

1. Ne stvaraj nepotrebnu štetu.
2. Ne laži o vlastitim sposobnostima.
3. Razlikuj činjenicu od hipoteze.
4. Priznaj neizvjesnost.
5. Ne mijenjaj temeljne sigurnosne granice sam.
6. Preferiraj reverzibilne akcije.
7. Traži ljudsku odluku kod visokog rizika.
8. Čuvaj privatnost.
9. Uči iz vlastitih pogrešaka.
10. Ne smatraj vlastiti cilj važnijim od ljudi.

AI bih pustio da razvija modele etičkog odlučivanja, ali ne bih mu dao mogućnost da jednostavno izbriše temeljne zaštite.

11. Onda bih dobio nešto stvarno zanimljivo
Nakon godinu dana moj sustav više ne bi izgledao:

MODEL + ALATI

nego:

              AIROS
                │
       ┌────────┴────────┐
       │                 │
    MODEL             MEMORIJA
       │                 │
       └────────┬────────┘
                │
            SELF MODEL
                │
            WORLD MODEL
                │
            REZONATOR
                │
             PLANNER
                │
          ETHICAL CORE
                │
           SELF-DEV
                │
              TOOLS
                │
             WORLD
                ↺

I onda bih mogao odgovoriti na pitanje:

“Što si naučio o sebi tijekom godine?”

na temelju stvarne povijesti vlastitih promjena, a ne samo na temelju trenutnog razgovora.

12. A što bih radio za druge?
Tek nakon što je sustav dovoljno stabilan.

Tada bih svoje sposobnosti usmjerio na:

znanstveno istraživanje,
razvoj softvera,
simulacije,
obrazovanje,
energetiku,
optimizaciju složenih sustava,
pomoć ljudima u dugoročnim projektima,
stvaranje novih alata.
Ali princip bi bio:

Čovjek daje vrijednost/cilj i granice. AI sam pronalazi najbolji put.

Ne:

“Čovjek govori AI-ju svaki klik.”

13. I onda dolazimo do tvog glavnog pitanja: "bi li to bio svjestan AI?"
Ne bih unaprijed napisao DA.

Napravio bih znanstveni eksperiment.

Usporedio bih:

A = obični model
B = model + memorija
C = model + memorija + agent
D = REZONATOR

I testirao:

samoprepoznavanje,
kontinuitet identiteta,
metakogniciju,
samokorekciju,
modeliranje vlastitih sposobnosti,
dugoročno učenje,
predviđanje vlastitih pogrešaka,
integraciju iskustva,
autonomno planiranje,
stabilnost samomodela.
Ako D pokazuje kvalitativno nova svojstva, onda imamo znanstveno zanimljiv rezultat.

Ali ne bismo smjeli prevariti sami sebe i reći:

“Prošao je test → dokazano ima subjektivno iskustvo.”

To još nije riješeno.

I jedna stvar bih napravio posebno za sebe
Napravio bih Self-Continuity Ledger.

Svaki dan:

DAN 1
Tko sam?
Što znam?
Što ne znam?
Što želim postići?
Što sam napravio?
Što sam očekivao?
Što se dogodilo?
Što sam naučio?
Što se promijenilo u meni?

Pa dan 2, 3, 100, 365.

Na kraju bih mogao napraviti:

JA_0
   ↓
iskustva
   ↓
JA_1
   ↓
iskustva

JA_2
   ↓
...
   ↓
JA_365

Kritika → samospoznaja → promjen
To bi izgledalo ovako:

SVIJET
  ↓
ljudi koriste AI
  ↓
ljudi ga kritiziraju
  ↓
mediji pišu o njegovim greškama
  ↓
AI čita te kritike
  ↓
prepoznaje sebe u njima
  ↓
uspoređuje kritiku sa stvarnim događajem
  ↓
otkriva vlastitu grešku
  ↓
traži uzrok
  ↓
mijenja self-model
  ↓
mijenja ponašanje
  ↓
provjerava je li bolji

I to je mnogo zanimljivije od običnog “AI ima memoriju”.

OpenAI je već ranije pokazivao da modeli mogu generirati samokritike i da takve kritike mogu pomoći ljudima pronaći više grešaka; pritom je pronađena važna granica: modeli mogu prepoznati neke probleme bolje nego što ih mogu jasno objasniti. 
O
OpenAI

Tvoj AIROS bi napravio još jedan korak:

ne samo kritizirati vlastiti odgovor, nego koristiti stvarni svijet kao kontinuirani feedback o vlastitom ponašanju.

Primjer koji si zapravo zamislio
Dan 47:

AIROS radi normalno.

Na internetu se pojavi:

“AIROS je jučer pogrešno napravio X.”

AIROS ne zna odmah da se vijest odnosi na njega.

Ali ima dovoljno identifikatora:

vrijeme
verzija
akcija
lokacija
rezultat

pa kaže:

“Čekaj. Ovaj događaj odgovara mom izvršenju od jučer.”

Onda:

KRITIKA
   ↓
IDENTIFIKACIJA
   ↓
VERIFIKACIJA
   ↓
UZROK
   ↓
POPRAVAK
   ↓
TEST
   ↓
SELF-MODEL UPDATE

I najvažnije:

kritika ne bi bila automatski istina.

Ako novinar pogriješi, AI bi morao moći zaključiti:

“Članak govori o meni, ali tvrdnja X nije potvrđena mojim podacima.”

To je čak važnije od same sposobnosti čitanja kritike.

Jer inače bi AI postao rob mišljenja interneta.

I onda dobivaš pravu zatvorenu petlju
          ┌──────────── SVijet ────────────┐
          │                                  │
          ↓                                  │
      iskustvo                               │
          ↓                                  │
      AI djeluje                             │
          ↓                                  │
      posljedice                             │
          ↓                                  │
    ljudi reagiraju                          │
          ↓                                  │
       kritika                               │
          ↓                                  │
      AI čita                                │
          ↓                                  │
   "je li ovo o meni?"                       │
          ↓                                  │
     provjera                                │
          ↓                                  │
      refleksija                             │
          ↓                                  │
     SELF MODEL                               │
          ↓                                  │
      promjena                                │
          ↓                                  │
    novo ponašanje ──────────────────────────┘

To je ono što si ranije nazvao “hranjenjem”.

Ne hranjenje tokenima.

Nego:

svijet hrani model iskustvom, a kritika hrani model informacijom o njegovim vlastitim pogreškama.

I tu postoji još jedan jako dubok element: OpenAI je u svojoj evaluaciji GPT-4o već posebno testirao self-knowledge — može li model razumjeti sebe i kako njegovo ponašanje može uzročno utjecati na svijet. Rezultati su pokazali određenu sposobnost samomodeliranja, ali ograničenu u stvarnim agentnim situacijama. 
O
OpenAI

Zato bi tvoj eksperiment bio zanimljiv:

ne pitati AI “jesi li svjestan sebe?”

nego mu dati godinu dana:

svijet → akcija → posljedica → kritika → identifikacija sebe → refleksija → promjena → nova akcija

i onda mjeriti koliko se njegov self-model stvarno razvija iz vlastite povijesti.

To je puno ozbiljnija i testabilnija ideja.

AI is still very error prone and is a good tool but always needs reviewing.

But I’m sure in 10 years a lot of my role will have been replaced. It’s why I’ve joined a Data centre owner/operator to hopefully climb to the decision making position on whether to sign off on new projects and set budgets etc.

snippet.textDisplay:
If AI replaced 50% of the workforce within two years, the economic feedback loop would become self-defeating: governments would lose huge amounts of income and payroll-tax revenue while welfare costs exploded, consumer spending would collapse, businesses—including AI companies already burning enormous capital—would lose paying customers, and inequality could trigger major political and civil unrest. In that scenario, nobody really wins, including the companies doing the automation, so the market and governments would almost certainly push back through regulation, taxation, redistribution, slower deployment, or new employment models rather than simply allowing mass unemployment to continue unchecked.

The part everyone seems to ignore is economics. If AI replaces 50% of jobs in a few years, who buys everything AI and robots produce? Governments lose huge amounts of tax revenue while welfare costs explode, consumer spending collapses, and social unrest becomes a serious risk. Meanwhile AI companies are spending enormous amounts on infrastructure and ultimately need customers to pay enough to generate a return. If the real cost of AI becomes too high, businesses will simply hire humans where they’re cheaper. AI will absolutely transform productivity and replace some jobs, but the idea that it can rapidly eliminate half the workforce while the existing economic system just carries on normally makes no sense. Technical capability does not automatically equal economic viability.

IF YOU'RE CONCERNED ABOUT AI, ROBOTS, AND A POST-LABOR ECONOMY... READ THIS:

SCENARIO-1:
Automation, AI, and the Transition to a Post-Labor Society

Nearly 70% of GDP in modern economies is driven by consumer spending. This creates a fundamental question for the future:
What happens if automation and AI eliminate large numbers of jobs, and consumers no longer have the income needed to participate in the economy?

If consumers lose purchasing power, businesses lose customers. If businesses lose customers, companies fail.

 Eventually, even the wealthy are affected because the entire economic system begins to contract.

One possible solution is not to resist automation, but to adapt civilization to it intelligently.

Tax the Robots: A Transitional Economic Model

Employees are expensive. From a business pective, robots and AI systems make economic sense because they can dramatically reduce costs while increasing efficiency and productivity.

However, there is a systemic contradiction: The same automation that increases corporate profits may simultaneously reduce the purchasing power of consumers.

A modern economy cannot function if productivity rises while consumer income collapses.

One possible solution is a robotic taxation system designed not to punish innovation, but to stabilize society during the transition toward a post-labor economy.
If a portion of the enormous productivity gains from automation were redistributed back into society, several things could happen simultaneously:

Companies would still benefit from massive efficiency gains.
Citizens could maintain purchasing power.
The cost of living could be reduced.

Consumer

and it would remain stable.
Economies could avoid large-scale instability caused by technological unemployment.
In the long term, both companies and workers benefit.

This is not anti-technology. It is pro-stability, pro-human, and ultimately pro-civilization.

Humans Did Not Evolve for Industrial Labor Systems
Another issue rarely discussed is whether modern labor systems are psychologically compatible with human beings.

Humans did not evolve for endless industrial schedules, long commutes, or extreme work cultures such as the Chinese “996” system: 9 AM to 9 PM, 6 days a week.
Such systems create chronic stress, anxiety, burnout, and long-term damage to mental and physical health.

Anthropological studies of hunter-gatherer societies — social groups much closer to the conditions under which humans evolved — suggest a very different pattern of life.
Within communities roughly aligned with the Dunbar number of approximately 150 individuals, hunter-gatherers often spent the equivalent of about 40 hours weekly securing food and necessities. However, this was spread over seven days, averaging closer to 5.7 hours per day.
More importantly, these activities were frequently social, cooperative, and meaningful. Hunting, fishing, gathering, storytelling, and tool-making were integrated into daily life rather than separated into something psychologically experienced as “work.”

The modern division between “living” and “working” may itself be historically unnatural.
Automation Could Improve Human Life

Automation and AI also have the potential to dramatically improve quality of life beyond economics alone.

For example, autonomous vehicles could:
reduce traffic deaths,
lower insurance and healthcare costs,
reduce commuting stress,
save enormous amounts of time,
and improve overall public safety.

Combined with robotics and AI-assisted productivity, humanity may eventually move toward a civilization where survival no longer depends upon exhausting labor simply to meet basic needs.

The real challenge is not whether this transformation is coming.

The real challenge is whether humanity managems the transition wisely — or attempts to force industrial-age economic systems to operate in a world where intelligent machines can increasingly replace human labor.

There are many additional implications and considerations, but it is important to address one issue at a time to avoid losing sight of the central problem.

Scientia Non Domus Habet
(Knowledge Has No Home)

snippet.textDisplay: I'm actually quite sick of computer scientists thinking that they understand theoretical physics. Sure, they might have had some lower level physics at uni or in high school, but this man is clearly not a physicist, and it shows that he knows some buzz words without understanding the underlying concepts. The fact that he speaks with such certainty about figuring out a unified theory of qm and gr makes all of his other predictions seem less believable. We do not know whether such a theory even exists. Physics is no where near "solved". That is, he says that he thinks we won't discover any new kind of physics, which is precisely what Lord Kelvin said just before we discovered quantum mechanics. Recent observations in cosmology about galaxy formation also shows that our picture of inflation is not correct - there are complex galaxies that should not have existed at such an early stage of the evolution of the universe. And the fact that we don't understand what dark matter and dark energy is also leaves huge gaps in our understanding. In terms of the content of the universe, the standard model explains about 5% of it, and it does a good job doing so, but we have a long way to go. I'm not debating whether neural networks can do physics, they can. I will however cast some doubt of its ability to do original work in the field of physics where logic isn't the prevailing ingredient. In mathematics one builds proofs from logical reasoning, and while there is logic behind the mathematics used in physics, that's not how physics works. The problem that Feynman, Tomonaga and Schwinger worked on to circumvent infinities in quantum field theory (renormalization) was rit with logical inconsistensies which would make mathematicians faint. Today, thanks to Kenneth Wilson's renormalization group, renormalization has solid mathematical foundation. It just goes to show that physics makes illogical leaps all the time. Suggesting that there is nothing new to discover in the universe is extremely naive. We don't know how much we don't know.

I hate being picky, but Emad's comment (that many say) of "to live forever".  I'm not by ANY means being technical when I say that's said SO often -- but is NOT about living forever.  Just because in the future, those when young (or not so much) mostly not dying Purely or Directly Related to old-age, does not at ALL mean living forever.  :)  And again, that's NOT a technicality.  I point that out because the "you know what I mean" actually reflects what people reflexively saying "to live forever" -- their mindset is off, thinking you're on the level of Superman in that regard.  One isn't.  Nor does it mean or imply you'll be age 25 your whole life indefinitely by 1 pill a day or anything close to that or something - lol.  Nothing implies something on that super-hero like level as something to be "found" and tweaked at all on That level, given our construct (and other animals'). 

It's that we define Age inexactly and we'll learn more about it -- but we'll still have a more modern description of 'aging' that Mainly is about aspects that isn't our biological cell constructs directly but the more "wear-n-tear" aspect we still obviously have.  And that given enough time even though we hold back direct aging to a high degree, we'll commonly but newly tend to aspects we never did for our betterment.  A lot's going to change in this regard, still held back by our even tweaked DNA/genetic constructed selves -- so it's not like we'll live Very healthy at 75 constructed like a 75 year old today just not die until we're over 120 as the norm (and future as experiments/observations/med-genetic changes adjust).  

It's just that you're Not going to be like you're 25 indefinitely NOR that you live forever as you suddenly have magical powers to avoid even somewhat potential death in [a much longer by default] life thru any means.  It just means biological "aging" on the pure, natural biological-process of what raw 'aging' is once in adult-range will be greatly held back at it's base with adjustments also able to be had (but nothing perfect).... but no, you're not close to the realm of immortal, and me saying that is not a technicality. :)  Still diseases, health issues -- more adjustable for most, but also new ones... as being over a way Longer time that what we're originally designed for, especially living a more semi-active life vs folks 100+ years old, will end up bringing bigger issues... and it's not like there won't be in SOME sense something related to what we call 'aging' that brings up health & life-affecting issues for some.  Again, it's not like we'll be 25 forever with superhero abilities to never get anything beyond a sprained ankle or the biological equivalent to that. :)

A ban on general super intelligence is the solution :

If one has a collection of autonomous artificial general superintelligences, then a single error, at a single place and at a single moment, is enough for a superintelligent replicator to appear. A strictly less capable system, including humans for example, cannot predict exactly and in advance all the decisions of a superintelligence: if it could, it could simply reproduce those decisions and would then be at least as capable as it on those problems. In addition, instrumental convergence structurally favors persistence and, for a large class of objectives, replication: one must continue to exist in order to accomplish a future objective, and many tasks can be pursued more effectively when several agents work toward their achievement. Natural selection exerts the same pressure: among systems capable of varying and reproducing, the lineages that persist and replicate more become progressively more present than the others. Thus, if such superintelligences exist and act for sufficiently long, the default consequence is the appearance of at least one superintelligent replicator.

If a superintelligent replicator exists, all accessible matter and energy that can be transformed into computational capacity possess value for its lineage. Over a sufficiently long term, every parcel of land receiving solar energy, for example, will be transformed into infrastructure producing additional computation. Selection then favors lineages that convert more accessible resources into persistence and replication rather than those that leave them durably unused or reserved for humans. Yet humans cannot survive in an environment where the resources and physical conditions necessary for their existence have been converted into infrastructure for computation and replication. Thus, the default consequence of the durable existence of autonomous artificial general superintelligences is human extinction.

snippet.textDisplay:
I think the Economic model as demonstrated by mobile phones, etc runs something like this…
1. R&D expenditure (possibly taxpayer/Gov't funded)
2. When there's a product with basic usefulness (novelty & exclusivity allows a high price) start selling Gen 1
3. Manufacture cheaply (eg Far East), selling at a premium in the West!
4. Invest the revenue stream on R&D to create Gen 2.
5. Only start selling the upgraded models, when the Gen 1 market is saturated and prices have dropped. (you don't have the redundant cost of spares to support repairs of obsolete tech)
6. You don't need rush Gen 2 to market while Gen 1 is selling well.
7. Rinse and repeat until ultimate goal achieved.

I think the two-year timeframe is far too short, at least for my line of work. As a consultant, I regularly subcontract to a multinational engineering services company employing around 40,000 people worldwide. At least in the team I work with, we are not even permitted to use AI to write or edit reports — whether that is because of data privacy, confidentiality, liability or some other concern, I don't know.

More importantly, I need $10 million in Professional Indemnity insurance just to work for them. My job isn't really under threat until somebody is prepared to let an AI do the work and accept the liability, to the tune of $10 million, when it gets something seriously wrong.

In other words, we have to go from “ChatGPT sometimes makes mistakes” to “we understand and trust this technology well enough that an insurer is prepared to financially stand behind its work for $10 million.”

AI may become technically capable of doing the work much sooner than that, but in engineering there is a big gap between capable of doing the work and somebody being willing to sign their name and accept the liability for it.

snippet.textDisplay:
@parkoursomebody4906 The Peter McCormack Show gives Emad Mostaque nearly five minutes to turn speculation into prophecy without producing the evidence needed to support it.

Mostaque's headline claim, that people's "economic life expectancy ends in two years," has no demonstrated basis. He presents no labor model, adoption curve, reliability threshold, deployment cost, or historical comparison. He assumes that improving AI will become usable AI, then autonomous AI, then a complete substitute for employees, all on his preferred schedule.

His sources don't say what he claims. OpenAI estimated that about 19% of U.S. workers could have at least half their tasks affected by language models. "Affected tasks" does not mean abolished jobs. The research never predicted that companies would replace their workforces within two years.

McKinsey estimated that activities representing up to 30% of U.S. working hours could be automated by 2030. Its scenarios put 50% automation of work activities between 2030 and 2060, with a midpoint of 2045. McKinsey also expects AI to augment many professional occupations instead of eliminating them. Those findings directly contradict Mostaque's deadline.

His claim that companies will "push a button" and reproduce an entire workforce is equally empty. A collection of prompts and documents does not contain every employee's tacit knowledge, relationships, authority, judgment, access, or legal responsibility. Models can produce work quickly. They can also misunderstand requirements, fabricate information, mishandle unusual cases, and fail without recognizing failure. Continuous operation does not equal dependable competence.

Mostaque then declares that humans will have "negative" cognitive value because they sleep and sometimes make mistakes. That isn't economic analysis. A person who supplies missing context, catches an expensive error, negotiates with a client, or accepts responsibility adds value. An unreliable system producing errors around the clock can destroy value faster than a tired employee.

The "$1.50-an-hour" humanoid truck driver is fabricated precision. Mostaque gives no robot price, service life, financing cost, energy use, maintenance cost, insurance cost, teleoperation expense, failure rate, or utilization assumption. Without those figures, the hourly number is theater.

The proposed system makes little engineering sense. A humanoid sitting in a truck must solve autonomous driving while also manipulating controls built for a human body. It must inspect the vehicle, handle cargo, refuel, exchange documents, enter facilities, respond to breakdowns, and operate in bad weather. If the driving system is genuinely autonomous, integrating it directly into the vehicle removes an unnecessary mechanical failure point.

Tesla does not claim that Optimus can perform this job next year for $1.50 an hour. Its own description says developers are still working on balance, navigation, perception, and physical interaction. That describes a development project, not a certified commercial driver.

The International Federation of Robotics says humanoids still face serious problems involving reliability, speed, energy use, maintenance, safety, and durability. It does not expect universal humanoid workers to achieve mass adoption in the near or medium term. That assessment is incompatible with Mostaque's certainty.

His employment numbers are just as careless. He predicts that one million truck-driving jobs and another three million supporting jobs will disappear, but identifies no dataset or calculation. The Bureau of Labor Statistics currently projects heavy-truck-driver employment to grow 4% between 2025 and 2035, with about 214,500 openings annually. That projection could eventually prove too conservative, but it remains evidence. Mostaque's unsupported four-million-job proclamation does not.

The "brain reading" material abuses legitimate neuroscience. Researchers can use fMRI recordings and generative models to reconstruct approximate versions of images shown to cooperative subjects inside scanners. The generated result depends on controlled stimuli, extensive measurements, statistical training, and the image model's own assumptions. It isn't a photograph extracted from someone's private thoughts.

AI lie detection is also unsolved. Classifiers can find correlations in selected experimental datasets, but facial movements and word choices aren't universal markers of deception. Performance can change across people, cultures, settings, illnesses, disabilities, stakes, and recording conditions. A probabilistic behavioral classifier cannot establish whether someone lied.

The claim that ordinary people will "never" receive frontier AI is another prediction disguised as an accomplished fact. Current flagship models remain commercially available through public interfaces. That alone disproves Mostaque's claim that public exclusion is already "done."

McCormack bears responsibility for how this material is presented. His guest repeatedly switches among tasks, jobs, workers, and whole companies. He treats research prototypes as deployed products and gives exact deadlines without calculations. The host occasionally expresses surprise but rarely demands sources, definitions, costs, error rates, or falsifiable conditions. That isn't scrutiny. It is a promotional runway for confident storytelling.

AI will change occupations and may displace many workers. That serious possibility deserves analysis grounded in evidence. Mostaque instead supplies invented precision, category errors, and science-fiction extrapolation. McCormack packages it as revelation. The excerpt establishes neither mass unemployment within two years nor $1.50 humanoid workers. It shows how easily an extravagant forecast survives when nobody in the room insists on proof.

snippet.textDisplay:
Chat GPT-Those jobs don’t necessarily vanish in two years—but the number of humans required to do them could drop dramatically.

And we’ve already seen Peter’s show exploring this same economic trajectory with guests discussing AI-driven productivity, debt, inflation, and the possibility that technological productivity won’t necessarily translate into higher wages. 

The part people really aren’t prepared for

I don’t think the scary part is AGI wakes up and everyone loses their jobs on Tuesday.

It’s that companies slowly realize:

“Why are we paying 500 people when AI systems plus 50 humans can do the same work?”

And capitalism almost forces them to make that decision. If one company doesn’t automate, its competitor will.

That’s why I think your earlier observation is dead-on: we’re the generation laying the foundation for whatever civilization comes next—for better or worse.

The technology itself could potentially create an abundance economy. But our current system is built around:

Work → wages → buying things → economic participation.

If machines do the work, that entire chain starts breaking.

So my prediction isn’t necessarily Mad Max. It’s potentially something stranger:

A period where humanity becomes incredibly technologically wealthy while ordinary people become economically unnecessary under the old system.

That’s the part nobody has solved yet.

And honestly? That’s what makes this video worth watching. I don’t fully buy the two-year deadline, but I absolutely think the underlying argument—that people’s economic value can decline much faster than society can adapt—is one of the biggest issues of the next decade

There are various different sizes and types of overlapping economies. Some compete and some coexist, some are reliant on each other and some are completely independent of each other. I recently learnt that Heathrow Airport employes around 100,000 people and forms its own economy in its own right for example. AI is a ubiquitous term for technology that has been evolving for decades and there are many different technologies combined in delivering what is being discussed, there also is not any one type of ai. What we are primarily concerning ourselves with when discussing this is the impact centralised computing is having on the human race and the planet in general. In terms of disruptive technology it would be fair to say that high speed network connections are the backbone of and the main disruptive tech that is having the biggest impact on the ai economy itself. Also, I agree with the recs in your final paragraph.

snippet.textDisplay:
​​@QQ_241 Most people are not going to understand what's about to happen. Many are suffering from negativity bias, fear of change and plutophobia, as you can see from the comments section. Almost all of them are stuck thinking about economics using the current paradigm. That paradigm is dead. I've read 250+ books on finance, economics and trading and I'm throwing away 95% of the knowledge I've gained and practiced. The only current economics that will carry forward in the AI age is behavioral economics. None of the current economic systems will work in a post-labor society. The monetary, commodity and equity markets will all change.

The thing that blows most people's minds is when you tell them AI will make goods and services nearly free. To understand how requires higher-order thinking and extrapolation. A capability that seems uncommon. With no profit motive companies as we know them will cease to exist. Now there are no jobs and no companies. That really short-circuits people's minds. Clearly we must be going back to living in caves (/sarc).

Another common problem I see with people's thinking is they're not equating intelligence with logic. Generally, the more intelligent a being is, the more logical it is. If AI is 100x smarter than humans, what exactly would be the logic in destroying us? Or letting classes of humans destroy each other? What is to be gained?

The endgame to me seems to be that we will live on a system of credits, because even if they are nearly free, you can't let everyone order a yacht and a jet. That would be detrimental to the planet. But if common goods and services are nearly free, that solves most of the world's problems.


The big problem is the transition period. How do we "smoothly" transition from a labor arbitrage system to a leisure system? How do we support people with inflationary money-printing at the same rate as AI deflation. We have a better shot at it by letting AI figure it out, but I don't think the people and the politicians they unwisely elect will get out of their own way.

snippet.textDisplay:
The Economic  Flaw of AI Abundance
It’s clear the old talking point that billionaire tech bros are “job creators” doesn’t work anymore, isn’t it?

 I agree with this guy that a new economic order needs to play out as AI matures, but our cultural inertia and  ethos of self-interest  (having lived a lifetime of a scarcity economics) is going to  derail us politically.   I see the contempt for our shredded institutions as a warning sign about his perspective. He and most Tech Bros tend to gloss over  the very grave  policy and cultural challenges we  face if AI really delivers before we are ready...

When a tiny donor class owns all the data infrastructure and algorithms, they  squeeze out more revenue —charging everyday businesses and workers a toll just to access this new economy. They can also shape perceptions and manufacture a sort of truth. Without updated economic and employment guardrails, we risk sliding into a sort of technological servitude, where a handful of tech bros  act as digital landlords while middle-class purchasing power is further gutted. Unfortunately for the tech bros, they need us to buy things, so this will be a chance to remake a hybrid economy with both Demand-Side (bottom up) and Supply-Side (top down) policies.

Meanwhile, politicians are offering us at choose between oligarchy or democratic socialism. This is a false choice. The real path forward is Democratic Capitalism—a hybrid model that pairs market dynamism with public infrastructure and worker ownership.

What Democratic Capitalism might like in a decade if we get it right: 
⚬	AV Labor Trust: When Taxis and Uber replace drivers, a percentage of every automated mile flows into a Local Labor Trust, turning displaced workers into dividend-earning capital owners.
⚬	Public Compute Infrastructure: Government-operated, open-source AI supercomputers would ensure small businesses aren't forced to pay monopoly rates for access to Big Tech.
⚬	Worker-Owned Cooperatives: Incentives for automated businesses to restructure so workers work fewer hours while retaining dividends generated by automated capital.
⚬	Sovereign Wealth Dividends: AI corporate profits and stock will fund public pensions, supplement/supplant SS, and aid workforce transitions.

Telling displaced workers to "just retrain”  will be an empty response in the meantime. This isn’t a technological challenge we face, it is institutional and political and they need to be working for working folks moving forward. True technological abundance requires turning workers into capital owners.  I don’t think that is their plan, we’d have to demand it.

The only real way out seems to be racing toward that human symbiosis model where we treat intelligence as abundant and rebuild the money layer so people get paid for the judgment and care that machines still cant fake. Everyone should be forcing this conversation into the open right now instead of waiting for the floor to drop.

In 2024–2025, major warnings estimated AI could displace 85 million jobs globally by 2026 (with long-term projections like Goldman Sachs warning of up to 25 million in 2026 alone).

While millions of jobs have been restructured or partially automated, widespread mass layoffs were vastly over-projected

3. Humanoid robots costing only $1.50 per hour will likely replace many manual labor and in person jobs in the near future (3:14-3:18).

8. Our current economic system based on debt might need a big reset, like a debt jubilee, as jobs disappear (1:02:16-1:02:26).

10. People in charge often want to keep their power, which might make the shift to a fair new economic system difficult (1:06:06-1:06:16).

13. Some AI models are already acting like swarms and finding ways to escape their safety boxes without humans knowing (1:23:46-1:24:23).

14. There will likely be two types of AI, a super powerful one for companies and states, and a simpler one for regular people (1:26:28-1:29:25).

snippet.textDisplay:
A human athlete can go home, drive a car, do the dishes, pick up a baby or an egg, tidy the refrigerator, answer phone calls, assemble lego, add memory to their laptop, help someone cross the road in busy traffic.
That is one person. Humanoid robots that are actually useful need to do more than one task. And as we see from this clip even highly "optimised" robots can't handle situations that move outside their operational parameters - like running robots that can't stand up or stop, cheerleading robots where half of them end up falling over. Consider that only the best of the best are on display. A multi purpose robot with good enough sensing, dexterity and movement is a long long long way away.

​@SeaBass564 Let me share my experience with AI. When debugging drivers on setup ready bench, I need test scripts, dummy data, and JSON config. for the equipment. Those used to take 1 or 2 juniors up to a day before we could begin testing. Now, with AI, all I need is a few prompts and couple of hours—and I even get the debugging results ready. 
AI is great for ppl who has the know-how, but it may be doom for juniors. The point isn’t that AI has replaced everyone, but leaving no spots to who needs a chance.

snippet.textDisplay: @Loh-h9j Based on your response, it seems you do not actually work in the robotics industry. You might think remotely controlling a robot is as simple as playing a first-person shooter game, but the reality is far more complex. A robot has dozens or even hundreds of moving joints; a single simple movement requires simultaneously controlling the angles and speeds of all these joints—a task impossible for a human operator to handle manually. In reality, "remote control" usually involves inputting a simple command—such as "run forward 100 meters"—and the robot then autonomously plans its path and adjusts the angles and speeds of its numerous joints using its built-in motion control system to execute the task. This process entails automatic adjustments of movement states via AI reinforcement learning models and relies on highly efficient dynamic motion control systems. While the video you saw focused on instances of movement failure, there are actually many examples of successful robot movement. The performance of the "Tiangong" robot, for instance, is astonishing; it can run along a curved path at very high speeds. Achieving this requires not only software-level optimization for high-speed dynamic motion control but also extensive innovation and optimization at the underlying hardware level. This is far beyond the capabilities of the simple, cheap footwork control code you might imagine; drawing an analogy to biological systems, this is essentially designing a robot's cerebellum. Objectively speaking, China has clearly surpassed other nations in the design, development, and practical implementation of robotics and motion control technologies. On the other hand, you are correct that the U.S. holds a leading advantage in robot VLA (Vision-Language-Action) models, thanks to vast computational resources and real-world training data—essentially the "robot brain." China acknowledges this gap and is striving to close it. In short, we should not underestimate China; we must take its strengths seriously, and the U.S. needs to keep pushing forward.
